article.title: Omega-3 and Fish Oil for Arthritis: An Honest Evidence Review (UK)
article.excerpt: Omega-3 fats from oily fish have the strongest evidence of any food supplement for inflammatory arthritis, but the benefits are modest and the evidence for osteoarthritis is weak. This review explains what the trials show, food versus supplements, doses used in research, the difference between fish oil and fish liver oil, and important safety checks if you take anticoagulants or NSAIDs.
article.content:
Quick answer: Long-chain omega-3 fats (EPA and DHA) from oily fish or fish oil can modestly reduce joint tenderness and morning stiffness in rheumatoid arthritis, but they work slowly and do not replace medicines. Evidence for osteoarthritis is weak. Eat oily fish at least once a week, and check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking fish oil if you use blood thinners or NSAIDs.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against Arthritis UK's fish oils information, the BDA omega-3 fact sheet, NHS fish guidance and the trials listed below.

Of all the supplements people with arthritis ask about, fish oil has the most research behind it. That does not mean it works for everyone, or for every type of arthritis. This review explains what omega-3 fats are, what the studies suggest, how food compares with supplements, and how to use fish oil safely if you decide to try it.

What are omega-3 fats?

Omega-3s are a family of polyunsaturated fats. The BDA explains the main types:

  • ALA (alpha-linolenic acid): an essential fat found in plant foods such as walnuts, flaxseed (linseed), chia seeds and rapeseed oil.
  • EPA and DHA: long-chain omega-3s found mainly in fish, especially oily fish. Your body can make small amounts from ALA, but this happens slowly.

Most arthritis research has looked at EPA and DHA from fish oil. These are thought to reduce the production of some substances involved in inflammation, which is why they have been studied in inflammatory arthritis.

Evidence in rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis

Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) summarises the evidence like this:

  • A report combining data from 10 trials found that fish body oil reduced the number of tender joints and shortened morning stiffness compared with placebo, but did not significantly change other measures such as grip strength, blood tests for disease activity or overall severity. The trials were of low to moderate quality.
  • A review of 17 randomised trials, using doses of about 1.6 to 7.1g of omega-3 a day, found fish oil was generally well tolerated and reduced joint pain, morning stiffness, the number of tender or swollen joints and the use of painkillers.
  • Arthritis UK's overall conclusion is that marine oils can modestly reduce pain and inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis and may reduce the need for painkillers.

Arthritis UK also says omega-3 can be helpful in other inflammatory types of arthritis, such as psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis. It notes that fish oils act slowly, so it suggests trying them for about three months to judge any benefit.

What this means in practice: fish oil is a reasonable thing to try alongside your prescribed treatment if your rheumatology team agrees. It is not a substitute for disease-modifying medicines, which protect your joints from long-term damage. NICE guidance on rheumatoid arthritis (NG100) says complementary therapies should not replace conventional treatment.

Evidence in osteoarthritis

The evidence for osteoarthritis is much weaker:

  • An Australian trial in knee osteoarthritis (Hill and colleagues, 2016) compared a high dose of fish oil with a low dose. There was no extra benefit from the high dose. Unexpectedly, the low-dose group did slightly better on pain at two years, which the authors said needs more research.
  • A 2024 trial in JAMA (Laslett and colleagues) found that 2g a day of krill oil, another source of omega-3, did not improve knee pain over 24 weeks compared with placebo in people with knee osteoarthritis and joint inflammation on MRI.
  • Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that cod liver oil makes a difference to osteoarthritis.

So for osteoarthritis, the most effective things remain exercise and, if relevant, weight management, as NICE guidance NG226 recommends. Omega-3 from oily fish is still good for your heart, which is a sensible reason to eat it.

Why omega-3 matters for your heart too

The NHS says long-chain omega-3 can help to prevent heart disease. Arthritis UK points out that omega-3 fats also help lower cholesterol and triglyceride levels, which may reduce the risk of heart disease and stroke in people with inflammatory arthritis, who have a higher risk of these conditions. This is a good reason to eat oily fish regularly even if it makes no obvious difference to your joints. It fits naturally into an anti-inflammatory, Mediterranean-style diet.

Can omega-3 prevent arthritis?

The large VITAL trial in older US adults (Hahn and colleagues, BMJ 2022) tested omega-3 supplements for preventing autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis. The omega-3 group had fewer new autoimmune diagnoses than the placebo group, but the difference was not statistically significant, so it does not show that fish oil prevents arthritis.

Evidence at a glance

ConditionEvidenceBottom line
Rheumatoid arthritisSeveral trials and reviews; benefits modestMay reduce tender joints, stiffness and painkiller use. Try for about 3 months alongside treatment
Other inflammatory arthritisLess researchArthritis UK says it can be helpful; discuss with your team
OsteoarthritisTrials mostly negative or uncertainNot expected to ease joint pain; eat oily fish for heart health
GoutNot a recommended treatmentAsk your GP or a dietitian about oily fish in your diet

Food first: oily fish

UK guidance is food first. The NHS advises at least 2 portions of fish a week (a portion is about 140g), 1 of which should be oily. Oily fish includes:

  • salmon, trout and mackerel
  • sardines, pilchards and herring (including kippers)
  • anchovies and sprats

Fresh and tinned tuna do not count as oily fish. Tinned fish is cheap, keeps well and needs no preparation, which helps on bad days. Tinned sardines, pilchards and salmon with soft bones also provide calcium.

How much is too much?

The BDA says that if you are past childbearing age or not planning to have children, you can eat up to four portions of oily fish a week. If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, planning a pregnancy or may become pregnant in future, the limit is two portions a week, because of pollutants. Avoid shark, swordfish and marlin if you are pregnant, planning a pregnancy or under 16, because of mercury.

If you do not eat fish

You can get ALA from walnuts, ground flaxseed, chia seeds, rapeseed oil and some fortified foods. Arthritis UK notes that we do not know whether plant omega-3s are as beneficial as the EPA and DHA in fish oil. Algae-based omega-3 supplements contain EPA and DHA and are suitable for vegetarians and vegans; the omega-3 in fish originally comes from algae.

For meal ideas, see our simple oily fish meals and our guide to oily fish and arthritis.

If you choose a supplement

Fish oil is not the same as fish liver oil

This is the most important point. Fish body oil comes from the flesh of oily fish. Fish liver oil, such as cod liver oil, also contains vitamins A and D. Arthritis UK warns that large doses of fish liver oil could lead to too much vitamin A, which can cause liver problems and is particularly dangerous in pregnancy. The BDA says you should not have more than 1.5mg (1,500 micrograms) of vitamin A a day from food and supplements combined, and should not take supplements containing vitamin A if you are pregnant or planning a pregnancy.

If you want omega-3 for arthritis, Arthritis UK recommends pure fish oil rather than fish liver oil.

Doses

Doses vary a lot, and labels can be confusing. Look at the amount of EPA plus DHA, not the total amount of oil in each capsule.

  • The BDA notes that omega-3 supplements are not recommended for the general population, because evidence of benefit is inconclusive. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • For inflammatory arthritis, Arthritis UK says quite large amounts are needed for the best effects and mentions concentrated products providing 3g of EPA and DHA a day. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Because higher doses have more potential for side effects and interactions, agree a dose with your rheumatology team, GP or pharmacist rather than choosing one yourself.

Reading a label: a worked example

A capsule might say "1000mg fish oil" on the front. On the back, the nutrition panel might show that each capsule contains 180mg EPA and 120mg DHA, which is 300mg of EPA plus DHA. So reaching a particular amount of EPA and DHA could take several capsules a day. Concentrated "omega-3" products contain more EPA and DHA per capsule, which means fewer capsules but usually a higher price. Always compare the EPA plus DHA content, the number of capsules per daily dose and whether vitamin A is included.

Quality and storage

Fish oil can go rancid, which may cause a fishy taste or burps. Store it as the label says, check the use-by date, and do not buy more than you will use in a few months. Arthritis UK notes that very high doses of fish oil raise concerns about environmental contaminants, and that most supplement companies test their products for purity.

Side effects

Arthritis UK says side effects are usually minor, most commonly stomach upset, with wind or diarrhoea in some people. Taking the dose in two or three smaller amounts with meals can help.

Important safety: blood thinners and NSAIDs

Arthritis UK advises that people taking blood-thinning medicines, such as warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban or aspirin, or anti-inflammatory painkillers, should seek medical advice before using fish oil, because it can increase the risk of bleeding.

  • Warfarin: the NHS says to tell your doctor if you take any vitamins or supplements and to speak to your doctor before starting new ones. Your INR may need checking.
  • NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen can already cause stomach bleeding. Adding something else that affects bleeding needs a conversation with your pharmacist.
  • Before surgery or dental extractions: tell the team you take fish oil.
  • Allergy: if you are allergic to fish, avoid fish oil and ask about algae-based alternatives.

Our full guide to medicine and supplement interactions covers other combinations.

How to try fish oil sensibly

  1. Talk to your rheumatology team, GP or pharmacist, especially if you take any blood thinner or NSAID.
  2. Choose pure fish oil (or algae oil), not fish liver oil, and check the EPA and DHA content.
  3. Write down your symptoms before you start: morning stiffness, number of painful joints, painkiller use.
  4. Take it consistently for about three months.
  5. Review your notes. If you cannot see a difference, it is reasonable to stop and save the money.
  6. Do not stop or reduce prescribed medicines without talking to your team.

When to see a dietitian

A registered dietitian can help if you do not eat fish, have a fish allergy, follow a vegan diet, have gout, or are trying to balance fish intake with pregnancy plans. Ask your GP or rheumatology team about a referral.

When to get medical help

Stop fish oil and get urgent medical advice if you notice signs of bleeding, such as black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, blood in your urine, or unusual bruising, especially if you take a blood thinner. Speak to your GP or rheumatology team if your arthritis is getting worse, rather than increasing supplements. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

Does fish oil help rheumatoid arthritis?

It can modestly reduce joint tenderness, morning stiffness and painkiller use for some people, according to reviews summarised by Arthritis UK. It works slowly and does not replace disease-modifying medicines.

Does fish oil help osteoarthritis?

The evidence is weak. Trials of fish oil and krill oil in knee osteoarthritis have not shown clear benefits. Exercise and weight management are more effective.

Is cod liver oil good for arthritis?

Arthritis UK says there is no evidence that cod liver oil helps osteoarthritis, and large doses risk too much vitamin A. Choose pure fish oil if you want omega-3.

Can I take fish oil with warfarin?

Only after speaking to your doctor or anticoagulant clinic. Fish oil can increase bleeding risk, and your INR may need closer monitoring.

How long does fish oil take to work?

Arthritis UK suggests trying it for about three months before deciding whether it helps.

Is eating oily fish better than taking a supplement?

UK advice is food first. Oily fish also provides protein, vitamin D, selenium and, in tinned fish with bones, calcium. Supplements may help if you want the higher doses used in inflammatory arthritis trials, with medical advice.

article.title: Arthritis and Pet Ownership – UK Guide
article.excerpt: Can you keep a pet with arthritis? UK guide to the benefits and challenges of pet ownership when living with arthritis, plus practical adaptations.
article.content:
Pets can bring immense joy, companionship, and even health benefits to people with arthritis. But pet ownership also presents practical challenges when you have limited mobility or painful joints. Here's how to make it work.

Quick answer: Pet ownership can benefit people with arthritis by providing motivation to move, reducing loneliness, distracting from pain, and encouraging routine. Challenges like dog walking, feeding, and grooming can be managed by using adapted equipment, choosing appropriate pets, and utilising services like dog walkers or professional groomers. Organisations such as Cinnamon Trust offer support.

Benefits of Pet Ownership with Arthritis

  • Motivation to move — dog walking ensures regular low-impact exercise
  • Reduced loneliness — companionship reduces social isolation
  • Pain distraction — stroking a pet releases oxytocin and reduces pain perception
  • Routine — pets encourage a structured daily routine
  • Mental health — pet owners report lower rates of depression and anxiety
  • Studies suggest pet owners with chronic pain use fewer pain medications

Practical Challenges and Solutions

Dog Walking

  • Use a dog walking harness or lead with padded handle to reduce grip strain
  • Choose routes with benches for rest stops
  • Consider a dog walking service on flare days (from £10 per walk in most UK areas)
  • Smaller dogs are easier to manage on lead
  • Look into Cinnamon Trust — a UK charity that helps people with illness walk their dogs

Feeding

  • Raised feeding bowls eliminate bending
  • Use a scoop rather than lifting heavy bags
  • Store food in a container at waist height
  • Automatic feeders for cats can reduce daily effort

Grooming

  • Choose breeds with low grooming needs if getting a new pet
  • Use ergonomic grooming brushes with thick handles
  • Consider professional grooming every 6-8 weeks

Litter Trays (Cats)

  • Self-cleaning litter trays reduce manual scooping
  • Place the tray at a comfortable height
  • Use lightweight clumping litter that's easier to handle

Choosing the Right Pet

  • Low-energy dog breeds — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, Shih Tzu, Greyhound (surprisingly lazy!)
  • Cats — independent, require less physical management
  • Small pets — rabbits, guinea pigs — lower physical demands
  • Consider an older rescue pet — less energetic, already trained

UK Support Services

  • Cinnamon Trust — volunteers help walk dogs and foster pets if you're hospitalised
  • PDSA — free vet care for eligible pet owners
  • Blue Cross — financial assistance for pet healthcare
  • Dogs for Good — assistance dogs for people with physical disabilities

A pet can be a wonderful companion on your arthritis journey. With the right planning and support, pet ownership is absolutely possible.

Practical next steps for Arthritis and Pet Ownership – UK Guide

If you came here about Arthritis and Pet Ownership – UK Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Quick questions about Arthritis Ownership Guide

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

article.title: Arthritis and Pregnancy in the UK
article.excerpt: Planning a pregnancy with arthritis? UK guide to medication safety, disease management during pregnancy, NHS preconception services, and breastfeeding.
article.content:
If you're living with arthritis and planning a pregnancy, or are already pregnant, there's good news: many women with arthritis have healthy pregnancies. However, careful planning with your rheumatologist is essential, particularly around medication management.

Quick answer: Managing arthritis during pregnancy requires careful planning with your rheumatologist. Some medications like methotrexate must be stopped months before conception, while others like hydroxychloroquine are considered safe. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Regular monitoring throughout pregnancy and planning for potential postpartum flares are crucial for a healthy outcome.

Before You Conceive

Ideally, speak to your rheumatology team 3-6 months before trying to conceive:

  • Some arthritis medications must be stopped well before conception
  • Your disease should be well-controlled before pregnancy — active inflammation increases risks
  • Ask your GP or hospital for a preconception counselling appointment
  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Medication Safety

Generally Safe During Pregnancy

  • Hydroxychloroquine — considered safe and often continued throughout
  • Sulfasalazine — generally safe but requires folic acid supplementation
  • Low-dose prednisolone — may be used for flare management
  • Paracetamol — first-line pain relief in pregnancy

Must Be Stopped Before Pregnancy

  • Methotrexate — must be stopped at least 3 months before conception (men and women)
  • Leflunomide — requires a washout period
  • NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — avoid after 20 weeks; discuss with doctor before 20 weeks

Discuss with Your Rheumatologist

  • Biologics — some are safer than others during pregnancy; many are stopped in the third trimester
  • JAK inhibitors — generally stopped before conception

During Pregnancy

Many women with inflammatory arthritis experience improvement during pregnancy, particularly in the second and third trimesters. However:

  • Some women experience flares, especially in the first trimester
  • Regular monitoring with both rheumatology and obstetric teams is important
  • Stay as active as possible — swimming and walking are excellent during pregnancy
  • Physiotherapy can help with joint pain and posture changes

After Birth

  • Flares are common in the first 3-6 months postpartum — plan medication restart with your team
  • Breastfeeding is possible with many arthritis medications — check each one individually
  • Ask for help at home — managing a newborn with arthritis requires support
  • Contact your rheumatology team early if symptoms worsen

UK Resources

  • UK Teratology Information Service (UKTIS) — bumps.org for medication safety data
  • NHS preconception clinics — ask your rheumatologist for a referral
  • NRAS — leaflets on RA and pregnancy

With proper planning and support from your healthcare team, arthritis need not prevent you from having a healthy pregnancy and baby.

article.title: Arthritis and sleep problems: what's keeping you awake? (UK)
article.excerpt: Night pain, medicines, toilet trips, restless legs, snoring or worry: find what is disturbing your sleep with arthritis and who can help. UK guide.
article.content:
Quick answer: Sleep problems with arthritis are not always caused by joint pain alone. Common causes include night pain and stiffness, more active inflammatory arthritis, medicines such as steroids, needing the toilet at night, restless legs, sleep apnoea, worry or low mood, and fibromyalgia. Work out what is waking you, then ask the right person: your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. Do not change prescribed medicines yourself.

"I can't sleep" can have several causes when you live with arthritis, and joint pain is not always the only one. Working out what is actually waking you makes it much easier to fix, and to ask the right person for help. Use this page as a checklist. For tonight's routine, see our main how to sleep with arthritis guide, and for the link between bad nights and worse pain, read poor sleep and arthritis pain.

Common causes, what helps and who to ask

1. Night pain and stiffness

Joints often ache when you are still, and turning over can hurt. What helps: settle pain before bed and support sore joints with pillows; see our sleep positions guide and pain relief guide. Who to ask: your GP or pharmacist about your pain relief plan.

2. More active inflammatory arthritis

In rheumatoid arthritis, pain and stiffness are often worse in the morning and after rest, and morning stiffness often lasts longer than 30 minutes. Night pain, swelling or long morning stiffness that is new or getting worse can mean your arthritis is more active. Who to ask: your rheumatology team or advice line, as your treatment may need reviewing. See the rheumatoid arthritis hub and the flare-up guide.

3. Medicines

Some medicines can affect sleep. For example, the NHS advises taking prednisolone in the morning, with breakfast, so it is less likely to affect your sleep. Some painkillers can cause drowsiness in the day, which can upset your sleep pattern. Who to ask: your pharmacist or GP. Do not stop, skip or change the timing of prescribed medicines yourself, and never stop steroid tablets suddenly.

4. Needing the toilet at night

Getting up to pee is harder with stiff joints, and night trips in the dark raise the risk of falls. What helps: a night light and a clear path; see our night-time toilet trips guide and falls prevention guide. Who to ask: your GP if night-time peeing is new or getting worse.

5. Restless legs

Restless legs syndrome causes a strong urge to move your legs, often with tingling, throbbing or pain, and is usually worse at night when resting. It can be linked to iron deficiency anaemia, kidney disease and some medicines. What helps: the NHS suggests a regular sleep routine, a warm bath or stretching before bed, and no caffeine after midday. Who to ask: your GP if it is stopping you sleeping.

6. Snoring and daytime sleepiness

Loud snoring, gasping or choking noises in your sleep and feeling very tired during the day are the main signs of sleep apnoea. Who to ask: your GP. Read our sleep apnoea guide. If you drive and feel very sleepy in the day, check the driving advice with your GP.

7. Worry and low mood

Stress, anxiety and depression are among the most common causes of insomnia, and they are common with long-term pain. Who to ask: your GP, or in England you can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies. See our arthritis and mental health guide and depression guide.

8. Fibromyalgia

Fibromyalgia can stop you sleeping deeply enough to feel refreshed, so you may wake tired even after plenty of sleep. Who to ask: your GP. See our fibromyalgia overview.

9. Your bedroom and habits

The NHS lists noise, a room that is too hot or cold, an uncomfortable bed, and alcohol, caffeine or nicotine among the common causes of insomnia. What helps: try one change at a time. There is no single best mattress for arthritis; something supportive that does not sag suits many people, and a topper is a cheaper first step.

Before you see your GP

  • Keep a two-week sleep diary noting what woke you each night; our sleep and pain guide has a simple template
  • Bring a list of all your medicines and supplements, with the times you take them
  • Ask: "Could any of my medicines be affecting my sleep?", "Could this be restless legs or sleep apnoea?" and "Is CBT for insomnia available here?"
  • If a carer or partner notices snoring, gasping or kicking, bring them or their notes

When to get urgent help

  • Call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain, severe breathlessness or sudden confusion
  • Get urgent advice from NHS 111 or your rheumatology team if a joint becomes hot, red and very swollen, especially with fever
  • If you feel you cannot keep yourself safe, call 999. You can also call Samaritans free on 116 123

Frequently asked questions

Can I take an over-the-counter sleep aid?

Ask a pharmacist first, as some can interact with arthritis medicines or leave you drowsy the next day, which raises the risk of falls. Our sleeping tablets and falls guide explains more.

Is it my arthritis or something else keeping me awake?

It can be both. Pain is a common cause, but restless legs, sleep apnoea, toilet trips, medicines and worry are all worth ruling in or out with your GP.

I care for someone who sleeps badly. What can I do?

Note what you see at night, help them keep a regular get-up time, and make the route to the toilet safe and well lit. A carer's assessment can help if your own sleep is suffering.

article.direct_answer: Sleep problems with arthritis are not always caused by joint pain alone. Common causes include night pain and stiffness, more active inflammatory arthritis, medicines such as steroids, needing the toilet at night, restless legs, sleep apnoea, worry or low mood, and fibromyalgia. Work out what is waking you, then ask the right person: your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. Do not change prescribed medicines yourself.

faqs.q: Can I take an over-the-counter sleep aid?

faqs.q: Is it my arthritis or something else keeping me awake?

article.title: Travelling with Arthritis – UK & Abroad Guide
article.excerpt: Planning a holiday with arthritis? UK guide to travel insurance, accessible accommodation, flying tips, medication management, and making the most.
article.content:
Arthritis doesn't have to stop you travelling. With proper planning, you can enjoy holidays in the UK and abroad. This guide covers everything from travel insurance to managing medications while away.

Quick answer: When travelling with arthritis, declare your condition for travel insurance and carry medications in hand luggage with a GP letter. Request airport assistance, reserve an aisle seat, and move frequently during flights. Choose accessible accommodation, such as ground-floor rooms or those with lifts and walk-in showers. Pace yourself, use a fold-up walking stick, and consider a RADAR key for accessible toilets.

Before You Go

Travel Insurance

Standard travel insurance may not cover pre-existing conditions like arthritis. You need to:

  • Declare arthritis when buying travel insurance
  • Specialist providers: AllClear, InsureWith, Avanti, Staysure
  • Cover should include emergency treatment for flare-ups abroad
  • GHIC (Global Health Insurance Card) provides access to state healthcare in EU countries — apply free at nhs.uk

Medications

  • Carry medications in original packaging with prescription labels
  • Take enough for your trip plus a few extra days
  • Keep medications in hand luggage (never checked luggage)
  • Carry a letter from your GP listing your medications — especially for controlled drugs or injectable biologics
  • Check destination country rules on medication imports

Flying with Arthritis

  • Request assistance — airports provide free assistance from check-in to the gate (book 48 hours ahead)
  • Aisle seat — easier to get up and move during the flight
  • Move regularly — walk the aisle every 30-60 minutes to prevent stiffness
  • Compression socks — reduce swelling on long flights
  • Support pillows — neck and lumbar pillows for comfort
  • Stay hydrated — cabin air is very dry
  • Time medication — adjust for time zones on long-haul flights

Accessible Accommodation

  • Look for ground-floor rooms or properties with lifts
  • Check for walk-in showers (no bath step-over)
  • UK: search "accessible holiday cottages" on DisabledHolidays.com or AccessAble
  • Hotels: Travelodge accessible rooms are reliably equipped
  • Cruise ships: often excellent for accessibility

UK Accessible Breaks

  • Calvert Trust — accessible activity holidays in Exmoor, Lake District, Kielder
  • Center Parcs — adapted lodges and accessible facilities
  • National Trust — many properties have accessibility guides on their website
  • Seaside towns — many have beach wheelchairs available

During Your Trip

  • Pace yourself — don't try to pack every day full of activities
  • Build in rest days
  • Carry a fold-up walking stick or portable seat for queues
  • Apply for a RADAR key (£5 from Disability Rights UK) — opens 10,000+ accessible toilets across the UK
  • Keep a cool bag for biologic medications if they need refrigeration

Don't let arthritis stop you exploring. With the right preparation, you can travel comfortably and create wonderful memories.

Practical next steps for Travelling with Arthritis – UK & Abroad Guide

If you came here about Travelling with Arthritis – UK & Abroad Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Quick questions about Travelling with Arthritis Abroad

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on travelling with arthritis – uk & abroad guide. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Healthy Weight and Arthritis: A Practical UK Guide to Losing Weight Safely When Your Joints Hurt
article.excerpt: Weight is one of the few things that has strong evidence for easing osteoarthritis pain, and it matters for inflammatory arthritis too. This guide explains what NICE says, how to check your weight, free NHS support, realistic steps that work with painful joints, weight-loss medicines, and why being underweight is also a concern.
article.content:
Quick answer: If you have osteoarthritis and are living with overweight or obesity, NICE says losing weight improves pain, function and quality of life, and any amount helps, though losing 10% of your body weight is likely to be better than 5%. Aim to lose weight steadily, about 0.5 to 1kg a week, with a balanced diet and activity you can manage. Free NHS tools and your GP can help, and a dietitian can tailor advice.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against NICE NG226, the NHS overweight and obesity and Better Health pages, Arthritis UK's weight guidance and published trials.

Weight can be a sensitive subject, and many people with arthritis have been told to "just lose weight" without any real help. That is not fair or useful. Losing weight is genuinely hard, and it is harder when walking hurts and fatigue makes cooking difficult. But weight is also one of the few things with strong evidence for easing joint pain, so it is worth understanding why it matters and what support is available.

This guide is about reaching a weight that is healthy for you, which for some people means losing weight and for others means gaining or keeping weight steady.

Why weight matters with arthritis

Osteoarthritis

NICE guidance on osteoarthritis (NG226) names therapeutic exercise and weight management (where appropriate) as core treatments. For people with osteoarthritis who are living with overweight or obesity, NICE says healthcare professionals should:

  • advise them that weight loss will improve their quality of life and physical function, and reduce pain
  • support them to choose a weight-loss goal
  • explain that any amount of weight loss is likely to be beneficial, but losing 10% of their body weight is likely to be better than 5%

Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) explains that the force going through your knees when walking can be two or three times your body weight, so even a small weight loss can make a difference to the load on your joints.

Research supports this. In the US IDEA trial (Messier and colleagues, JAMA 2013), adults with knee osteoarthritis and overweight or obesity who followed a diet, with or without exercise, lost more weight and had greater falls in an inflammation marker than those who only exercised, and the diet group had lower compressive forces on the knee. A 2025 systematic review (Asadi and colleagues) found that reduced-energy diets improved pain, physical function and body weight in people with osteoarthritis.

Rheumatoid arthritis, gout and other types

Arthritis UK says being overweight can increase inflammation in the body and is linked with a higher risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis, gout, back pain and osteoarthritis. For people with gout, losing excess weight can help lower uric acid levels. Excess weight also adds to the higher risk of heart disease that comes with inflammatory arthritis.

Before joint surgery

If you are waiting for a joint replacement, your surgical team may talk to you about weight, because it can affect the anaesthetic, wound healing and recovery. Ask what support is available while you wait.

How to check your weight

The NHS uses body mass index (BMI) as a starting point, alongside waist-to-height ratio. You can use the free NHS BMI calculator online.

BMI (most adults)BMI (South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean background)Category
18.5 to 24.918.5 to 22.9Healthy range
25 to 29.923 to 27.4Overweight
30 or more27.5 or moreObese

The NHS explains that people from these ethnic backgrounds are at risk of health problems at a slightly lower BMI. BMI cannot tell the difference between muscle and fat, so it is only a rough guide.

Waist-to-height ratio: the NHS says you should try to keep your waist size to less than half your height. Measure around your middle, halfway between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone.

Setting a realistic goal

  • Start small. The NHS says losing just 5 to 10% of your body weight can improve your health. For someone weighing 90kg, 5% is 4.5kg.
  • Go steady. The NHS suggests aiming to lose 0.5 to 1kg (1 to 2lb) a week.
  • Measure more than the scales. Notice changes in pain, walking distance, stairs, sleep and how clothes fit.
  • Plan for plateaus. Weight loss is rarely a straight line. Keeping weight off is a success in itself.

Eating to lose weight

To lose weight, you need to take in less energy than your body uses. The NHS says that on average women use around 2,000 calories a day and men around 2,500, but this varies, and many people with arthritis are less active than average. This guide does not set a calorie target for you; a dietitian or NHS weight management service can help with that.

Practical changes that follow NHS advice:

  • Fill half your plate with vegetables or salad. They are filling and low in energy.
  • Choose wholegrain starchy foods and watch portion sizes and added fats such as butter and oil.
  • Include protein at each meal to stay full and protect muscle. See our protein guide.
  • Cut down on sugary drinks, snacks and alcohol. The NHS points out that alcohol is high in calories.
  • Read labels and use the traffic-light system to choose foods lower in fat, saturated fat, sugar and salt.
  • Plan meals ahead so you are not relying on takeaways on bad days. Our meal plans for arthritis can help.
  • Eat mindfully. Sit at a table, eat slowly and avoid eating in front of a screen.

An anti-inflammatory, Mediterranean-style diet works well for weight loss because it is filling, flexible and not overly restrictive.

Approaches to be cautious about

  • Very low calorie diets (under 800 to 1,200 calories a day). The NHS says these are not suitable or safe for everyone and should only be followed with support from a dietitian or specialist service.
  • Cutting out whole food groups without advice, which risks missing out on calcium, fibre or protein.
  • Unregulated "fat burner" supplements or slimming pills bought online, which can be unsafe.
  • Fasting if you take medicines that must be taken with food, or have diabetes, without speaking to your healthcare team first.

Being active with painful joints

Activity helps with weight, but it matters even more for your joints, muscles, mood and heart. NICE recommends therapeutic exercise for everyone with osteoarthritis. Arthritis UK notes that adults need at least two and a half hours of moderate aerobic activity a week plus strengthening exercise, but any amount is better than none.

  • Low-impact options: swimming, aqua aerobics, cycling or an exercise bike, walking on flat ground, chair-based exercise.
  • Strengthening: sit-to-stands, step-ups, resistance bands. Stronger muscles support your joints.
  • Start low, go slow: some extra discomfort while you exercise is normal, but pain should settle within a day or so. If it does not, do a little less next time.
  • Get help: a physiotherapist can design a programme around your joints. Many areas offer self-referral to NHS physiotherapy and exercise programmes for joint pain.

Exercise alone usually leads to modest weight loss. Combining it with changes to eating works best, as the IDEA trial showed.

Free NHS and local support

  • NHS Weight Loss Plan app: a free 12-week plan to help you build healthier habits.
  • NHS Better Health: free tools, healthy eating tips, home workout videos and information on discounted weight-loss programmes.
  • Local weight management services: the NHS says you may be able to refer yourself; check your GP surgery website or ask reception.
  • NHS Digital Weight Management Programme (England): a 12-week online programme for adults living with obesity who also have diabetes, high blood pressure or both, accessed by referral, usually from your GP practice.
  • Specialist weight management services: your GP can refer you if you need more support, including dietitian-led programmes.

Services differ in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Ask your GP practice what is available locally.

Weight-loss medicines and surgery

Depending on your BMI and other health conditions, your doctor may discuss medicines. The NHS lists GLP-1 and GIP medicines such as semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide, which reduce appetite, and orlistat, which reduces fat absorption. They are prescribed alongside diet and activity changes. Our guide to weight-loss injections and arthritis explains these in more detail, including what to tell your rheumatology team.

Weight-loss surgery may be offered if your BMI is 40 or over, or 35 or over with conditions that could improve with weight loss (with lower thresholds for some ethnic groups). This is a specialist decision.

If you lose a lot of weight, tell your rheumatology team, as some medicine doses depend on body weight.

Common barriers and what helps

BarrierWhat may help
Pain stops me exercisingWater-based or chair exercise, a physiotherapy programme, and a pain relief review with your GP
Steroid tablets increase my appetiteAsk your rheumatology team about the dose and duration; keep filling, lower-energy snacks such as fruit and vegetables to hand
Cooking is too tiringBatch cooking on good days, frozen vegetables, simple meals, and an occupational therapy assessment
I eat when I feel lowTalk to your GP; NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral in England) can help with mood and eating habits
Poor sleep makes me snackWork on sleep habits and discuss night pain with your GP

Keeping weight off

Many people lose weight and then regain it, which can feel discouraging. Things that tend to help include:

  • Weighing yourself regularly, as the NHS suggests, so small gains are noticed early.
  • Keeping the habits that worked, such as planning meals and keeping active, rather than going back to old routines.
  • Planning for flares. When your arthritis flares, activity often drops. Have a list of easy, healthy meals and gentle exercises ready for those weeks.
  • Getting support. Friends, family, a weight management group or an app can help you stay on track.
  • Being kind to yourself. The NHS reminds us that changing habits and losing weight is not easy and takes time.

If you stop weight-loss medicines, the NHS says you should be offered support to help you stay a healthy weight.

Being underweight is a concern too

Arthritis UK points out that being underweight can be a symptom of some conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis, and is linked to an increased risk of fractures related to osteoporosis. If your BMI is below 18.5, or you are losing weight without trying, see your GP. A dietitian can help you gain weight in a healthy way.

When to see a dietitian

Ask your GP about a referral to a registered dietitian if you have tried to lose weight without success, have diabetes, kidney disease or another condition affecting your diet, are considering a very low calorie diet, are underweight, or have a history of disordered eating.

When to get medical help

See your GP if you lose weight without trying, as unexplained weight loss should always be checked. See your GP if you think you may have an eating disorder, such as binge eating. Talk to your doctor before starting a weight-loss programme if you have diabetes, heart disease or take medicines that need adjusting. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

How much weight do I need to lose to help my knees?

NICE says any amount of weight loss is likely to help, but losing 10% of your body weight is likely to be better than 5%. Even small losses reduce the load on your knees.

Will losing weight cure my arthritis?

No, but for people with osteoarthritis who are overweight it can reduce pain and improve function and quality of life. It also helps heart health and some inflammatory conditions.

How fast should I lose weight?

The NHS suggests a steady 0.5 to 1kg (1 to 2lb) a week.

What is the best diet to lose weight with arthritis?

The one you can stick to. A balanced, Mediterranean-style diet with smaller portions is a good choice. A dietitian can tailor it to you.

Can I get weight-loss injections on the NHS?

Possibly, depending on your BMI, other health conditions and local services. Talk to your GP; see our weight-loss injections guide for details.

I cannot exercise because of pain. Can I still lose weight?

Yes. Changes to eating have the biggest effect on weight. Gentle activity, even seated, still helps your joints and mood, and a physiotherapist can help you find what you can manage.

article.title: Managing Arthritis at Work in the UK: Your Rights, Adjustments
article.excerpt: In the UK, arthritis is considered a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it significantly affects daily activities for at least 12 months.
article.content:
For the millions of people in the UK living with arthritis, managing the condition alongside employment presents unique challenges. Joint pain, stiffness, fatigue and unpredictable flare-ups can make the demands of a typical working day feel overwhelming. Yet with the right adjustments, legal protections and strategies, most people with arthritis can continue to work successfully and enjoy fulfilling careers. This comprehensive guide explains your rights as an employee with arthritis in the UK, the adjustments available to you, and practical techniques for managing symptoms at work.

Quick answer: In the UK, arthritis is considered a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it significantly affects daily activities for at least 12 months. This protects employees from discrimination and obliges employers to make 'reasonable adjustments', such as providing ergonomic equipment, flexible working hours, or modifying tasks. The Access to Work scheme also offers grants for workplace adjustments.

Your Legal Rights Under the Equality Act 2010

Arthritis is classified as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on your ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. "Long-term" means it has lasted, or is likely to last, at least 12 months. Most forms of arthritis — including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis — will meet this definition.

What This Means for You

  • Protection from discrimination — Your employer cannot treat you less favourably because of your arthritis, whether in recruitment, promotion, training or dismissal
  • Reasonable adjustments — Your employer has a legal duty to make reasonable adjustments to remove disadvantages you face because of your condition
  • Protection from harassment — Colleagues or managers cannot make offensive comments or create a hostile environment related to your disability
  • Right to flexible working — All employees can request flexible working from day one in a job, and employers must consider requests reasonably

Telling Your Employer

You are not legally obliged to tell your employer about your arthritis during recruitment. However, disclosing your condition — especially to your line manager and HR department — is usually beneficial because it triggers the duty to make reasonable adjustments, provides context for any absences or performance variations, allows your employer to support you proactively, and protects you more effectively if problems arise. Many people worry about stigma, but UK employment law strongly protects you once a disclosure is made. If you experience negative consequences after disclosing, you may have a claim for disability discrimination.

Reasonable Adjustments at Work

Reasonable adjustments are changes your employer makes to ensure you can do your job effectively. What is "reasonable" depends on the size and resources of the employer, the cost, and the practicality of the adjustment. Common adjustments include:

Physical Workspace

  • Ergonomic chair — A chair with lumbar support, adjustable height and armrests can significantly reduce pain
  • Sit-stand desk — Alternating between sitting and standing prevents stiffness from prolonged positions
  • Ergonomic keyboard and mouse — Split keyboards, vertical mice and trackballs reduce hand and wrist strain
  • Voice recognition software — Dragon NaturallySpeaking can reduce typing if hand arthritis is severe
  • Accessible parking — A closer parking space to reduce walking distance, especially in bad weather
  • Ground-floor workspace — Avoiding stairs if knee or hip arthritis is problematic

Working Patterns

  • Flexible start/finish times — Starting later allows morning stiffness to ease before commuting
  • Working from home — Reducing commuting and providing a comfortable environment on difficult days
  • Regular breaks — Short breaks every 30–45 minutes to move and stretch
  • Reduced hours — Temporary or permanent reduction during flare-ups or medication changes
  • Phased return — Gradually increasing hours after a period of absence

Task Modifications

  • Reallocating physical tasks — Swapping heavy lifting or prolonged standing duties with colleagues
  • Modified targets — Adjusting output expectations during flare-ups
  • Additional time for tasks — Allowing extra time for activities affected by your condition
  • Changed meeting formats — Virtual meetings to reduce travel; walking meetings for gentle movement

The Access to Work Scheme

Access to Work is a government programme that provides grants to cover the costs of workplace adjustments beyond what is considered "reasonable" for your employer. It can fund specialist equipment (ergonomic furniture, assistive technology), support workers or job coaches, travel to work if public transport is difficult (taxi fares), mental health support, and communication support. To apply, visit the gov.uk website or call the Access to Work helpline on 0800 121 7479. The scheme is available to employees, self-employed workers and people starting a new job. Applications can be made at any time — you don't need to be starting a new role.

Practical Strategies for Managing Symptoms at Work

Morning Routine

  • Allow extra time in the morning for stiffness to ease — set your alarm 30 minutes earlier if needed
  • Take a warm shower to loosen joints before dressing
  • Do 5–10 minutes of gentle stretches before leaving the house
  • Prepare your work clothes and bag the night before to reduce morning rushing
  • Take any morning medications with breakfast to ensure they have time to work

During the Working Day

  • Move regularly — Set a timer to remind you to stand, stretch or walk every 30–45 minutes
  • Pace yourself — Alternate between demanding and less demanding tasks throughout the day
  • Stay hydrated — Dehydration worsens stiffness; keep a water bottle at your desk
  • Manage pain proactively — Don't wait until pain becomes severe; take medication at regular intervals as prescribed
  • Use gadgets and aids — Jar openers, electric can openers, padded pen grips and lightweight equipment all reduce joint strain
  • Protect your joints — Carry bags on your forearm rather than gripping with your hands; use both hands to carry heavy items

Managing Flare-Ups at Work

Have a flare-up plan agreed with your manager in advance. This might include working from home on bad days, access to a quiet rest room, permission to take additional short breaks, pre-agreed modified duties during flares, and clear communication channels so your team knows when you need support without lengthy explanations.

Occupational Health Assessments

Many UK employers offer occupational health services. An OH assessment involves a meeting with an occupational health professional who will assess how your arthritis affects your ability to work, recommend specific adjustments, advise on any limitations or concerns, provide your employer with a report (with your consent), and help plan any return to work after absence. You can request an OH referral through HR or your line manager, or your employer may suggest one. These assessments are confidential between you and the OH professional — your employer only receives the recommendations, not your full medical details.

Sickness Absence and Arthritis

If arthritis causes you to take time off work, remember that disability-related absences should be recorded separately from general sickness, they should not normally trigger absence management procedures or be counted towards absence thresholds, your employer should consider whether adjustments would reduce future absences, and you are entitled to Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) from the fourth day of absence. If you feel your employer is treating disability-related absences unfairly, seek advice from ACAS (0300 123 1100) or Citizens Advice.

Self-Employment and Freelancing

Many people with arthritis find self-employment offers greater flexibility. If you work for yourself, structure your day around your symptoms (e.g., working when stiffness has eased), build in rest days and buffer time for flare-ups, invest in ergonomic equipment, consider Access to Work for self-employed support, use technology to automate repetitive tasks, and set clear boundaries with clients about response times and deadlines.

Financial Support

  • Personal Independence Payment (PIP) — For extra costs of living with a disability (not means-tested, available whether or not you work)
  • Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) — If you cannot work or have limited capability for work
  • Universal Credit — Work allowances may be higher if you have a health condition
  • Disabled Facilities Grant — For home adaptations that help you remain independent and able to work

Getting Support

  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) — Employment advice line and guides at arthritis-uk.org
  • ACAS — Free workplace advice including disability rights (0300 123 1100)
  • Citizens Advice — Help with employment rights, benefits and adjustments
  • Disability Rights UK — Factsheets and advice on employment and disability
  • Your GP or rheumatologist — Can provide supporting letters for workplace adjustments

Working with arthritis is challenging but achievable. With the right adjustments, support and self-management strategies, you can maintain a productive and satisfying career. Don't hesitate to ask for help — it's your legal right. Our virtual assistant can provide personalised advice on workplace adjustments for your specific type of arthritis.

  • GOV.UK: Definition of disability under the Equality Act 2010
  • GOV.UK: Access to Work

  • Arthritis UK: Work and arthritis

Educational information for people in the United Kingdom — not personal legal, benefits or medical advice. Charity no. 1218461. Reviewed by Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483. Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.

/blog/arthritis-and-your-heart-lowering-.answer: Inflammatory types of arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, lupus and gout, are linked with a higher risk of heart disease and stroke. Ongoing inflammation can damage blood vessels, and some medicines and reduced activity add to the risk. Keeping inflammation well controlled, not smoking, staying active and having regular blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar checks all help lower it.

article.title: Turmeric for Arthritis: Evidence, Dose Context and UK Safety
article.excerpt: Does turmeric help arthritis? What curcumin trials show, why absorption matters, safety with medicines, and how it fits UK diet and pain-care plans.
article.content:
Quick answer: Curcumin (from turmeric) has some clinical evidence for osteoarthritis pain when taken as an enhanced-absorption extract for several weeks. Plain culinary turmeric delivers little curcumin. It is not a substitute for prescribed treatment. Tell your GP or pharmacist before starting high-dose supplements — especially if you take anticoagulants or have gallbladder disease.

Turmeric is widely marketed for “joint inflammation”. Some of the interest is justified; much of the marketing is not. This page summarises what UK patients and carers usually need to know, with links to diet, pain relief and medicines safety. Educational information only — not personal medical advice.

What UK sources emphasise first

NICE osteoarthritis guidance (NG226) centres on exercise, weight management where relevant, and carefully chosen topical or oral medicines — not turmeric. NHS osteoarthritis information and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) diet advice treat food patterns as supportive, while Arthritis UK complementary treatments pages urge caution with supplements that lack strong evidence or clear regulation. Use those pages as your baseline; treat curcumin as an optional adjunct you discuss with a clinician.

What the evidence actually says

Curcumin can influence inflammatory signalling pathways that also matter in arthritis care. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Results vary by product quality and study design.

Treat curcumin as an optional adjunct — not a replacement for evidence-based pain relief, topical or oral NSAIDs when appropriate, or DMARD therapy in inflammatory arthritis.

Absorption: why powder in tea is not the same as a trial dose

  • Curcumin alone is poorly absorbed
  • Formulations with piperine (black pepper extract), phytosomes or lipids are used in many studies
  • Cooking with turmeric powder is pleasant and low-risk for most people, but it is not equivalent to standardised trial extracts
  • “Golden milk” and supermarket spice jars are food, not a clinical dose

Practical dosing context (not a prescription)

Trial products often use standardised curcuminoid extracts rather than raw powder. Labels differ. Do not stack multiple “joint blends”. If you try a supplement, pick one clear product, take it with food as directed, and review after 8–12 weeks whether pain, stiffness or function actually changed. Stop and seek advice if you develop stomach pain, easy bruising, yellowing of the skin/eyes, or allergic symptoms.

Safety and medicine interactions

  • May interact with anticoagulants / antiplatelets — check with a pharmacist
  • Use caution with gallstones or bile duct problems
  • High doses can upset the gut
  • Always list supplements on your rheumatology and GP records

If you take methotrexate or other DMARDs, read our note on turmeric and methotrexate and confirm with your specialist nurse before combining.

Where turmeric fits with diet and lifestyle

No spice reverses arthritis. Patterns matter more: vegetables, pulses, wholegrains, olive oil and oily fish — see the diet hub and diet guide. Pair any supplement experiment with movement from the exercise guide and flare tactics in the pain relief guide.

If you are newly diagnosed

Supplements can distract from the first jobs that matter: understanding your arthritis type, starting prescribed treatment when offered, and learning pacing. Use the newly diagnosed guide first. Curcumin can wait until your core plan is clear.

Money and realistic expectations

Premium curcumin products are expensive. If cost is tight, prioritise NHS-prescribed care, footwear/exercise that help daily function, and benefits advice via the Benefits & PIP hub rather than unproven stacks. Arthritis UK and NHS pages remain the safest first reads for condition basics. For a deeper evidence walk-through, see turmeric and curcumin evidence and ginger vs turmeric.

Bottom line

Curcumin extracts have plausible, modest evidence for some osteoarthritis symptoms. Culinary turmeric is fine as food. Neither replaces clinical care. Review any supplement with your NHS team and keep expectations honest.

Quick questions

Can turmeric replace ibuprofen? No. Follow NICE/NHS medicines advice; ask a pharmacist before mixing supplements and painkillers.

How long before I judge it? Give a single product several weeks unless side effects appear sooner.

Who should avoid high-dose curcumin? People on blood thinners, with gallbladder disease, or who are pregnant should get individual advice first.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

article.title: Understanding Frailty in Older Adults
article.excerpt: Frailty is more than just getting older — it's a recognised medical syndrome. Here's what it means, what causes it, and how it can be managed.
article.content:
Quick answer: Frailty is a medical syndrome characterised by reduced strength, endurance, and physiological reserve, making individuals vulnerable to illness or injury. It is different from normal ageing, as many older people remain robust. Clinically, frailty is identified by unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking speed, and low physical activity. Early identification is crucial for effective intervention and improved outcomes.

Frailty is more than just getting older. It's a recognised medical syndrome characterised by reduced strength, endurance, and physiological reserve that leaves a person vulnerable to illness, injury, and disability following even minor stressors. Many people remain robust well into their eighties and nineties, while frailty can sometimes develop earlier when multiple health conditions overlap.

What Does 'Frailty' Actually Mean?

Frailty is a recognised medical syndrome characterised by reduced strength, endurance, and physiological reserve, which leaves a person more vulnerable to illness, injury, and disability following even relatively minor stressors, such as an infection or a fall. It's distinct from simply being older — many people remain robust well into their eighties and nineties, while frailty can sometimes develop earlier when multiple health conditions overlap.

Clinically, frailty is often identified using a set of measurable signs: unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness (often measured by grip strength), slow walking speed, and low physical activity levels. Meeting several of these criteria suggests a frailty syndrome rather than normal ageing. A healthcare professional can assess these markers and determine whether someone is experiencing frailty, pre-frailty, or neither.

The distinction is important because it changes how healthcare decisions should be made. A frail person may respond differently to surgery, medication, or hospitalisation than a non-frail person of the same age, and may need additional support to recover from illness.

What Causes Frailty?

Frailty develops from an interplay of multiple factors rather than a single cause. Age-related muscle loss, known as sarcopenia, is a fundamental driver. Starting around age 30, most people lose approximately 3-8% of their muscle mass per decade, with the rate of loss accelerating significantly after age 60. This loss of muscle translates directly to loss of strength and functional capacity.

Chronic inflammation is another key factor. As we age, baseline levels of inflammatory markers in the blood tend to increase, a phenomenon researchers call "inflammaging." This chronic, low-level inflammation damages tissues over time and contributes to both muscle loss and weakness.

Hormonal changes also play a role. Testosterone and growth hormone levels decline with age, and these hormones are important for maintaining muscle mass and strength. In women, the drop in oestrogen after menopause affects muscle strength and bone density.

The cumulative effect of chronic diseases — heart disease, diabetes, kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease — accelerates frailty. These conditions create a state of metabolic stress that the ageing body struggles to manage.

Poor nutrition, particularly inadequate protein intake, compounds the problem. Social isolation and inactivity create a vicious cycle: weakness leads to reduced activity, which leads to further weakness. Addressing these factors can interrupt the progression.

Why Identifying Frailty Matters

Recognising frailty early matters because it changes how healthcare decisions should be approached. A frail person undergoing surgery, for example, may need different perioperative management, longer rehabilitation, and closer monitoring. A frail person starting a new medication may experience different side effects or require dose adjustments.

More importantly, identifying frailty allows healthcare teams to be proactive rather than reactive. Instead of waiting for a fall, fracture, or hospitalisation, early recognition enables supportive interventions that can slow or even reverse the condition's progression.

Research consistently shows that frailty, particularly in its earlier stages, responds to targeted intervention. This means that identifying frailty is not a pessimistic diagnosis — it's an opportunity to intervene when intervention is most effective.

Can Frailty Be Reversed?

Importantly, frailty is not necessarily a one-way path. It is generally thought that frailty — particularly in its earlier stages, sometimes called "pre-frailty" — can often be improved or even reversed through targeted interventions. Resistance exercise to rebuild muscle strength, adequate protein and calorie intake, addressing underlying medical conditions, and reducing social isolation have all been shown to improve frailty markers in clinical studies.

Studies of older adults who began resistance training programmes showed meaningful strength gains and improved functional capacity even after years of decline. Some adults moved from a frailty classification back to pre-frailty or robust status. The key is consistency and starting sooner rather than later.

Supporting a Frail Loved One

If you're caring for someone who shows signs of frailty, encouraging regular movement appropriate to their ability, ensuring meals are nutritious and protein-rich, supporting social connection, and coordinating closely with their healthcare team can all make a meaningful difference. Small, consistent steps tend to be more sustainable and effective than dramatic changes.

If you notice signs of frailty in yourself or a loved one — unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, or a noticeable slowing of walking speed — it's worth raising this with a doctor, since early support can meaningfully improve strength, independence, and quality of life.

This article is for general information only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult with your healthcare provider before starting new exercise or dietary changes.

Practical next steps for Understanding Frailty in Older Adults

If you came here about Understanding Frailty in Older Adults, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Quick questions about Understanding Frailty Older Adults

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

/blog/universal-credit-and-arthritis-lim.question: ESA and Universal Credit for Arthritis: Limited Capability for Work, the WCA and What You Could Get
/blog/universal-credit-and-arthritis-lim.answer: If arthritis limits how much you can work, you may be able to claim Universal Credit, New Style ESA, or both. Universal Credit is means-tested; New Style ESA depends on your National Insurance record. Both use the Work Capability Assessment. If you are found to have limited capability for work and work-related activity, Universal Credit includes an extra monthly amount, which has had two rates for new claims since 6 April 2026.
