article.title: ESA and Universal Credit for Arthritis: Limited Capability for Work, the WCA and What You Could Get
article.excerpt: A practical UK guide to New Style ESA and Universal Credit when arthritis limits how much you can work: how the two benefits fit together, fit notes, the WCA50 questionnaire, the physical descriptors that often matter with arthritis, the two LCWRA rates from 6 April 2026, working while claiming, and how to challenge a decision.
article.content:
Quick answer: If arthritis limits how much you can work, you may be able to claim Universal Credit, New Style ESA, or both. Universal Credit is means-tested; New Style ESA depends on your National Insurance record. Both use the Work Capability Assessment. If you are found to have limited capability for work and work-related activity, Universal Credit includes an extra monthly amount, which has had two rates for new claims since 6 April 2026.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Health conditions, disability and Universal Credit, GOV.UK: Universal Credit – what you'll get and GOV.UK: Employment and Support Allowance. Amounts quoted are the ones shown on GOV.UK on that date. Rates usually change each April, so always check the current figures.

When arthritis means you cannot work, or can only work a little, money worries can pile on top of pain and fatigue. The benefits system for people who cannot work because of their health has changed a lot over the years, and the names (ESA, UC, WCA, LCW, LCWRA) can be confusing. This guide explains, in plain English, how it works now in England, Scotland and Wales, with notes on Northern Ireland.

This is separate from Personal Independence Payment (PIP), which helps with the extra costs of disability and can be claimed whether or not you work.

The two benefits: Universal Credit and New Style ESA

Universal CreditNew Style ESA
What it isA monthly payment to help with living costsA benefit for people whose disability or health condition affects how much they can work
Based onHousehold income, savings and circumstances (means-tested)Your National Insurance contributions, usually in the last 2 to 3 years (credits also count)
SavingsReduced if you have over £6,000; usually no entitlement over £16,000Savings and a partner's income do not count
How often paidMonthlyEvery 2 weeks
AssessmentWork Capability AssessmentWork Capability Assessment

You might be able to get both at the same time. If you do, your Universal Credit is reduced by the amount of New Style ESA you get. GOV.UK points out that New Style ESA is paid more regularly and gives you different National Insurance credits, which count towards your State Pension. If you claim both, you only have one Work Capability Assessment.

Income-related ESA is closed to new claims. If you already get it, you keep getting it while you are eligible, until you are moved to Universal Credit.

New Style ESA: key conditions

  • You must be under State Pension age.
  • You must have a disability or health condition that affects how much you can work.
  • You must have paid enough National Insurance contributions, usually in the last 2 to 3 years.
  • You cannot get it while you get Statutory Sick Pay (SSP), but you can apply up to 3 months before your SSP ends.
  • You can apply whether you are employed, self-employed or unemployed.

If you get more than £85 a week from a private pension, half of the amount over £85 is taken off your ESA each week.

Step 1: Report your condition and get fit notes

When you claim Universal Credit, you can report a health condition that affects your capability to work. GOV.UK says you must get a fit note if your condition affects your capability to work for longer than 7 days. Fit notes can come from a GP or hospital doctor, registered nurse, occupational therapist, pharmacist or physiotherapist, and can be printed or digital.

Keep getting fit notes until you have been sent your assessment decision. If you do not, you may be expected to work or look for work. You will get a reminder before your fit note expires. Our sick pay and fit notes guide explains fit notes in more detail.

Step 2: The Work Capability Assessment (WCA)

If your condition affects your capability to work for longer than 28 days, you may need a WCA. GOV.UK notes you might not get one if you earn over £881 a month.

  1. The questionnaire. You fill in the WCA50 "Capability for Work" questionnaire (ESA has its own version). You can send copies of medical information, such as treatment plans or test results.
  2. The assessment. It can be in person, by video call or by phone. You can have someone with you, such as a friend or support worker. The audio is recorded unless you contact the assessment provider to say you do not want this.
  3. The decision. DWP decides whether you are fit for work, have limited capability for work (LCW), or have limited capability for work and work-related activity (LCWRA).

The physical activities that often matter with arthritis

The WCA is a points-based test. The physical activities are set out in law in Schedule 6 of the Universal Credit Regulations 2013. You meet the LCW test if you score at least 15 points. The physical activities include:

ActivityWhat it looks at (summarised)Arthritis examples
1. MobilisingHow far you can move (for example 50, 100 or 200 metres) on level ground, with any aid you normally use, without stopping to avoid significant discomfort or exhaustion, and whether you can do it repeatedlyHip, knee or foot pain; fatigue
2. Standing and sittingWhether you can stay at a work station, standing, sitting or a mix, for more than 30 minutes or an hour before needing to move awayBack, hip and knee pain; stiffness
3. ReachingWhether you can raise either arm to a top pocket, to the top of your head or above head heightShoulder arthritis
4. Picking up and movingWhether you can pick up and move a half-litre or litre carton of liquid, or a light but bulky object such as an empty boxHand, wrist, elbow and shoulder problems
5. Manual dexterityWhether you can press a button, turn pages, pick up a £1 coin, use a pen or use a suitable keyboard or mouseHand arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis

The other activities cover things like communication, continence and mental, cognitive and intellectual function. You can read the exact wording on legislation.gov.uk.

Tips for the questionnaire

  • Focus on reliability. Can you do the activity repeatedly, without significant discomfort or exhaustion, and in a reasonable time? Explain what happens if you try.
  • Describe bad days and flares, how often they happen and how long they last. Do not describe your best day as if it is normal.
  • Include after-effects. If walking to the shop means you need to lie down for two hours, say so.
  • Mention aids such as walking sticks or adapted cutlery, and how much they help.
  • Send evidence that describes your function, not just your diagnosis: letters from your rheumatologist, physiotherapist or occupational therapist, and your medication list.
  • Keep a copy of everything you send, and note the date.

Our PIP evidence diary is designed for PIP, but the same approach of recording real days works well for the WCA.

Step 3: What the decision means

OutcomeWhat it means for Universal Credit
Fit for workYou agree to look for work suitable for your health. You get the standard allowance based on your circumstances.
Limited capability for work (LCW): need to prepare for work in the futureYour work coach agrees steps to prepare for work, such as writing a CV. You do not need new fit notes. There is usually no extra money unless your claim started before 3 April 2017.
Limited capability for work and work-related activity (LCWRA)You do not need to look for or prepare for work. You may get an extra monthly amount on top of your standard allowance.

For New Style ESA, the groups are called the work-related activity group (regular interviews with a work coach) and the support group (no interviews, and no sanctions). New Style ESA lasts 365 days in the work-related activity group. There is no time limit in the support group.

How much: the LCWRA changes from 6 April 2026

The Universal Credit Act 2025 changed the LCWRA extra amount from 6 April 2026 in England, Scotland and Wales. It now has two rates. On 10 October 2026, GOV.UK showed:

  • £429.80 a month if you have a severe health condition or disability that is unlikely to change, or you are nearing the end of life
  • £217.26 a month if your condition is assessed as less severe or may improve over time

You get the higher amount if you told DWP about your health condition before 6 April 2026, were already getting LCWRA before then, or had the ESA support group before then and continue to get it until you claim Universal Credit. You also get it at any time if you have a severe, lifelong condition or are nearing the end of life.

GOV.UK says you are treated as having a severe, lifelong condition if it means you cannot work, will last your whole life, will not get better and is officially diagnosed by a health professional. A health professional reviews your evidence as part of the WCA.

For New Style ESA, GOV.UK showed up to £95.55 a week in the work-related activity group and up to £145.90 a week in the support group, with an assessment rate for the first 13 weeks. For all current figures, see GOV.UK: what you'll get and GOV.UK: ESA.

If you live with your partner and you both have LCWRA, you only get one extra amount. You also cannot get the Universal Credit carer element as well as LCWRA.

Working while claiming

  • Universal Credit: you can work if you feel able to, even with LCW or LCWRA. If you have LCW or LCWRA, you can earn up to a certain amount (the work allowance) before your payment is affected. If you start working, you will not usually need another assessment unless your health changes.
  • ESA: you can usually work while claiming if you work less than 16 hours a week and earn no more than £203.50 a week (checked 10 October 2026). Fill in the ESA permitted work form first.

If arthritis is making work harder rather than impossible, look at Access to Work and reasonable adjustments too.

If you disagree with a decision

  1. Ask for mandatory reconsideration. You usually need to ask DWP to look at the decision again first, normally within one month of the date on your decision letter.
  2. Appeal to the tribunal. If you still disagree, appeal to the independent Social Security and Child Support Tribunal within one month of your mandatory reconsideration notice.

Many of the tips in our PIP appeal guide apply to WCA challenges too: go back through the descriptors and show which ones apply and why.

Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

  • Scotland and Wales: Universal Credit, ESA and the WCA follow the rules above.
  • Northern Ireland: Universal Credit and ESA are run by the Department for Communities. The process is similar but contact details, questionnaires and some details differ. Check nidirect. The April 2026 LCWRA guidance quoted above says it applies to England, Scotland and Wales.

Free, independent advice

Citizens Advice, Turn2us (including its benefits calculator), Scope and Disability Rights UK all offer free information. In Northern Ireland, Advice NI can help. We are not connected to these organisations. A welfare rights adviser can be especially useful before a WCA or an appeal.

When to get medical help

If your arthritis is getting worse, or you are struggling to cope, speak to your GP or rheumatology team. Treatment might need adjusting, and a clear record of how your condition affects you can also support your claim. If money worries are affecting your mental health, tell your GP. If you are in crisis, call NHS 111 (option 2 for mental health in England), or Samaritans on 116 123.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get Universal Credit for arthritis?

Universal Credit depends on your household income, savings and circumstances, not your diagnosis. If arthritis limits your capability to work, you can report it, and a WCA may decide whether you get extra support.

What is the difference between LCW and LCWRA?

LCW means you have limited capability for work now and need to prepare for work in the future. LCWRA means you do not need to look for or prepare for work, and you may get an extra monthly amount.

Can I claim ESA and Universal Credit at the same time?

Yes, you may be able to. Your Universal Credit is reduced by the New Style ESA you get, and you only have one WCA.

Do I need fit notes while waiting for my WCA?

Yes. Keep getting fit notes and providing the details until you have been sent your assessment decision.

Can I get PIP as well?

Yes. PIP is separate and is not means-tested. Getting PIP does not mean you will get LCWRA, or the other way round, because the tests are different.

Does the April 2026 change affect me if I already get LCWRA?

GOV.UK says the changes do not affect you if you have been getting LCWRA since before 6 April 2026.

How long do I have to challenge a decision?

Usually one month from the date on your decision letter to ask for mandatory reconsideration, and one month from the mandatory reconsideration notice to appeal.

article.title: University With Arthritis: Disability Support and DSA
article.excerpt: Disabled Students’ Allowance can help students with arthritis access tailored university support, including specialist equipment, non-medical helpers.
article.content:
Quick answer: Disabled Students’ Allowance can help students with arthritis access tailored university support, including specialist equipment, non-medical helpers and academic adjustments. The article advises applying early, contacting disability services, tracking symptoms, maintaining gentle movement and self-care, and involving support networks. It also recommends speaking to a GP, physiotherapist or rheumatologist if symptoms worsen or affect study.

Overview

The Disabled Students' Allowance opens doors most students miss.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews and clinical guidelines consistently highlight the positive impact of appropriate support for students with long-term health conditions, including arthritis. It is generally thought that tailored adjustments and financial aid can significantly improve academic attainment, reduce dropout rates, and enhance overall university experience.

Randomised controlled trials and observational studies have demonstrated that early identification of needs and proactive provision of disability support services are key. This approach helps students manage their conditions effectively alongside their studies, leading to better mental wellbeing and a smoother transition into their chosen careers post-graduation.

The evidence base strongly supports a personalised approach, acknowledging that the specific requirements of students with arthritis can vary widely. Effective support systems are often multi-faceted, combining financial assistance for specialist equipment or non-medical helpers with academic adjustments like extended deadlines or alternative examination formats.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Not applying for support early enough: Apply for the Disabled Students' Allowance (DSA) as soon as you accept your university place.
  • Assuming your university already knows your needs: Proactively communicate with the disability support team to discuss your specific arthritis symptoms and requirements.
  • Hiding your struggles from family or friends: Involve your support network so they can help you navigate challenges and advocate for your needs.
  • Neglecting self-care amidst studies: Prioritise rest, balanced nutrition, and gentle movement to manage your arthritis symptoms alongside your academic commitments.
  • Underestimating the benefits of assistive technology: Explore ergonomic equipment or dictation software that could significantly ease your workload and reduce discomfort.

When to Speak to a Clinician

Staying on top of your health while studying is crucial. If you notice significant changes in your arthritis or experience new symptoms that affect your ability to study or carry out daily activities, it’s important to contact your general practitioner, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. They can assess your situation and make any necessary adjustments to your treatment plan or provide additional support.

  • Sudden increase in joint pain or swelling that doesn't settle.
  • New or worsening fatigue that impacts your ability to concentrate.
  • Persistent stiffness, especially in the mornings, lasting longer than 30 minutes.
  • Difficulty performing tasks essential for studying, like writing or typing.
  • Signs of infection around a joint (redness, warmth, severe tenderness).

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get support for more than one health condition?

Yes, the Disabled Students' Allowance (DSA) can cover support for multiple eligible health conditions, including arthritis, if they impact your ability to study. You will typically be assessed for all your conditions simultaneously.

What if my symptoms change during my course?

If your arthritis symptoms worsen or change significantly during your university course, you can request a review of your Disabled Students' Allowance support. Contact your university's disability services team; they can guide you through the process of reappraising your needs.

Does applying for DSA affect my student finance?

No, applying for or receiving the Disabled Students' Allowance does not affect any other student finance you receive, such as student loans or grants. DSA is provided in addition to these and is specifically for costs related to your disability.

Practical next steps for University With Arthritis: Disability Support and DSA

If you came here about University With Arthritis: Disability Support and DSA, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Finding people who understand

Local arthritis groups, hospital patient panels and moderated online communities can reduce isolation. Ask your rheumatology nurse, library, or council adult social care pages for current lists. Choose spaces that feel practical and kind; leave any that push unproven cures or shame medication use.

Mood, sleep and joint symptoms

Pain, poor sleep and low mood often reinforce each other. Protect a regular bedtime, limit late caffeine, and use wind-down habits you can keep on flare days. If worry about pain is growing, ask your GP about NHS talking therapies or local peer support — mood care is part of joint care, not an optional extra.

Quick questions about University With Arthritis Disability

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

article.title: UTIs and sudden confusion with arthritis: signs in older people and who to call (UK guide)
article.excerpt: NHS UTI signs in older or frail people, when sudden confusion means 999, when to call NHS 111, methotrexate and antibiotics, and easier toilet trips.
article.content:
In older or frail people, a urine infection (UTI) does not always cause the usual burning or needing to pee often. The NHS says it can show up as new agitation or confusion, leaking more urine than usual or new shivering. Anyone who suddenly becomes confused needs 999 or A&E. If you are 65 or over, have a weakened immune system from arthritis medicines or have kidney pain, ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111.

This guide is for people with arthritis and the family members and carers who notice when something is not right. It covers the signs to look out for, who to call, how arthritis can make UTIs more likely, and the medicines questions to ask. It does not replace a clinical assessment: confusion has many causes, and a UTI should not be assumed.

Signs of a UTI

The NHS lists the usual symptoms as:

  • pain or burning when peeing
  • needing to pee more often, more urgently or more at night
  • cloudy pee or blood in your pee
  • pain low in the tummy, or in the back just under the ribs
  • a high temperature, feeling hot or cold and shivery, or a very low temperature below 36C
  • feeling tired or weak

In older, frail people, people with memory problems such as dementia and people with a catheter, the NHS says a UTI may also cause:

  • changes in behaviour, such as acting agitated or confused (delirium)
  • leaking pee that is worse than usual
  • new shivering or shaking (rigors)

Dark or smelly pee on its own is often a sign of not drinking enough, not an infection.

Sudden confusion is an emergency

Call 999 or go to A&E if someone suddenly becomes confused, drowsy or has difficulty speaking. The NHS says many causes of sudden confusion, including infection, stroke, low blood sugar, a head injury and some medicines, need to be assessed straight away. Do not drive them to A&E yourself; ask someone else to drive or call 999. Take their medicines, or a list, and any steroid card.

While you wait, the NHS suggests you stay with them, tell them who you are and where they are, use short simple sentences, avoid asking lots of questions and only stop them moving around if they are in danger. Signs of sepsis, such as fast breathing, blotchy or blue skin and a rash that does not fade, also need 999.

When to get an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if you think you or someone you care for has a UTI and any of these apply:

  • you are 65 or older
  • you are a man
  • you have a weakened immune system, which can include steroids, methotrexate, biologics or JAK inhibitors
  • you have diabetes, use a catheter or are pregnant
  • you have a very high or low temperature, or shivers
  • you have pain in the back just under the ribs, or blood in your pee
  • symptoms get worse quickly or do not improve within 48 hours
  • you keep getting UTIs (2 in 6 months or 3 in 12 months)

The NHS says some of these can be signs of a kidney infection, which can lead to sepsis if it is not treated. Women aged 16 to 64 who are not pregnant can usually see a pharmacist first.

Arthritis medicines and UTI treatment

  • Do not stop, skip or pause arthritis medicines yourself. If you take methotrexate, biologics, JAK inhibitors or steroids, ask your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology advice line what to do while you have an infection
  • Never stop steroid tablets suddenly. If you carry a steroid card, show it. See our steroid emergency card guide
  • Methotrexate and antibiotics: the NHS lists trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole among the medicines that affect methotrexate, and asks you to show your methotrexate card. Always tell the prescriber or pharmacist you take methotrexate before you start an antibiotic
  • Anti-inflammatory painkillers: if you are dehydrated or unwell, ask a pharmacist before taking ibuprofen or similar tablets. The NHS suggests paracetamol for UTI pain and temperature. Our painkillers guide explains why
  • Take the whole antibiotic course you are prescribed, even if you feel better

Why arthritis can make UTIs more likely

Some links are practical rather than medical. Painful hips, knees or hands can make getting to the toilet slow or hard, so people sometimes drink less or hold on longer. Reduced movement can lead to constipation, and difficulty wiping or managing pads can make hygiene harder. All of these are worth tackling:

  • drink enough so your pee is pale through the day, spread out rather than all at once. A jug or bottle within easy reach helps
  • do not hold on when you feel the urge, and take your time to empty your bladder fully
  • wipe from front to back, and change pads promptly
  • ask your GP for an occupational therapy assessment for a raised toilet seat, grab rails, a commode or bottle at night, or wiping aids
  • plan night-time toilet trips safely: a night light, clear path and walking aid by the bed. Our falls prevention guide has more
  • if you take warfarin, the NHS says avoid cranberry products

After a UTI: recovering strength

An infection, especially with confusion, can leave someone weaker and less steady for days or weeks. Restart usual movement gently, keep eating and drinking regularly, and ask for physio or a falls service if walking has become harder. If confusion does not clear as the infection settles, tell the GP. NICE guidance on delirium (CG103) highlights that it can last and that it needs follow-up. Carers can ask for a carer's assessment for extra support.

Frequently asked questions

Is every bout of confusion in an older person a UTI?

No. The NHS lists many causes, including other infections such as a chest infection, stroke, low blood sugar, a head injury and medicines. That is why sudden confusion needs a proper assessment. Our chest infection guide covers another common winter cause.

Do cranberry drinks treat a UTI?

The NHS says there is no evidence that cranberry products ease symptoms or treat a UTI once it has started, though they may help some people prevent them. They can contain a lot of sugar.

Can I prepare for this in winter?

Yes. Write down your medicines, who to call and what to do on a sick day. Our winter viruses guide and printable flare action plan help you plan ahead.

The NHS says it can show up as new agitation or confusion, leaking more urine than usual or new shivering. Anyone who suddenly becomes confused needs 999 or A&E. If you are 65 or over, have a weakened immune system from arthritis medicines or have kidney pain, ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111.

faqs.q: Is every bout of confusion in an older person a UTI?
faqs.a: No. The NHS lists many causes, including other infections such as a chest infection, stroke, low blood sugar, a head injury and medicines. That is why sudden confusion needs a proper assessment. Our chest infection guide covers another common winter cause.

faqs.q: Do cranberry drinks treat a UTI?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no evidence that cranberry products ease symptoms or treat a UTI once it has started, though they may help some people prevent them. They can contain a lot of sugar.

faqs.q: Can I prepare for this in winter?
faqs.a: Yes. Write down your medicines, who to call and what to do on a sick day. Our winter viruses guide and printable flare action plan help you plan ahead.

article.title: Vaccines When You Take DMARDs or Biologics: A UK Guide
article.excerpt: Arthritis medicines that calm the immune system make vaccines more important. This guide explains which vaccines are recommended, which live vaccines to avoid, timing and how to book in the UK.
article.content:
Quick answer: If you take DMARDs, biologics, JAK inhibitors or steroids, most non-live vaccines, such as flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal and the non-live shingles vaccine, are safe and recommended because infections can hit harder. Live vaccines may need to be avoided or carefully timed. Ask your rheumatology team for advice before any vaccine, and never pause or change your arthritis medicines without their advice.

Why vaccines matter more on arthritis medicines

Many arthritis medicines work by calming the immune system. That helps control inflammation, but it can also make it harder for your body to fight some infections. Infections such as flu, pneumonia, COVID-19 and shingles may be more likely or more serious. Vaccines are one of the simplest ways to lower that risk. Some inflammatory conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, can also raise infection risk on their own.

The medicines this guide applies to include methotrexate, leflunomide, azathioprine, mycophenolate, biologics (such as anti-TNF medicines, rituximab, tocilizumab and others), JAK inhibitors and steroid tablets. Hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine on their own are usually considered to have little effect on the immune system, but check with your team, especially if you take them with other medicines.

Live and non-live vaccines: the key difference

Vaccines fall into two broad groups.

  • Non-live (inactivated) vaccines contain no living germs. They cannot cause the infection they protect against, so they are safe for people with a weakened immune system. They may work slightly less well if your immune system is suppressed, but they still give valuable protection.
  • Live vaccines contain a weakened form of the germ. In people whose immune systems are significantly suppressed, there is a small risk the weakened germ could cause illness. Live vaccines are therefore often avoided or given only after specialist advice.

Examples of live vaccines include MMR (measles, mumps and rubella), chickenpox, yellow fever, BCG (for TB), oral typhoid and the nasal spray flu vaccine given to children. Whether you can have a live vaccine depends on which medicines you take and how strongly they affect your immune system, so always ask your rheumatology team first.

Vaccines usually recommended

The NHS offers several vaccines to people whose immune system is weakened by a condition or treatment. Eligibility rules are reviewed regularly, so check the NHS website or ask your GP practice for the current offer.

Flu

The injected flu vaccine is offered free every autumn to people with a weakened immune system due to treatment, and to many people with long-term conditions. It is not live. Having it every year is important because flu strains change. Close household contacts of people with weakened immune systems may also be eligible, which adds another layer of protection. Our flu jab guide has more.

COVID-19

COVID-19 vaccines used in the UK are not live. People with weakened immune systems have been included in seasonal booster programmes. Check the NHS website each season to see whether you are eligible and how to book.

Pneumococcal (pneumonia)

The pneumococcal vaccine helps protect against a common cause of pneumonia, meningitis and blood infections. It is not live. It is offered to people with weakened immune systems and to everyone from a certain age. Some people may need more than one dose, so ask your GP practice.

Shingles

The shingles vaccine now used by the NHS, Shingrix, is not live, so it is suitable for people taking immune-suppressing medicines. People with a severely weakened immune system can be offered it at a younger age than the general population. Shingles can be very painful and can cause long-lasting nerve pain, so it is worth asking about. See our shingles vaccine guide.

RSV and others

An RSV vaccine, which protects against a virus that can cause serious chest infections, is offered to older adults in certain age groups. Other vaccines, such as hepatitis B, may be recommended depending on your circumstances. Your GP practice can tell you what you are due.

Timing: before, during and after starting treatment

  • Before you start a new medicine is often the ideal time to catch up on vaccines, especially any live vaccines, which may need to be given a few weeks before immune-suppressing treatment begins. Ask about this at the appointment where a new medicine is discussed.
  • Non-live vaccines can usually be given while you continue your arthritis treatment. Your team may suggest timing a vaccine around certain medicines so it works better. For example, vaccines tend to work best before a rituximab infusion rather than shortly after one. Only adjust medicine timing if your own team advises it.
  • If you are unwell with a fever, vaccines are usually postponed until you are better.

Do not stop, pause or change the dose of your arthritis medicines for a vaccine unless your rheumatology team has told you to.

Travel vaccines

If you are travelling abroad, see a travel clinic or your GP practice at least six to eight weeks before you go, and tell them about all your medicines. Some destinations need vaccines, such as yellow fever, that are live and may not be suitable. If you cannot have a required vaccine, you may be given an exemption letter, and you may need to reconsider some destinations. Our guide to travelling with arthritis covers medicines, insurance and planning.

Family, grandchildren and people you live with

It is usually helpful for the people you live with to be fully vaccinated, as this reduces the chance of infections being brought into the home. Most routine childhood vaccines are fine for your household to have. After a baby has the rotavirus vaccine, which is live and given by mouth, the virus can be passed in nappies for a short time, so wash your hands well after nappy changes or ask someone else to do them if you are significantly immunosuppressed. If you have questions about a specific vaccine a family member is due, ask your GP or practice nurse.

Practical tips

  • Keep a list of your medicines on your phone to show at vaccine appointments.
  • Tell the person giving the vaccine about your arthritis medicines, especially if a live vaccine is mentioned.
  • Record which vaccines you have had and when.
  • Mild soreness, tiredness or aches for a day or two after a vaccine are common and usually settle. Seek advice if you feel very unwell afterwards.
  • Carry on with everyday infection precautions, such as hand washing, as vaccines do not give complete protection.

Frequently asked questions

Can I have the flu jab if I take methotrexate?

Yes. The injected flu vaccine is not live and is recommended every year for people taking methotrexate. Ask your team whether they have any timing advice, and do not change your methotrexate yourself.

Which vaccines should I avoid on biologics?

Live vaccines, such as yellow fever, MMR, chickenpox, BCG and oral typhoid, are usually avoided while taking biologics unless a specialist advises otherwise. Non-live vaccines are generally safe.

Can I have the shingles vaccine on a JAK inhibitor?

The non-live shingles vaccine used by the NHS is suitable for people on JAK inhibitors and other immune-suppressing medicines. Ask your GP practice or rheumatology team about eligibility.

Will vaccines work if my immune system is suppressed?

They may give a slightly weaker response, but they still offer important protection. That is one reason why timing and booster doses can matter.

Can my grandchildren have their live vaccines?

Most childhood vaccines are fine. Wash your hands carefully after nappy changes for a short time after a baby has the rotavirus vaccine, and ask your GP if you are unsure.

Should I stop my arthritis medicine before a vaccine?

Not unless your rheumatology team specifically advises it. Stopping medicines can cause a flare.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Vaccinations
  • NHS: Flu vaccine
  • NHS: Shingles vaccine
  • UKHSA: Immunisation against infectious disease (the Green Book)

This guide is for general education and is not a substitute for personal medical advice. Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.

article.title: Vision, falls and arthritis in frail adults (UK)
article.excerpt: How eyesight and hearing changes add to falls risk with arthritis and frailty, free NHS eye tests, lighting, and practical steps to stay steady at home.
article.content:
Seeing clearly helps you judge steps, kerbs and obstacles. When arthritis already makes moving harder, poor vision adds to falls risk.

This guide explains how vision and hearing affect falls and what can help. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

How vision affects falls

  • Blurred vision or cataracts make hazards harder to see.
  • Bifocal or varifocal glasses can make steps hard to judge.
  • Changes in light can be hard to adjust to.
  • Reduced side vision can make you miss obstacles.

Practical steps

  • Have regular eye tests. They are free on the NHS for people aged 60 and over.
  • Keep glasses clean and well-fitting.
  • Consider single-vision glasses for walking outside.
  • Improve lighting, including night lights.
  • Mark step edges with contrasting colours.

Hearing and balance

Hearing loss is linked to a higher risk of falls, and inner ear problems can affect balance. Ask your GP about a hearing test if you are having difficulty hearing, and seek advice about dizziness.

Getting help

NICE recommends that falls assessments include checking vision. Ask your GP about a falls assessment if you have fallen or feel unsteady.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if you have sudden loss of vision, a drooping face, arm weakness or slurred speech.
  • Get urgent help from NHS 111 or an eye service for sudden eye pain, flashes, new floaters or a shadow in your vision.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

How often should I have an eye test?

Usually every two years, or as your optometrist advises.

Can cataract surgery reduce falls?

Treating cataracts can improve vision. Ask your optometrist or GP.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Free NHS eye tests and optical vouchers
  • NHS: Hearing loss
  • NICE NG249: Falls — assessment and prevention in older people
  • NHS: Falls

article.title: Vitamin D and falls with arthritis: what it can and cannot do (UK guide)
article.excerpt: Vitamin D supports bones and muscles but is not proven to prevent falls on its own. NHS 10 microgram advice, who needs it all year and what helps (UK).
article.content:
Vitamin D helps keep bones and muscles healthy, and the NHS says most adults should consider a daily 10 microgram supplement in autumn and winter — and all year if you are frail, housebound or live in a care home. But NICE says there is not enough evidence that vitamin D on its own lowers the risk of falls. What does help is strength and balance exercise, a medicines review, eyesight checks and a safer home. If you have fallen, see a GP, and ask about your bones too, especially if you broke a bone in a minor fall.

This page answers one question: does vitamin D help with falls? For the full winter guide — who should take it, food sources and safe limits — see our vitamin D in autumn and winter guide. For what the evidence says about vitamin D and arthritis itself, see vitamin D and arthritis. For the full falls checklist, use our falls prevention guide.

What vitamin D does — and what it does not do

The NHS explains that vitamin D helps control the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body, which are needed to keep bones, teeth and muscles healthy. A lack of vitamin D can lead to bone pain caused by a condition called osteomalacia in adults.

That makes vitamin D part of looking after your bones and muscles. It does not make it a falls treatment. NICE falls guidance (NG249) says that although there is insufficient evidence to support taking vitamin D supplements specifically to lower the risk of falls, people should be encouraged to follow NHS advice on vitamin D to maintain bone and muscle health. So: take it if NHS advice applies to you, but do not rely on it to keep you on your feet.

Vitamin D is not a treatment for osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis either. It will not replace your prescribed medicines, exercise or physiotherapy.

NHS vitamin D advice in plain words

  • Autumn and winter: between October and early March we do not make enough vitamin D from sunlight, so the NHS says everyone should consider a daily supplement containing 10 micrograms
  • All year round: the NHS advises a daily 10 microgram supplement throughout the year if you are not often outdoors (for example, if you are frail or housebound), live in a care home, or usually cover most of your skin outdoors. People with dark skin, for example from an African, African-Caribbean or south Asian background, should also consider taking it all year
  • Do not take too much: the NHS says do not take more than 100 micrograms (4,000 IU) a day, as taking too much over a long time can cause too much calcium to build up in the body, which can weaken the bones and damage the kidneys and the heart
  • If a doctor prescribed vitamin D: follow their instructions and do not add a shop-bought supplement on top without asking your pharmacist
  • If you have other health conditions: some people cannot safely take as much vitamin D. If you have kidney problems or take several medicines, check with your GP or pharmacist first

Food helps but is rarely enough on its own: oily fish, egg yolks, red meat and fortified foods such as some breakfast cereals and fat spreads all contain some vitamin D.

What actually lowers your risk of falling

The NHS says a GP can check your balance and may refer you to a falls service. Help from a falls service may include checking for problems such as muscle weakness, weak bones or eyesight problems, strength and balance training, checking your home is safe, and reviewing your medicines. In some areas you can refer yourself.

  • Strength and balance exercise. The NHS says adults aged 65 and over should do activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week. Start with our balance training guide or tai chi for balance
  • A medicines review. Some tablets cause dizziness or drowsiness, especially in combination. Ask for a medication review, and see sleeping tablets and night falls. Do not stop prescribed medicines yourself
  • Eyes, ears and feet. Regular eye tests, a hearing check and well-fitting shoes with good grip
  • A safer home. NICE recommends offering a home hazard assessment to people at risk. Clear clutter and loose rugs, light the route to the toilet at night, and ask about grab rails
  • Winter extras. Icy pavements and dark evenings add risk — see our ice and snow guide

If you have already fallen and feel shaky about going out, our guide to rebuilding confidence after a fall covers a step-by-step return to walking.

Bones: the other half of the falls conversation

Falls matter more when bones are fragile. The NHS says osteoporosis develops slowly over several years and is often only diagnosed when a fall or sudden impact causes a bone to break. The most common breaks are the wrist, hip and spinal bones.

Ask your GP about your bone health if any of these apply:

  • you broke a bone after a minor fall, such as from standing height
  • you take, or have taken, long-term steroid tablets — see bone protection on steroids
  • you have rheumatoid arthritis, or you have lost height or noticed a more curved upper back

Your GP may estimate your fracture risk and, if needed, arrange a bone density (DEXA) scan. Our bone density and osteoporosis guide explains what to expect. For calcium, the NHS says you should be able to get all you need from a varied and balanced diet — dairy or fortified dairy alternatives, green leafy vegetables and tinned fish with soft bones are good sources.

Questions to take to your GP or pharmacist

  • Should I be taking vitamin D all year, or only in autumn and winter?
  • Is it safe alongside my other medicines and my kidney function?
  • Do any of my medicines make me dizzy, drowsy or unsteady?
  • Could I be referred to a falls service, or can I refer myself here?
  • Do I need a bone health check or a bone density scan?

If you care for someone

  • If they are housebound or rarely go outside, NHS advice is a daily vitamin D supplement all year round — ask their GP or pharmacist
  • In a care home, ask staff whether residents are offered vitamin D all year and whether a falls and medicines review has been done
  • Encourage practice of everyday movements rather than taking over every task, and ask for a carer's assessment for yourself

When to get urgent help

  • Call 999 if someone has fallen and cannot get up, or may have hurt their head, neck, back or hip
  • Call 999 for severe hip or groin pain after a fall, being unable to put weight on a leg, or a leg that looks shorter or turned outwards
  • Contact NHS 111 if you have fallen and may be injured or unwell, or you hit your head and take a blood-thinning medicine
  • See a GP after any fall, or if you are worried about your balance or bones

Frequently asked questions

Should I take a high-dose vitamin D to stop me falling?

No. NICE says there is not enough evidence that vitamin D supplements specifically lower the risk of falls, and the NHS warns that taking too much can be harmful. Follow the NHS 10 microgram advice unless a doctor has prescribed something different.

Can I get enough vitamin D from the sun in winter?

Not in the UK. The NHS says that between October and early March we do not make enough vitamin D from sunlight, which is why a supplement is advised in autumn and winter.

Will vitamin D help my arthritis pain?

Vitamin D is not a treatment for arthritis. If your joint pain is getting worse, speak to your GP or rheumatology team. See vitamin D and arthritis for what the evidence does and does not show.

article.excerpt: Vitamin D matters for bones and muscles, and people with arthritis are often in groups who need it most. This guide explains NHS advice (10 micrograms a day), who should take it all year, what the research shows for osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, safe limits, testing, and when to speak to your GP or pharmacist.
article.content:
Quick answer: The NHS advises everyone in the UK to consider a daily 10 microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter, and all year round if you are rarely outdoors, live in a care home, cover most of your skin or have dark skin. Vitamin D is important for bones and muscles, but trials have not shown that it treats osteoarthritis pain. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against NHS: Vitamin D, the BDA vitamin D food fact sheet and published trials listed below.

Vitamin D is one of the few supplements that UK health advice actually recommends for most people, at least for part of the year. It is also surrounded by bold claims online, from "cures joint pain" to "everyone needs a high dose". This guide sets out what the NHS advises, what the research suggests for arthritis specifically, and how to take vitamin D safely alongside your other treatment.

Why vitamin D matters

The NHS explains that vitamin D helps regulate the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body, which are needed to keep bones, teeth and muscles healthy. A lack of vitamin D can cause bone pain from a condition called osteomalacia in adults. The British Dietetic Association (BDA) adds that vitamin D helps maintain muscle strength, which helps prevent falls, and supports the immune system.

For people with arthritis, this matters in a few specific ways:

  • Bone health. Some types of arthritis, and some treatments such as long-term steroid tablets, increase the risk of osteoporosis.
  • Muscle strength and falls. Strong muscles protect painful joints and help you stay steady. See our guide to vitamin D and falls.
  • Less time outdoors. Pain, stiffness and fatigue can mean spending more time indoors, which reduces the vitamin D your skin makes.
  • Aches that overlap. Osteomalacia can cause bone pain and muscle weakness that can be mistaken for, or add to, arthritis symptoms.

How much do you need?

The NHS says children from the age of 1 and adults need Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.. This is the same as 400 international units (IU)Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

WhoNHS advice

Adults who are not often outdoors, for example frail or houseboundSpeak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

People with dark skin, for example of African, African-Caribbean or south Asian backgroundSpeak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

From about late March or early April to the end of September, the NHS says most people can make all the vitamin D they need from sunlight on their skin. Between October and early March, the sun is not strong enough in the UK.

Food and sunlight

Vitamin D is found in a small number of foods. The NHS lists:

  • oily fish, such as salmon, sardines, trout, herring and mackerel
  • red meat
  • egg yolks
  • fortified foods, such as some fat spreads and breakfast cereals
  • liver (avoid if you are pregnant)

The BDA adds some mushrooms and fortified unsweetened soya drinks. But both the NHS and BDA say it is difficult to get enough vitamin D from food alone. In the UK, cows' milk is generally not fortified, so it is not a good source.

Eating oily fish twice a week helps, and also gives you omega-3 fats, which are part of an anti-inflammatory style of eating. The NHS advises at least 2 portions of fish a week, 1 of which should be oily.

In summer, short periods of sun on bare skin help your body make vitamin D. You cannot overdose on vitamin D from sunlight, but the NHS reminds you to cover up or protect your skin to reduce the risk of sunburn and skin cancer. Some medicines can make your skin more sensitive to the sun, so check your medicine leaflets and ask your pharmacist if you are unsure.

What the research suggests for arthritis

This is where claims online often go further than the evidence.

Osteoarthritis

A two-year randomised trial published in JAMA in 2016 (Jin and colleagues) gave vitamin D or a placebo to people with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis who had low vitamin D levels. Vitamin D did not make a significant difference to knee cartilage volume measured on MRI or to knee pain scores. The authors concluded that the results do not support vitamin D supplements to prevent cartilage loss or improve knee pain in osteoarthritis.

So vitamin D is important for your bones and muscles in general, but it should not be expected to ease osteoarthritis pain.

Rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmune conditions

Low vitamin D levels are often reported in people with inflammatory arthritis, but that does not prove that low vitamin D causes it, or that supplements treat it. The large VITAL trial in the United States (Hahn and colleagues, BMJ 2022) found that five years of vitamin D supplements, with or without omega-3, reduced the number of new autoimmune disease diagnoses in older adults compared with placebo. This was a prevention study in people without autoimmune disease, so it does not show that vitamin D treats rheumatoid arthritis once you have it.

NICE does not recommend vitamin D as a treatment for rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis. Your rheumatology team may still check or recommend it to protect your bones.

Summary

QuestionWhat the evidence says
Do I need vitamin D for healthy bones and muscles?Yes. NHS advice applies to people with arthritis too
Will vitamin D ease osteoarthritis pain?A good-quality trial found no benefit for knee pain
Will vitamin D treat rheumatoid arthritis?Not shown. One large trial suggests it may help prevent autoimmune disease, but that is different from treatment
Is a higher dose better?No. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Taking too much

The NHS warns that taking too much vitamin D over a long period can cause too much calcium to build up in the body (hypercalcaemia), which can weaken bones and damage the kidneys and heart.

  • Adults, including older people and those who are pregnant or breastfeeding, should Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. unless a doctor advises it.
  • Some people have medical conditions that mean they cannot safely take as much. If in doubt, ask your doctor.
  • If your doctor has prescribed a different dose, for example a short high-dose course for deficiency, follow their advice.

Check the labels of everything you take. Vitamin D can be in multivitamins, calcium tablets, fish liver oils and "joint" supplements, and amounts can add up. Fish liver oil (such as cod liver oil) also contains vitamin A, which can be harmful in large amounts and should be avoided in pregnancy.

Vitamin D and arthritis medicines

  • Steroid tablets such as prednisolone, taken for a long time, can weaken bones. Your doctor may prescribe calcium and vitamin D, sometimes with a bone-protecting medicine. Take what is prescribed rather than adding your own supplement on top, unless your doctor agrees.
  • Prescribed calcium and vitamin D tablets already contain vitamin D. You usually do not need an extra over-the-counter vitamin D supplement as well. Ask your pharmacist.
  • Kidney disease, sarcoidosis or high calcium levels can change how much vitamin D is safe. Check with your doctor before taking a supplement.
  • Methotrexate: the NHS advises not taking supplements that contain folic acid if you are already taking prescribed folic acid. Some multivitamins with vitamin D also contain folic acid, so check the label.

Tell your doctor or pharmacist about every vitamin and supplement you take, as the NHS advises for many arthritis medicines.

Do I need a blood test?

You do not need a blood test to follow NHS advice on a daily 10 microgram supplement. Your GP may arrange a vitamin D test if you have symptoms that could be due to deficiency, such as bone pain or muscle weakness, if you have osteoporosis or a condition that affects how you absorb nutrients, or before some treatments. If a test shows a deficiency, your doctor will advise on a treatment dose and how long to take it for.

Private home test kits are widely sold. If you use one, discuss the result with your GP or pharmacist rather than starting a high-dose supplement on your own.

Choosing a supplement

  • Dose: Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. Many products contain much more; that is not necessary for most people.
  • Form: most supplements contain vitamin D3. Vitamin D2 and some D3 products are suitable for vegans; check the label.
  • Cost: basic vitamin D supplements from pharmacies and supermarkets are usually inexpensive. You do not need a "joint health" product to get vitamin D.
  • Healthy Start: women and children who qualify for the Healthy Start scheme can get free vitamin supplements containing vitamin D.

A simple plan

  1. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  2. If you rarely go outside, live in a care home, cover most of your skin, or have dark skin, take it all year round.
  3. Eat oily fish and eggs regularly, and choose fortified foods if you like them.
  4. In summer, spend short periods outside when you can, without burning. Even sitting in a garden or by an open window helps more than staying indoors all day.
  5. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  6. Tell your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team what you take.

Pair vitamin D with calcium-rich foods such as milk, yoghurt, cheese, fortified plant drinks, tinned fish with soft bones and green leafy vegetables. Our calcium foods guide has easy ideas. For older adults and people who struggle to get outdoors, see our guide to vitamin D in winter.

When a dietitian can help

If you eat a restricted diet (for example vegan, dairy-free or very low in fish), have a condition that affects absorption such as coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease, or have had weight-loss surgery, ask your GP about a referral to a registered dietitian. They can check whether you are getting enough vitamin D, calcium and other nutrients.

When to get medical help

See your GP if you have bone pain, muscle weakness or aches that are not explained by your arthritis, if you have broken a bone after a minor fall, or if you take long-term steroids and have not had your bone health discussed. Seek medical advice if you take vitamin D supplements and develop symptoms that could suggest high calcium, such as feeling very thirsty, passing a lot of urine, feeling sick, constipation or confusion. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

How much vitamin D should I take with arthritis?

The same as the general NHS advice: 10 micrograms (400 IU) a day in autumn and winter, or all year if you are in an at-risk group. Your doctor may advise a different dose if you have a deficiency or osteoporosis.

Can vitamin D help joint pain?

A good-quality trial in knee osteoarthritis found that vitamin D did not improve knee pain. Correcting a genuine deficiency can ease bone pain and muscle weakness caused by osteomalacia, which is different from arthritis pain.

Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Not for most people. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

Can I take vitamin D with methotrexate?

Vitamin D on its own is not known to be a problem, but some multivitamins contain folic acid. The NHS advises not taking extra folic acid if you are already prescribed it. Check with your pharmacist.

Do I need vitamin D in summer?

Most people can make enough from sunlight between late March or early April and September. If you rarely go outside or cover your skin, the NHS advises taking it all year.

Should I get my vitamin D level tested?

Not routinely. You can follow NHS supplement advice without a test. Your GP may test if you have symptoms of deficiency or certain conditions.

article.title: Vitamin D in autumn and winter with arthritis (UK guide)
article.excerpt: NHS vitamin D advice for October to March: who should take 10 micrograms a day, who needs it all year, safe limits, bones and steroids. UK guide.
article.content:
Quick answer: Between October and early March, the NHS says everyone should consider taking a daily vitamin D supplement of 10 micrograms (400 IU), because UK sunlight is too weak for your skin to make enough. If you are frail or housebound, live in a care home, usually cover your skin outdoors, or have dark skin, consider taking it all year. Vitamin D helps keep bones and muscles healthy but is not a treatment for arthritis itself. Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.

October is when UK sunlight becomes too weak for your skin to make the vitamin D your body needs, and that lasts until about early March. If arthritis already keeps you indoors more, or you are older or living with frailty, winter can leave you short. This guide explains what the NHS advises, who should take vitamin D all year, how to take it safely alongside arthritis medicines, and what vitamin D can and cannot do for your joints.

What the NHS advises this autumn and winter

  • Between October and early March, the NHS says everyone should Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you.
  • From about late March or early April to the end of September, most people can make enough vitamin D from sunlight on their skin, so you may choose not to take a supplement in those months
  • Vitamin D supplements are sold in most pharmacies and supermarkets. A pharmacist can help you choose one and check it fits with your other medicines

Who should consider vitamin D all year round

The NHS advises a daily 10 microgram supplement throughout the year if you:

  • are not often outdoors, for example because you are frail or housebound
  • live in a care home or other institution
  • usually wear clothes that cover most of your skin when outdoors
  • have dark skin, for example if you have an African, African-Caribbean or south Asian background

If painful joints mean you rarely get outside, the first point may apply to you even if you would not call yourself frail.

What vitamin D can and cannot do for arthritis

Vitamin D helps your body control calcium and phosphate, which keep bones, teeth and muscles healthy. A real lack of vitamin D in adults can cause bone pain and muscle weakness (a condition called osteomalacia), which is worth getting checked if your aches feel different from your usual arthritis.

The NHS advice on vitamin D is about bone and muscle health. It is not a treatment for arthritis itself, so keep up your usual treatment, exercise and pain relief plan. NICE guidance for osteoarthritis puts exercise and weight management at the centre of care. Our supplements guide and supplements hub explain the evidence on other products.

Bones, steroids and falls

  • Long-term use of high-dose steroid tablets, and conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, can raise the risk of osteoporosis (thinning bones). If you take steroid tablets long term, ask your GP or rheumatology team whether you need bone protection. Our bone protection on steroids guide explains the questions to ask. Never stop steroid tablets suddenly or change the dose without advice
  • Bones and muscles both matter for falls. Strength and balance exercise helps most; see the exercise hub, our falls prevention guide and vitamin D and falls guide
  • If you have been told you have osteoporosis, our osteoporosis and arthritis guide covers bones and joints together

Taking vitamin D safely

  • Speak to your GP or pharmacist about the right dose for you. More is not better
  • The NHS says adults should not take more than 100 micrograms (4,000 IU) a day, as too much over a long time can raise calcium levels and harm bones, kidneys and the heart
  • Some medical conditions mean you may not be able to safely take as much. If in doubt, ask your GP or pharmacist first
  • If your doctor has prescribed a different dose, for example to treat a low level, follow their advice
  • Check labels so you do not double up. Multivitamins and some calcium tablets already contain vitamin D
  • Tell your pharmacist about any supplements you take alongside arthritis medicines, and do not stop or change prescribed medicines yourself

Food sources of vitamin D

Only a few foods contain vitamin D, which is why food alone is unlikely to be enough in winter. Sources include oily fish such as salmon, sardines, trout, herring and mackerel, red meat, egg yolks, and fortified foods such as some fat spreads and breakfast cereals. Liver also contains it, but avoid liver if you are pregnant. In the UK, cows' milk is generally not a good source. For eating well with arthritis, see the diet hub and our protein and frailty guide.

If you care for someone

If the person you care for is housebound or lives in a care home, the NHS advice is to consider vitamin D all year, not just in winter. Ask their GP or pharmacist if you are unsure, especially if they take several medicines. A carer's assessment can help if shopping and medicines are becoming hard to manage.

When to get help

  • See your GP if you have bone pain, new muscle weakness, or aches that feel different from your usual arthritis
  • See your GP if you have fallen, or you take steroid tablets long term and have never discussed bone health
  • Call 999 after a fall if you cannot get up or put weight on a leg, or you have severe hip or groin pain
  • For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland)

Frequently asked questions

Does vitamin D help arthritis pain?

The NHS recommends vitamin D for healthy bones and muscles, not as a treatment for arthritis. If you have pain that feels new or different, see your GP rather than taking more vitamin D.

Do I need a blood test before taking vitamin D?

The NHS advice to consider 10 micrograms a day in autumn and winter applies to everyone, so it does not depend on a blood test. Your GP may check your level if you have symptoms such as bone pain or you are at higher risk.

Can I take vitamin D with methotrexate or other arthritis medicines?

Ask your pharmacist or rheumatology team, who can check your full list of medicines. Keep taking your prescribed medicines as directed while you check.

article.title: Seated volunteering with arthritis and frailty (UK)
article.excerpt: Volunteering roles that suit arthritis and frailty: seated and home-based options, pacing, telling organisations what you need, and finding local roles.
article.content:
Arthritis and frailty need not stop you contributing.

This guide covers suitable roles. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Seated roles

  • Telephone befriending.
  • Reception or admin.
  • Craft groups.

Telling organisations what helps

  • Shorter shifts.
  • Seating.
  • Accessible venues.

Pacing

Plan rest around volunteering.

Finding roles

Local volunteer centres and charities.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can I volunteer from home?

Yes, some roles are remote.

Will it affect benefits?

Ask an adviser.

  • NHS England: Social prescribing

article.title: Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan
article.excerpt: Walking daily with arthritis is generally safe and recommended, especially when gentle and progressive. Regular, moderate intensity exercise, including.
article.content:
Quick answer: Walking daily with arthritis is generally safe and recommended, especially when gentle and progressive. Regular, moderate intensity exercise, including walking, improves joint function, reduces pain, and boosts overall quality of life. Tailored activity, alongside medication, helps keep muscles strong and supports heart health. Listen to your body and adjust if experiencing pain; consistency is more important than intensity.

Overview

Gentle aerobic activity boosts mood and joint health alongside treatment.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Many studies, including large randomised trials, have consistently shown the benefits of regular, moderate-intensity exercise for people living with inflammatory arthritis. Systematic reviews, which look at many studies together, confirm that staying active can improve joint function, reduce pain, and boost overall quality of life. This is true even for those taking disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs).

The evidence suggests that exercise works best when it's tailored to the individual and includes a mix of aerobic activities, like walking, and strength training. Clinical guidelines from leading rheumatology organisations across the UK strongly recommend incorporating physical activity into the treatment plan from early diagnosis, alongside medication. This combined approach is highlighted as the most effective way to manage long-term conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or psoriatic arthritis.

Regular movement helps to keep muscles strong around affected joints, which can provide better support and reduce pain. It also plays a role in keeping your heart healthy, which is especially important as some types of arthritis can increase the risk of heart problems. The research supports the idea that 'little and often' is key to sustainable benefits.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Doing too much, too soon: Start with short walks and gradually increase your time.
  • Ignoring pain: Differentiate between muscle fatigue and new joint pain; dial back if it's the latter.
  • Wearing unsuitable footwear: Invest in supportive, comfortable shoes that cushion your feet.
  • Not warming up or cooling down: Spend 5 minutes gently preparing and recovering your body.
  • Stopping completely during a flare: Modify your activity, but try to keep moving gently if possible.
  • Becoming discouraged by initial discomfort: Consistency builds stamina and comfort over time.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While walking is generally very beneficial, there are times when you should seek advice from your general practitioner, physiotherapist, or rheumatology team. It's always best to get a professional opinion if you're unsure or worried about new symptoms.

  • Sudden, severe pain that doesn't go away with rest.
  • New, persistent swelling or redness in a joint.
  • Fever, chills, or generally feeling unwell alongside joint symptoms.
  • Rapid loss of movement or function in a joint.
  • If your walking ability significantly worsens despite regular activity.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can walking help reduce the side effects of DMARDs?

Walking itself doesn't directly reduce DMARD side effects. However, regular physical activity can improve overall wellbeing, energy levels, and mood, which can help you cope better with any challenges from your medication. It's important to discuss any medication side effects with your rheumatology team.

How do I know if I'm overdoing it when walking?

A good rule of thumb is that you should still be able to hold a conversation while walking. If you're too breathless to talk, you're likely working too hard. Also, listen to your joints: a little stiffness might be normal, but sharp or increasing pain during or after your walk is a sign to slow down or rest.

Is it safe to walk every day with arthritis?

For most people with arthritis, walking every day is not only safe but highly recommended, provided it's gentle and progressive. Consistency is more important than intensity. If you have active inflammation or are experiencing a flare-up, you might need to adjust your routine and walk for shorter periods or on alternate days.

Practical next steps for Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan

If you came here about Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Quick questions about Walking Minutes While DMARDs

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
