article.title: Choosing Mobility Aids for Arthritis: Sticks, Rollators, Wheelchairs and Scooters (UK)
article.excerpt: A UK guide to choosing mobility aids with arthritis, with no brand rankings: getting assessed, walking sticks, crutches, frames and rollators, NHS wheelchair services, mobility scooter rules from GOV.UK, buying criteria, VAT relief and safety.
article.content:
Quick answer: Get assessed first by a physiotherapist or occupational therapist so you get the right aid at the right height. The NHS can lend some sticks and frames, and wheelchairs come through your local wheelchair service after an assessment. Mobility scooters are not generally available on the NHS. Class 2 scooters go up to 4mph on pavements; class 3 go up to 8mph, can use roads and must be registered with DVLA.

Checked on 11 October 2026 against the NHS guide to walking aids, wheelchairs and mobility scooters and the GOV.UK rules for mobility scooters and powered wheelchairs. Prices quoted are the NHS's published ranges and change over time. We have not tested or reviewed any products, and there are no affiliate links.

A mobility aid can help you stay active, reduce pain, improve balance and keep doing the things that matter, from walking to the shops to a day out with family. Choosing the wrong one, or using the right one at the wrong height, can make things worse. This guide explains the main types of aid, how to get one through the NHS or council, what to look for if you buy, and how to stay safe. It does not rank brands.

Before you choose: get assessed

A physiotherapist or occupational therapist (OT) can assess how you walk, your balance, your strength and your home, and recommend the right type of aid and the right height. The NHS says you can speak to a GP, physiotherapist, occupational therapist or hospital staff about borrowing a walking stick or frame. In many areas you can also refer yourself to NHS community physiotherapy or musculoskeletal (MSK) services.

Getting assessed matters because:

  • the wrong aid can increase strain on other joints, such as wrists, shoulders and hands
  • an aid at the wrong height can affect your posture and make pain worse
  • some aids are better indoors, others outdoors
  • exercise and strength work may be needed alongside the aid, not instead of it

Walking sticks

The NHS says a walking stick can give you extra support, help you balance, give you confidence and make walking less painful.

Getting one

You can borrow some types of walking stick from the NHS, possibly with a small deposit. You can also buy them online or from mobility shops. The NHS gives a price range of £15 to £50.

What to think about

The NHS suggests considering:

  • Height: the stick must be the correct height for you, so ask for advice when you get it. Physiotherapists usually check that your elbow is slightly bent when you hold the handle.
  • Base: whether you need one that stands up on its own, with 3 or 4 feet.
  • Handle: whether it needs to be right- or left-handed. With hand or wrist arthritis, a wider, moulded or padded handle can spread pressure. Ask an OT or physio.
  • Seat: whether you need a seat so you can rest.
  • Steps: whether you need advice on using it on stairs. The NHS says to speak to a physiotherapist.

Which hand?

For a painful hip or knee, physiotherapists usually advise holding a single stick in the hand opposite the painful side. Check with your physiotherapist, as this depends on your situation.

Folding or fixed?

Folding sticks are handy for travel but can be less sturdy. Adjustable sticks are useful while you work out the right height, but check that the locking clip is secure every time.

See our guide to choosing a stick or a frame.

Crutches

Elbow crutches are often used for a short time, for example after surgery or an injury, and are usually provided by the hospital with instructions. Using crutches long-term can put strain on hands, wrists and shoulders, which matters if these are affected by arthritis. Ask your physiotherapist before using them for long periods.

Walking frames and rollators

The NHS says a walking frame gives you more support than a walking stick.

Getting one

You can borrow a frame from the NHS, possibly with a deposit, or your local authority may provide one free after a needs assessment. You can also buy them. The NHS gives a range of £40 to £200.

What to think about

The NHS suggests considering:

  • whether it is the correct height for you
  • whether you only want to use it indoors, where frames without wheels are best
  • whether you are strong enough to lift a frame without wheels
  • whether you want to get out and about, where frames with wheels are better
  • whether you need a seat, basket or tray
  • whether you need to fold it to fit in a car

Extra points for arthritis

  • Brakes: on a rollator, check you can squeeze and lock the brakes comfortably. Some designs need less grip strength than others.
  • Weight: check you can lift it into a car or up a step.
  • Handles: padded or shaped handles may be easier on painful hands.
  • Seat: only sit on a rollator seat with the brakes locked, and never be pushed while sitting on it unless it is designed for that.

Wheelchairs

A wheelchair can help if walking is difficult or you can walk only short distances. Some people use one only for longer trips. See our guide to using a wheelchair for distance.

NHS wheelchair services

The NHS says you need an assessment by your local wheelchair service before you can get an NHS wheelchair. Ask a GP, physiotherapist, OT or hospital staff to refer you, or check whether you can refer yourself by contacting your local wheelchair service or integrated care board (ICB). The service helps you decide if you need a wheelchair and what type.

In England, you may be eligible for a personal wheelchair budget, which lets you pay towards a different type of wheelchair. Our guide to the local wheelchair service explains more. In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, wheelchair services are run by NHS boards and health and social care trusts, and referrals usually come through your GP, physiotherapist or OT.

Borrowing and hiring

The NHS says you can sometimes borrow an NHS wheelchair for a short while, for example after an operation. Red Cross branches often hire wheelchairs weekly, and some shopping centres have a Shopmobility scheme where you can borrow a wheelchair, usually at low cost or free.

Buying

The NHS gives a range from about £150 for a manual wheelchair to around £2,000 for a basic electric wheelchair. The Motability Scheme allows some people to use their mobility benefits to hire or buy an electric wheelchair.

What to think about

  • whether you will push yourself or be pushed. Self-propelling can be hard on arthritic hands and shoulders
  • how often you need it, and whether indoors, outdoors or both
  • comfort, including the cushion and backrest
  • weight and folding, if it needs to go in a car
  • maintenance and repair costs

The NHS advises asking to try different types before you decide.

Mobility scooters and powered wheelchairs

The NHS says mobility scooters can be useful if you struggle to walk, need to travel longer distances, and can get on and off easily. They are not generally available on the NHS. The NHS gives a price range from £500 to more than £5,000. You might get a grant or charity help, and the Motability Scheme can help some people hire or buy one.

What to think about

The NHS suggests considering how often you will use it, whether on roads or pavements, whether it needs to go in a car, where you will store and charge it, maintenance costs, and whether you can steer it. It notes that some scooters have special steering levers if you have arthritis in your hands.

The rules

GOV.UK sets out the rules:

  • Who can use one: you can only drive a mobility scooter or powered wheelchair if you have trouble walking because of an injury, physical disability or medical condition (with a few exceptions, such as taking it for repair).
  • Class 2 vehicles have a maximum speed of 4mph and can be used on pavements and pedestrian areas.
  • Class 3 vehicles have a maximum speed of 8mph, can also be used on the road, and must be registered with DVLA. On the road they need features including lights, indicators, a horn and a rear-view mirror. You cannot use them in bus lanes, cycle lanes or on motorways.
  • On pavements, the maximum speed is 4mph, and you must give way to other people.
  • Eyesight: for class 2 and 3, you should be able to read a car's registration number from 12.3 metres (40 feet).
  • Tax and insurance: you do not pay vehicle tax if it is registered with DVLA as a mobility scooter or powered wheelchair. Insurance is not required for class 2 or 3 but is recommended.

Our guide to mobility scooters has more detail. Driving Mobility centres offer assessments and advice on mobility options, including scooters.

Buying an aid: criteria and red flags

Look for

  • adjustable height that locks securely
  • handles that suit your hands
  • a maximum user weight that is right for you
  • good rubber ferrules (tips) on sticks and frames, which can be replaced when worn
  • the chance to try it before buying
  • clear returns, warranty and servicing terms

Be wary of

  • buying a scooter or powered wheelchair without trying it on the routes you will use
  • pressure selling, especially at home
  • second-hand items without checking brakes, tyres, batteries and frames
  • products that are not adjustable or come in one size only

If you are disabled or have a long-term illness, GOV.UK says you will not be charged VAT on products designed for disabled people for your own use, including wheelchairs. See our guide to choosing arthritis-friendly products for VAT relief and returns rights.

Using your aid safely

  • Check height and fit regularly, especially if your shoes change.
  • Check ferrules and replace them when worn or smooth.
  • Check brakes on rollators and wheelchairs.
  • Clear your home of trip hazards such as loose rugs and trailing wires.
  • Take care in wet or icy weather.
  • Charge batteries as the manufacturer advises.
  • Keep exercising. An aid supports you, but strength and balance work helps you stay mobile. Ask your physiotherapist for exercises.

Getting used to a new aid

  • Practise at home first, then on short, familiar routes.
  • Ask your physiotherapist to show you how to use it on steps, kerbs, slopes and stairs.
  • Expect some aches in your hands, wrists or shoulders at first. Tell your physio if this does not settle.
  • Review your aid if your condition changes, after surgery, or if you are using it more than before.

Travelling with a mobility aid

Plan ahead when you travel. Railway companies offer free Passenger Assist, which you can book in advance. Airlines and airports must provide free assistance for disabled passengers and carry mobility equipment, so tell your airline when you book. Check the size and weight limits for scooters and powered wheelchairs, and the rules for their batteries. Folding sticks and lightweight rollators can make travelling easier. Our guide to flying with arthritis has more detail.

Feeling self-conscious

Many people put off using an aid because they worry about how it looks or feel it means "giving in". An aid that lets you walk further with less pain can help you stay active and independent. You might use one only on bad days or for longer trips. Talk to your physiotherapist or OT about options that suit your lifestyle.

When to get medical help

See your GP or physiotherapist if walking is getting harder, you are falling or nearly falling, or your aid no longer feels right. Get urgent help if you fall and are hurt, cannot get up, or cannot put weight on a leg. Call 999 if you have a serious injury.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get a walking stick on the NHS?

You can borrow some types of walking stick from the NHS. Speak to a GP, physiotherapist, OT or hospital staff. You might pay a small deposit.

How do I get an NHS wheelchair?

You need an assessment by your local wheelchair service. Ask a GP, physio, OT or hospital staff to refer you, or check whether you can refer yourself.

Can I get a mobility scooter on the NHS?

Mobility scooters are not generally available on the NHS. You might get help through the Motability Scheme, a grant or a charity.

Do I need a licence or insurance for a mobility scooter?

Not for class 2 or 3 scooters, although insurance is recommended. Class 3 scooters must be registered with DVLA.

Which hand should I hold my stick in?

For a painful hip or knee, usually the opposite hand. Check with your physiotherapist.

Is a rollator better than a stick?

A frame or rollator gives more support than a stick. Which is best depends on your balance, strength and where you will use it. Get assessed.

Do I pay VAT on a wheelchair?

Not if you are disabled or have a long-term illness and it is for your own use. Confirm this in writing with the supplier.

article.excerpt: Choosing between a walking stick and walking frame with arthritis and frailty: what each offers, getting assessed, correct height and using a frame indoors.
article.content:
The right walking aid can make you safer.

This guide compares sticks and frames. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Sticks

  • Light support.
  • Use in the hand opposite the painful leg.

Frames

  • More support for balance.
  • Wheeled or non-wheeled types.

Using a frame indoors

  • Clear routes and rugs.
  • Check doorways and turning space.
  • Do not carry things in your hands; use a bag or tray on the frame.

Getting assessed

Ask your GP or physiotherapist.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can I buy my own?

Yes, but get advice on height.

What about rollators?

They suit some people outdoors.

article.title: Walking With Arthritis: A Beginner's 8-Week Walking Programme (UK)
article.excerpt: A practical UK walking programme for beginners with arthritis: how to find your starting point, an 8-week plan that builds up safely, the 24-hour pain rule, technique, shoes, poles and sticks, what to do on bad days and during flares, staying motivated and when to get advice.
article.content:
Quick answer: To start walking with arthritis, find the time you can walk comfortably, even 5 minutes, then walk that most days and add a minute or two each week. Use the 24-hour rule: if pain settles by the next day, carry on. Supportive shoes, flat routes, poles or a stick help. Aim to build towards 150 minutes a week.

Walking is one of the simplest, cheapest and most useful things you can do for arthritis. It needs no special equipment, you can start from your front door, and you can adjust it to suit good and bad days. This guide is a beginner's programme: it shows you how to find your starting point, gives you an 8-week plan to build up safely, and explains how to deal with pain, flares and bad weather along the way.

Why walking is good for arthritis

  • It keeps joints moving. Regular movement helps reduce stiffness and keeps joints nourished.
  • It strengthens muscles in the legs and hips that support the knees, hips, ankles and back.
  • It builds fitness. NICE guideline NG226 recommends general aerobic fitness training, alongside strengthening, as part of exercise for osteoarthritis. Walking is the easiest way for most people to do this.
  • It helps with weight, which reduces load on weight-bearing joints.
  • It helps bones, heart, mood and sleep. The NHS says brisk walking counts towards your weekly activity target and benefits heart and lung health.

Walking is not bad for arthritic joints when it is built up gradually. Most people find that the right amount of regular walking reduces pain over time.

Before you start

Most people with arthritis can start walking without seeing a doctor. Speak to your GP or physiotherapist first if you have chest pain, breathlessness or dizziness with activity, have had a recent fall or injury, recent surgery, or a joint that is suddenly hot and swollen.

Find your starting point

On a normal day, walk at a comfortable pace on a flat route until you start to feel your usual pain increase or you feel tired, and note the time. Your starting walk is a little less than this, around two-thirds to three-quarters of that time. For some people this is 3 minutes; for others it is 20. Both are fine starting points. If you use a walking frame or a wheelchair for longer distances, you can still use this plan for the walking you do indoors or with your frame.

The 24-hour rule: how much pain is okay?

Some discomfort during and after walking is normal when you start, and is not a sign of damage. Use this simple guide:

How you feelWhat it meansWhat to do next time
Pain settles within an hour or two, back to normal by the next dayThe right amountKeep going, and build up as planned
Pain or stiffness is still worse the next morning but settles during the dayA little too muchRepeat the same amount, do not add more yet
Pain is worse for more than 24 hours, or the joint swellsToo muchDrop back to the previous week's amount
Sharp pain, the joint gives way or locksStopRest, and get advice if it continues

The 8-week beginner walking programme

Walk on at least 5 days a week. "Base" is your starting walk time. If you can only walk a few minutes at a time, do two or three short walks a day rather than one longer one.

WeekEach walkWalks per weekPace
1Base time5Comfortable, flat route
2Base + 1–2 minutes5Comfortable
3Base + 2–4 minutes5Comfortable
4Same as week 3 (consolidation week)5–6Comfortable; try 1–2 minutes a little brisker
5Week 3 + 2–3 minutes5–6Add a few brisker spells
6Week 5 + 2–3 minutes5–6Brisk for about a third of the walk
7Week 6 + 2–3 minutes5–6Try a gentle slope or varied surface
8Same as week 7, then review5–7Brisk for half the walk if comfortable

Move on to the next week only if the 24-hour rule says you are ready. It is fine to repeat a week, or to take 12 weeks rather than 8.

Example: starting at 6 minutes

Week 1: 6 minutes, 5 days. Week 2: 8 minutes. Week 3: 10 minutes. Week 4: 10 minutes again. Week 5: 12 to 13 minutes. Week 6: 15 minutes. Week 7: 17 to 18 minutes. Week 8: 18 minutes, with some brisk spells. That adds up to around 90 minutes a week, a big step towards the target.

After week 8: keep going

At the end of the programme, look back at your log. If walks feel comfortable and your joints settle by the next day, keep adding a couple of minutes a week until you reach around 30 minutes on most days, or the total that suits you. You can also:

  • add one longer, slower walk at the weekend
  • include gentle hills or a mix of surfaces
  • join a walking group or a Nordic walking class
  • combine walking with a weekly swim, cycle or strength session

If progress has stalled, repeat weeks 6 to 8 rather than starting again. Long-term, what matters most is walking regularly, not walking far.

Where you are heading

The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend that adults build up to at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week, such as brisk walking, plus muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days. Older adults should also include activities to improve balance and flexibility. These are long-term goals. Any increase from where you are now is worthwhile.

What does "brisk" mean?

The NHS describes brisk walking as walking fast enough to raise your heart rate and make you breathe faster, while still being able to talk but not sing. With arthritis, "brisk" may be slower than for others, and that is fine.

Tips for your main joint

JointHelpful tips
KneeShorter steps, flat routes at first, and poles or a stick for hills. Downhill is often harder than uphill, so take it slowly. Strengthen the thigh muscles with sit-to-stands.
HipA stick in the opposite hand can reduce limping. Avoid very long strides. Gentle hip stretches after walking help stiffness.
Foot and ankleCushioned, rocker-soled or stiffer-soled shoes reduce bending at painful joints. Choose smooth surfaces and avoid cobbles at first.
BackStand tall and keep walks regular; many people with back pain find walking eases stiffness. Break up long walks with short standing rests.
Several jointsUse shorter, more frequent walks, consider poles, and try water walking in a pool on bad days.

Try interval walking

Once you can walk for 15 to 20 minutes comfortably, alternating easy and brisker walking can build fitness without much extra time. For example, walk at your easy pace for 3 minutes, then a little faster for 1 minute, and repeat. Keep the brisk spells at a level where you could still talk. If your joints complain the next day, go back to steady walking for a week.

Walking technique

  • Stand tall, look ahead rather than down, and let your arms swing naturally.
  • Take comfortable, even steps; shorter steps are often easier on painful knees and hips.
  • Land gently on your heel and roll through to your toes.
  • Warm up with 2 to 3 minutes of slow walking, and finish with a slower few minutes and gentle calf stretches.

Shoes, poles and other aids

  • Shoes: choose cushioned, supportive shoes with a thick, flexible sole and enough room for your toes. Our guide to the best walking shoes for arthritis explains what to look for.
  • Walking poles: Nordic-style poles can take some load off the knees and hips and help balance. Ask for a quick lesson on technique.
  • Walking stick: hold it in the hand opposite the painful leg. A physiotherapist can check the height.
  • Insoles and knee supports: some people find these helpful, but they are not needed by everyone.
  • Bring: water, a phone, and layers in cold weather.

Choosing routes

  • Start on flat, even paths such as parks, pavements or seafronts.
  • Plan routes with benches or places to rest, and loops that keep you near home.
  • Indoors options when the weather is poor: shopping centres, large supermarkets, or walking around your home or garden.
  • Add hills and uneven ground gradually once flat walks are comfortable.

Bad days and flares

On a bad day, do not stop altogether unless a joint is hot and very swollen. Instead:

  • halve the time, or split it into two or three short walks
  • walk indoors or on the flattest route you have
  • use your stick or poles
  • add gentle seated exercises for the rest of the day

During a flare, rest the flaring joint more, keep gently moving the rest of your body, and return to walking with shorter walks, building back up over a week or two. Pacing helps prevent the boom-and-bust pattern of doing too much on good days.

Add strength and alternatives

Strong legs make walking easier and less painful. Add simple strength exercises such as sit-to-stands, step-ups and heel raises 2 or 3 times a week. Find joint-specific routines in our exercise hub. If walking is too painful, cycling (including on a static bike) and swimming or water exercise are good ways to build fitness with less load; see our swimming exercises for hip osteoarthritis.

Staying motivated

  • Walk with a friend, family member or dog, or join a group. Free, led health walks for beginners run in many areas, for example through Ramblers Wellbeing Walks in England and Paths for All in Scotland.
  • Keep a simple record: days walked, minutes and how you felt the next day.
  • Use a step counter or phone to see progress, but focus on minutes and how you feel rather than a fixed step number.
  • Set small goals linked to what matters to you, such as walking to the shops or round the park with grandchildren.
  • Vary your routes to keep it interesting.

Printable walking log

Copy or print this table to track your first few weeks. The "next day" column is the most important: it tells you whether you are ready to build up.

DateMinutesRoutePain during (0–10)Next day: better, same or worse?
     
     
     
     
     

Walking safely through the seasons

  • Winter: wear warm layers and shoes with good grip; walk in daylight; avoid icy paths and walk indoors if needed.
  • Summer: walk earlier or later in the day, drink water and wear sun protection.
  • Wet weather: take care on wet leaves and smooth surfaces.

When to get advice

  • Call 999 if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness or feel faint while walking and it does not settle with rest.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature, or after a fall if you cannot put weight on your leg.
  • Get urgent advice if your calf becomes painful, swollen and warm.
  • See your GP or a physiotherapist if pain keeps you from walking more than a few minutes, you are limping more, a joint gives way, or you are not improving after 8 to 12 weeks. In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy.

Is walking bad for knee arthritis?

No. For most people with knee osteoarthritis, regular walking built up gradually helps reduce pain and improve function. Use the 24-hour rule to find the right amount, wear supportive shoes and start on flat ground.

How far should I walk with arthritis?

There is no fixed distance. Start with the time you can walk comfortably, even 5 minutes, and add a minute or two each week. Over time, aim towards 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, which could be 30 minutes on 5 days, or shorter walks more often.

Should I walk if my joints hurt?

Mild pain that settles within a day is usually fine, and many people find walking eases stiffness. If a joint is hot and very swollen, rest it and use gentle movement instead. Sharp pain or a joint giving way means stop and get advice.

Do walking poles help arthritis?

They can. Poles share some of the load with your arms, improve balance and may make longer walks more comfortable for people with knee or hip arthritis. Learn the right technique and adjust the height to suit you.

What shoes are best for walking with arthritis?

Cushioned, supportive shoes with a thick, flexible sole, a firm heel and enough room for your toes. Lace-up or strap fastenings hold the foot securely. Replace walking shoes when the cushioning wears down.

How many steps a day should I aim for?

There is no single number for everyone. It is more useful to track minutes and build up gradually from your starting point. If you like counting steps, note your average for a week and aim to add a few hundred steps a day each week.

article.title: Weather and Arthritis Pain Explained: What Helps (UK)
article.excerpt: Many people with arthritis say they can feel the weather in their joints. This guide explains what research, including a large UK smartphone study, has found, why weather might affect pain, and practical steps to stay comfortable whatever the forecast.
article.content:
Quick answer: Many people with arthritis notice more pain in damp, cold or changeable weather. Research is mixed, but a large UK smartphone study found a small link between pain and humid, windy days with low air pressure. Weather does not damage joints. Keeping warm, staying active indoors, pacing and planning ahead usually help.

"I can tell it's going to rain because my knees are aching." It is one of the most common things people with arthritis say, and it has been said for centuries. But is it real, and if so, what can you do about it? This guide explains what the research suggests, why weather might affect some people's joints, and the practical steps that help in the British climate, whatever the forecast.

What people with arthritis report

Many people with osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, fibromyalgia and other conditions say their pain changes with the weather. The most common complaints are about cold, damp, grey days and about changes in the weather, such as a storm coming in. Some people notice the opposite and feel worse in heat. Others notice no link at all.

These experiences are real. Pain is personal, and you do not need a study to tell you how you feel. What research helps with is working out whether there is a consistent effect across many people, how big it is, and which kinds of weather matter.

What the research says

Studies over many years have given mixed results. Some found links between pain and temperature, humidity or air pressure; others found none. Part of the problem is that many studies were small, ran for short periods or relied on people remembering how they felt.

One of the largest studies was run in the UK. In the "Cloudy with a Chance of Pain" project, led by researchers at the University of Manchester, over 2,600 people living with long-term pain, many with arthritis, recorded their symptoms daily on a smartphone app over a 15-month period, while the phone's location was matched to local weather data. The results, published in npj Digital Medicine in 2019, found:

  • A small but real link between more pain and days with higher humidity, lower air pressure and stronger wind
  • That the combination of these, a damp, windy day with low pressure, was most associated with pain
  • That these links remained even after taking mood and physical activity into account
  • That temperature and rainfall did not show as clear a link in this analysis
  • That the effect was modest: weather was one influence on pain, not the main driver

In plain terms: there does seem to be something to it for many people, especially on damp, blustery days, but it is a nudge rather than a shove. Other things, such as activity, sleep, mood, stress and how well your arthritis is controlled, generally matter more.

Why weather might affect joint pain

No one knows for certain. Several explanations have been suggested, and more than one may play a part:

  • Air pressure changes. One theory is that falling pressure lets tissues in and around a joint expand slightly, which may be felt in joints that are already sensitive. This has not been proven.
  • Cold and stiffness. Cold can make muscles tense and joints feel stiffer, and people tend to move less when it is cold.
  • Less activity. Wet, dark or windy days mean fewer walks and more sitting, and inactivity often makes arthritis stiffness worse.
  • Mood and sleep. Grey, gloomy spells can lower mood, and low mood and poor sleep make pain feel worse. Some people have seasonal affective disorder in the darker months.
  • Expectation. If you expect a damp day to hurt, you may notice pain more. This does not mean the pain is imagined; the brain's processing of pain is affected by many things.

Weather does not damage arthritic joints

There is no evidence that cold, damp or changing weather damages joints or makes arthritis progress faster. A weather-related ache is uncomfortable, but it is not a sign of harm. This matters because it means you can keep moving on those days, and keeping active is one of the most helpful things you can do for arthritis. NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) recommends exercise as a core treatment.

Practical steps for damp, cold or changeable days

Keep warm

  • Dress in layers, which trap warm air better than one thick layer, and keep hands, feet and knees covered.
  • Thermal leggings under trousers, a scarf, gloves and warm socks make a real difference to stiff joints.
  • Keep your home warm. The NHS suggests heating rooms you use to at least 18°C if you can, especially if you are older or have a long-term condition.
  • Warm your clothes on a radiator before dressing on cold mornings.
  • If you have Raynaud's phenomenon, keeping your whole body warm, not just your hands, helps. The NHS notes cold is a common trigger.

Keep moving, indoors if needed

  • Have an indoor plan ready for bad weather: a seated exercise routine, a walk around a shopping centre or covered market, a home exercise video, or a session at a leisure centre.
  • Warm-water pools can be especially comfortable for stiff joints in cold months.
  • Break activity into short bursts through the day rather than skipping it altogether.
  • Our guide to staying active in winter has many ideas.

Use warmth on stiff joints

A warm shower, wheat bag or hot water bottle in a cover can ease stiffness on cold days, for about 15 to 20 minutes. Check your skin often and never use heat on numb skin. Read our guide to heat versus ice for arthritis.

Plan around the forecast

  • If a stormy or very wet week is coming, plan lighter tasks for those days and bigger jobs for drier spells.
  • Get shopping or prescriptions in before bad weather so you are not forced out on icy or very windy days.
  • Build in extra time for getting ready on cold mornings.
  • Keep a few easy meals in the cupboard or freezer for days when you do not want to go out.

Look after mood and sleep

  • Get daylight when you can, ideally in the morning, even on cloudy days.
  • Keep in touch with people. A phone call or meeting a friend can lift a grey day.
  • Keep a regular sleep routine through the winter months.
  • If your mood drops every autumn and winter, talk to your GP. Our guide to SAD and arthritis explains more.

Vitamin D in autumn and winter

In the UK, sunlight is not strong enough from about October to early March for the skin to make enough vitamin D. The NHS advises that everyone should consider taking a daily vitamin D supplement of 10 micrograms during autumn and winter, and some people all year round. Vitamin D is important for bone and muscle health, though it is not a treatment for arthritis pain. Check with your pharmacist if you take other medicines.

Weather and different types of arthritis

People with different conditions often describe the weather affecting them in different ways, though research has not clearly shown that one type of arthritis is more weather-sensitive than another.

  • Osteoarthritis: many people describe more aching and stiffness in cold, damp spells, often in knees, hips and hands.
  • Rheumatoid and other inflammatory arthritis: some people notice more stiffness in cold weather, and some feel more swollen and tired in heat and humidity. Persistent swelling, whatever the weather, is a reason to contact your rheumatology team.
  • Fibromyalgia: many people report widespread pain and tiredness changing with the weather.
  • Gout: hot weather can make dehydration more likely, and dehydration is one of the things that can trigger a gout attack, so drink enough fluids in warm spells.
  • Raynaud's phenomenon, which is more common in some inflammatory conditions: cold clearly triggers colour changes and pain in fingers and toes.

Hot weather and arthritis

Some people find their joints feel looser in warm weather, while others, including some people with inflammatory arthritis, find heat and humidity make swelling and tiredness worse. Heatwaves also bring their own risks, especially for older people and those taking certain medicines. Follow the NHS advice to stay out of the heat at the hottest time of day, drink plenty of fluids and keep rooms cool. Our guide to managing arthritis in a heatwave covers this in detail.

Moving somewhere warmer

Some people wonder whether moving to a sunnier, drier place would help. There is no good evidence that climate changes how arthritis progresses. A holiday somewhere warm may feel pleasant and help you be more active, but a big move is a major decision and should not be made for joint pain alone.

Track your own weather pattern

If you think weather affects you, it can be useful to check. For a month or two, note your daily pain score along with a quick description of the weather, for example "cold and wet", "windy", "mild and dry" or "hot". Also note how active you were and how you slept. You may find a pattern, or you may find that activity and sleep matter more than the weather. Either way, it helps you plan. Our pain tracking journal template has a notes column you can use.

When to get medical help

Weather-related aches are usually mild and settle. Do not put other symptoms down to the weather. Get help if:

  • A joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with fever or feeling unwell: call NHS 111 or go to A&E
  • You have new swollen joints, or morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes most days: see your GP
  • Your fingers or toes change colour in the cold and you also develop skin ulcers, or symptoms only affect one side: see your GP
  • You develop signs of hypothermia in cold weather, such as shivering, confusion and slurred speech, or heat exhaustion in a heatwave that does not improve within 30 minutes of cooling down: call NHS 111, or 999 if severe
  • Chest pain, severe breathlessness, signs of a stroke or collapse: call 999
  • Your arthritis pain is steadily getting worse whatever the weather: speak to your GP or rheumatology team about your treatment

Can weather really affect arthritis pain?

Many people with arthritis notice it, and a large UK smartphone study found a small link between pain and humid, windy days with low air pressure. The effect seems modest, and other factors such as activity, sleep and mood usually matter more.

Why do my joints hurt before it rains?

One theory is that falling air pressure before bad weather lets tissues in and around sensitive joints expand slightly. This has not been proven. Damp, grey days also tend to mean less activity and lower mood, which can make pain feel worse.

Does cold weather make arthritis worse?

Cold can make joints feel stiffer and muscles tenser, and people move less in cold weather, which can increase stiffness. There is no evidence that cold damages joints. Keeping warm and staying active indoors usually helps.

Is damp or cold weather worse for arthritis?

In the UK study, humidity, low pressure and wind together were more closely linked to pain than temperature alone. Many people find cold and damp together the hardest. Keeping warm, dry and active helps whichever affects you.

Would moving to a warmer country help my arthritis?

There is no good evidence that a warmer climate changes how arthritis progresses or reliably reduces pain. Some people feel better in warm, dry weather and others worse in heat. Do not make a major move for joint pain alone without discussing it with your clinicians.

Should I take vitamin D for arthritis in winter?

The NHS advises that everyone in the UK should consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. It supports bone and muscle health but is not a treatment for arthritis pain. Ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines.

article.excerpt: A practical, joint-friendly exercise plan to support weight loss with arthritis: why weight matters for joints, what exercise can and cannot do on its own, the best low-impact activities, a 12-week plan for three starting levels, adding everyday activity, pairing exercise with diet, NHS weight management support and when to get help.
article.content:
Quick answer: Exercise helps weight loss with arthritis most when combined with healthier eating. Choose low-impact activity such as walking, cycling or swimming, build towards at least 150 minutes a week, and add strength exercises twice a week to protect muscle. Start where you are, increase gradually over 12 weeks, and ask your GP about NHS weight management support.

If you have arthritis and are carrying extra weight, you have probably been told that losing some would help your joints. That is good advice: NICE guideline NG226 recommends weight loss for people with osteoarthritis who are overweight, alongside exercise. But exercise can feel hard when your joints hurt, and it is easy to start too hard and give up. This guide gives you a realistic, joint-friendly exercise plan to support weight loss, explains how to pair it with eating changes, and shows where to get NHS help.

Why weight matters for arthritis

  • Load on joints. Weight-bearing joints such as the knees, hips and feet carry more load with every step when you weigh more. Losing weight reduces that load.
  • Inflammation. Body fat is active tissue that produces substances linked to inflammation, which may affect joints throughout the body, including the hands.
  • Pain and function. NICE advises that any amount of weight loss is likely to help people with osteoarthritis who are overweight, and that losing more (such as 10% of body weight) is likely to bring more benefit.
  • Treatment and surgery. A healthier weight can make treatments, including joint replacement surgery and recovery, easier.

Our guide to arthritis and weight loss covers the reasons in more depth.

What exercise can and cannot do

It is worth being honest: exercise on its own usually leads to modest weight loss, because it is easy to eat back the energy you use. Weight loss is mainly driven by eating fewer calories than you use. But exercise matters a great deal because it:

  • helps you keep weight off once you have lost it
  • preserves and builds muscle while you lose fat, which protects your joints and keeps you strong
  • reduces arthritis pain and improves function in its own right
  • improves mood, sleep, blood pressure and blood sugar

So the best approach combines the two: eating changes for weight loss, and exercise for joints, muscle, health and keeping the weight off.

Before you start

  • Speak to your GP first if you have heart problems, chest pain, uncontrolled blood pressure, diabetes on insulin or tablets that can cause low blood sugar, or you are very inactive and have several health conditions.
  • Choose supportive, cushioned footwear and comfortable clothes.
  • Decide how you will track progress: steps, minutes of activity, or a simple diary.
  • Set a realistic goal. A loss of around 0.5 to 1 kg a week is a common safe target.

The best low-impact activities for weight loss with arthritis

ActivityJoint impactWhy it helpsTips
WalkingLow to moderateFree, easy to build into daily lifeStart with short walks on flat ground; use poles or a stick if helpful
Cycling (outdoor or stationary)LowUses large leg muscles; easy to adjust effortSet the seat height so your knee is slightly bent at the bottom
Swimming and aqua aerobicsVery lowWater supports body weightGood if weight-bearing is painful; warm pools are often more comfortable
Cross-trainerLowWorks arms and legs without impactStart at low resistance for short bouts
Rowing machineLow to moderateWhole-body exerciseAvoid if back or hands are painful
Seated exerciseVery lowOption for limited mobilitySeated marching, arm work and band exercises
Strength trainingLow to moderateBuilds muscle and protects joints2 to 3 times a week, see below

If your joints are painful when weight-bearing, water is a great place to start. See our guide to water-based exercise.

How hard should you work?

Most of your activity should be at a moderate intensity: you breathe faster and feel warmer, but can still talk. Use the "talk test" rather than chasing a high heart rate. As your fitness improves, you can include short spells of vigorous effort, where you can only say a few words, if your joints and health allow. Joint pain during exercise should stay at a level you find acceptable (often around 4 out of 10 or lower) and settle within 24 hours.

Your 12-week plan

Choose the starting level that suits you. Each week, do the aerobic minutes shown (spread over most days) and two strength sessions. If a week feels too hard, repeat it before moving on.

WeeksLevel A: very inactive or very painful jointsLevel B: some activityLevel C: fairly active
1–25–10 minutes a day (seated, pool or short walks), total 40–60 minutes a week15 minutes, 5 days (75 minutes)25 minutes, 5 days (125 minutes)
3–410 minutes, 6 days (60 minutes)20 minutes, 5 days (100 minutes)30 minutes, 5 days (150 minutes)
5–615 minutes, 6 days (90 minutes)25 minutes, 5 days (125 minutes)35 minutes, 5 days (175 minutes)
7–820 minutes, 5 days (100 minutes)30 minutes, 5 days (150 minutes)40 minutes, 5 days (200 minutes)
9–1025 minutes, 5 days (125 minutes)35 minutes, 5 days (175 minutes)45 minutes, 5 days (225 minutes)
11–1230 minutes, 5 days (150 minutes)40 minutes, 5 days (200 minutes)50 minutes, 5 days (250 minutes)

Minutes can be broken into shorter bouts, such as three 10-minute walks. UK guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week for health; for weight loss and keeping weight off, many people find they need more, built up gradually.

Strength sessions (twice a week)

Do 1 to 2 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions of each exercise, slowly and with control, resting a minute between exercises.

  1. Sit-to-stand from a firm chair, using your hands if needed.
  2. Wall press-up with hands on a wall at shoulder height.
  3. Step-ups on the bottom stair, holding the banister.
  4. Seated row with a resistance band around your feet.
  5. Bridge lying on your back, knees bent, lifting your bottom.
  6. Heel raises holding a support.
  7. Side leg raise standing and holding a support.

Make it harder over time by adding repetitions, then a second set, then light resistance. Our strength training guide explains progression in detail.

A sample week (Level B, weeks 7–8)

DayActivity
Monday30-minute walk (or 3 × 10 minutes)
TuesdayStrength session, plus 10 minutes on a stationary bike
Wednesday30-minute swim or aqua class
Thursday30-minute walk
FridayStrength session, plus 15 minutes of walking
Saturday30–40 minutes of cycling, gardening or a longer walk
SundayRest, or gentle mobility and a short stroll

For a step-by-step walking programme, see our guide to walking with arthritis.

Tips by joint

  • Knees: cycling and water exercise are often the most comfortable. Avoid deep squats and lots of stairs early on; build thigh strength with sit-to-stands and step-ups.
  • Hips: walking, cycling with a slightly higher seat and swimming usually suit. Strengthen your buttock muscles with bridges and side leg raises.
  • Feet and ankles: choose non-weight-bearing options such as cycling, rowing or swimming, and wear well-cushioned footwear for walking.
  • Back: walking and swimming are often helpful; keep strength exercises controlled and avoid heavy lifting.
  • Hands: use padded handles, cuffs or wrist loops for band exercises, and choose leg-based cardio.

Keeping the weight off

Staying active is widely recommended to help keep weight off over the long term. Once you reach your goal, keep your activity minutes at the level you built up, keep strength training twice a week, and keep weighing yourself weekly so you can act early if your weight starts creeping back. Planning ahead for holidays, illness and flares, with a simpler "minimum" routine, helps you stay on track.

Add everyday movement

Activity outside planned exercise adds up and is easier on joints than one long session. Ideas:

  • Stand up and move every 30 to 60 minutes.
  • Get off the bus a stop early or park further away, if your joints allow.
  • Do housework and gardening in short bursts, using joint protection.
  • Walk while on the phone.
  • Use a step counter and aim to add 500 to 1,000 steps a day each week or two.

Pairing exercise with eating changes

A few changes make the biggest difference:

  • Use the NHS Better Health resources, including the free NHS Weight Loss Plan app, which helps you set a calorie goal and plan meals.
  • Base meals on vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, beans and pulses, with lean protein such as fish, chicken, eggs or tofu. A Mediterranean-style diet is a good model.
  • Include protein at each meal to help preserve muscle while losing weight.
  • Cut down on sugary drinks, alcohol, and high-fat, high-sugar snacks.
  • Watch portion sizes; smaller plates can help.
  • Do not "reward" exercise with extra food. A 30-minute walk uses less energy than many snacks contain.

NHS weight management support

You do not have to do this alone. Options include:

  • Your GP practice can check your weight, discuss your options and refer you to local weight management services.
  • Local weight management services, which may offer group or one-to-one support, sometimes free through the NHS or your council.
  • The NHS Digital Weight Management Programme, available by referral for adults with a high BMI who also have diabetes or high blood pressure.
  • Medicines may be offered in some situations under NICE guidance, usually alongside a diet and activity programme. See our guide to weight loss injections and arthritis.
  • Exercise referral schemes at local leisure centres, which your GP or practice nurse may be able to refer you to.

Overcoming common barriers

BarrierTry
Joints hurt when I walkStart in water or on a bike; walk shorter distances more often
I feel self-consciousExercise at home, join a beginners or weight management group, or go at quiet times
I am not losing weightReview your eating; exercise alone rarely leads to big losses. Look at non-scale changes too
I am too tiredShort bouts help; regular activity often improves energy over time
Flares stop meScale back to gentle movement rather than stopping completely, then restart gradually

Track more than the scales

Weight can go up and down from day to day. Weigh yourself once a week at the same time, and also track your waist measurement, your weekly activity minutes, how far you can walk, how easily you manage stairs, and your pain levels. These often improve before the scales move much.

When to get medical help

  • Call 999 if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness or feel faint during exercise.
  • Stop and see your GP if you get chest discomfort, palpitations or unusual breathlessness with activity, or dizziness.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful.
  • See a physiotherapist if exercise keeps making your joint pain worse despite reducing it.
  • See your GP if you are losing weight without trying, or if you have diabetes and your blood sugars change as you become more active.

What is the best exercise to lose weight with bad knees?

Low-impact activities such as cycling, swimming, aqua aerobics and the cross-trainer are often the most comfortable. Walking is also good if built up gradually. Add strength exercises twice a week to support your knees.

How much exercise do I need to lose weight?

Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, building towards more if you can, plus strength exercises twice a week. Combining exercise with eating changes is the most effective way to lose weight.

How much weight do I need to lose to help my arthritis?

NICE advises that any weight loss is likely to help people with osteoarthritis who are overweight, and losing more, such as 10% of your body weight, is likely to bring more benefit.

Can I lose weight with arthritis if I cannot walk far?

Yes. Eating changes are the main driver of weight loss, and you can exercise in water, on a stationary bike or seated. Short, frequent bouts of activity add up.

Will exercise make my arthritis worse?

Exercise is a recommended treatment for arthritis. Some extra ache when starting is normal, but it should settle within a day. Building up gradually reduces the risk of flares.

Can I get help to lose weight on the NHS?

Yes. Your GP can discuss options, including referral to local weight management services, and you can use free NHS Better Health resources such as the NHS Weight Loss Plan app.

article.title: Weight-Loss Injections and Arthritis: Wegovy and Mounjaro
article.excerpt: Weight-loss injections such as Wegovy and Mounjaro are in the news. This guide explains how they might help arthritis, who can get them on the NHS, side effects, protecting muscle, and what to check if you take arthritis medicines.
article.content:
Quick answer: Weight-loss injections such as Wegovy (semaglutide) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) are licensed for weight management, not for arthritis. Losing weight can reduce knee and hip pain in osteoarthritis, and a large trial found semaglutide reduced knee pain in people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis. They are available on the NHS only for people who meet set criteria. Side effects are common, and protecting muscle strength matters.

What these medicines are

Wegovy contains semaglutide and Mounjaro contains tirzepatide. Both are weekly injections that copy natural gut hormones involved in appetite and blood sugar control. They make you feel fuller for longer and reduce hunger, which helps people eat less and lose weight. Similar medicines, under different brand names, are used to treat type 2 diabetes.

In the UK they are licensed for weight management in adults who meet certain criteria, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. They are not licensed as a treatment for arthritis itself.

How weight loss can help arthritis

Extra body weight increases the load on weight-bearing joints such as the knees and hips. Fat tissue also releases substances that promote inflammation. For people with osteoarthritis who are carrying extra weight, NICE recommends weight loss as part of core treatment, alongside exercise and education, because even modest weight loss can reduce pain and improve function.

There is growing research into weight-loss medicines specifically in people with arthritis. One large trial, published in 2024, found that people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis who took semaglutide lost more weight and reported less knee pain and better physical function than those given a placebo. Research is ongoing, including into whether these medicines have effects on joints beyond weight loss. For people with psoriatic arthritis and other inflammatory conditions, weight loss may help treatment work better, but more research is needed.

Who can get them on the NHS?

NICE has approved both medicines for use on the NHS for some adults living with obesity, usually with at least one weight-related health condition, and with specific body mass index (BMI) thresholds. Access has been phased, with priority given to people with the greatest clinical need, and the arrangements differ between specialist weight management services and GP-led care and across the four UK nations. Eligibility is based on weight and health conditions, not on having arthritis alone.

If you are interested, ask your GP whether you might be eligible and what local weight management support is available. Your GP can also discuss other options, such as NHS weight management programmes and the NHS Digital Weight Management Programme for people with diabetes or high blood pressure.

Buying privately: staying safe

Many people buy these medicines privately through online pharmacies. If you do:

  • Only use a UK-registered pharmacy. You can check registration with the General Pharmaceutical Council.
  • Expect a proper health assessment, including your weight, medical history and current medicines. Be honest about your arthritis and the medicines you take.
  • Never buy from social media, beauty salons or unregulated websites. The MHRA has warned about fake and unsafe weight-loss pens.
  • Tell your GP and rheumatology team that you are taking one, so it is on your record.

Side effects

Side effects are common, especially when starting or increasing the dose, and often improve with time. They include:

  • Feeling sick, vomiting, diarrhoea or constipation.
  • Indigestion, bloating and burping.
  • Tiredness and dizziness.
  • Hair thinning, sometimes linked to rapid weight loss.

Less common but serious side effects include inflammation of the pancreas (severe tummy pain spreading to the back, which needs urgent medical help) and gallbladder problems. Dehydration from vomiting or diarrhoea can affect the kidneys, which matters more if you also take anti-inflammatory painkillers. Read the patient leaflet and seek medical advice if you are worried.

Protecting muscle and bone

When people lose weight quickly, some of the weight lost is muscle. Muscle strength is vital for supporting arthritic joints, balance and staying independent, particularly as you get older. To protect it:

  • Do strength exercises at least twice a week. See our guide to resistance training for arthritis.
  • Eat enough protein at each meal, even when your appetite is low.
  • Keep active every day, for example with walking or swimming.
  • Ask your GP about bone health if you have other risk factors for osteoporosis.

Using them alongside arthritis medicines

  • There are no well-known major interactions with common DMARDs or biologics, but always check with your pharmacist or prescriber.
  • These medicines slow stomach emptying, which may affect how some tablets are absorbed. Your pharmacist can advise.
  • Mounjaro can make oral contraceptive pills less effective, particularly when starting or increasing the dose, so extra contraception may be needed. These medicines should not be used in pregnancy. This matters if you take arthritis medicines that also need careful pregnancy planning, such as methotrexate or leflunomide.
  • If you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhoea, ask your pharmacist or GP whether any medicines, such as NSAIDs, should be paused while you recover. Do not change doses of your arthritis medicines without advice.
  • Tell your surgical team and anaesthetist if you take one before any operation, including joint surgery.

What happens when you stop?

It is generally thought that many people regain weight after stopping these medicines. Building lasting habits around food, activity and sleep while taking them gives you the best chance of keeping benefits. The medicines work best as one part of a wider plan, not on their own.

Weight-loss support without injections

Injections are not suitable or available for everyone. Many people with arthritis lose weight through changes to diet and activity, with support from their GP, a dietitian, a weight management programme or a physiotherapist. See our diet guide and exercise guide.

Frequently asked questions

Can Mounjaro or Wegovy help knee arthritis?

They are not licensed for arthritis, but weight loss can reduce knee pain in osteoarthritis. A large trial found semaglutide reduced knee pain in people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis.

Can I get weight-loss injections on the NHS for arthritis?

Eligibility is based on your BMI and weight-related health conditions, not arthritis alone. Ask your GP whether you might qualify.

Can I take Mounjaro with methotrexate?

There is no well-known major interaction, but check with your pharmacist and tell your rheumatology team. Both need careful pregnancy planning.

Will I lose muscle on weight-loss injections?

Some muscle loss is common with rapid weight loss. Strength exercise and enough protein help protect muscle.

Are weight-loss injections safe to buy online?

Only buy from a UK-registered pharmacy that carries out a proper health assessment. Never buy from social media or unregulated sellers.

Do I need to stop weight-loss injections before joint surgery?

Tell your surgical team and anaesthetist. They will advise what to do, as these medicines slow stomach emptying.

article.title: Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence
article.excerpt: Every kilogram of weight loss removes roughly four kilograms of force from each knee step. The evidence on weight, inflammation and joint pain.
article.content:
Quick answer: Weight management is an effective strategy for managing arthritis symptoms. A 5% reduction in body weight can significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis symptoms. A 10% reduction in weight can even produce benefits comparable to some medications. This is achieved through consistent, small changes, tracking outcomes like pain on waking, longest pain-free intervals, and functional improvements.

What this guide covers

This piece summarises what the current evidence says about weight management and arthritis: the evidence, the practical steps that help most, and the red flags that mean you should speak to your GP or physiotherapist.

The underlying mechanism

Arthritis pain rarely has a single cause. Joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, surrounding muscle and the nervous system all contribute. Understanding which of these is driving your specific symptom is the first step toward targeted relief. For an in-depth condition overview, see our related guide.

Inflammatory and degenerative forms behave differently. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis (osteoarthritis) typically worsens with prolonged use. Knowing which pattern matches your day-to-day experience helps you choose the right management approach.

What helps — by strength of evidence

  1. Movement and graded exercise. NICE NG226 (2022) and Cochrane reviews place structured exercise as a first-line treatment. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, split into 20–30 minute sessions.
  2. Anti-inflammatory eating. A Mediterranean-style pattern — oily fish twice a week, plenty of vegetables, olive oil, whole grains — is linked to reduced pain scores in OA and RA trials.
  3. Weight management. A 5 percent reduction in body weight reduces knee-OA symptoms measurably; a 10 percent reduction can match the effect of some medications.
  4. Heat and cold. Heat eases stiffness; cold eases acute swelling. Twenty-minute applications, with a towel barrier.
  5. Sleep hygiene. Pain perception rises sharply on fewer than six hours of sleep. Prioritise a consistent bedtime.

A practical seven-day starting plan

Begin with the smallest dose that feels manageable — five minutes of movement, one anti-inflammatory meal a day, a 10 pm screen-off rule. Track only three things weekly: pain on waking (0–10), longest pain-free interval, and one functional win (e.g., climbed stairs without grabbing the rail). Small, consistent inputs outperform big sporadic efforts.

When to seek clinical advice

Book an appointment with your GP or a first-contact physiotherapist if you notice: sudden hot, red, swollen joints; unexplained weight loss alongside joint pain; morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour for more than two weeks; or new numbness or weakness. These can signal inflammatory disease that benefits from early treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Will this approach work alongside my medication? Yes. Exercise, diet and pacing complement prescribed treatments and often improve their effectiveness. Always check with your prescriber before stopping any medication.

How long until I notice a difference? Most people report meaningful improvement at 6–12 weeks of consistent practice. Earlier wins (less morning stiffness, better sleep) often appear within 2–3 weeks.

Is this safe if I have other conditions? The principles above are broadly safe for adults with stable cardiovascular, metabolic and respiratory conditions. If you are unsure, ask your GP for a referral to a first-contact physiotherapist for a tailored plan.

This article is general health information, not medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional for decisions about your individual care.

Practical next steps for Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence

If you came here about Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

article.title: Wet rooms and arthritis: washing when you are frail (UK)
article.excerpt: How a wet room or level-access shower can make washing safer with arthritis and frailty, what to include, assessments and grants that may help.
article.content:
Getting in and out of a bath is hard with painful hips and knees and less strength.

This guide explains wet rooms and other bathroom changes. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why bathrooms are risky

Wet floors, stepping over a bath edge and standing for long periods all increase the risk of falls.

What a wet room can include

  • A level floor with drainage.
  • A shower seat.
  • Grab rails.
  • Lever taps and a thermostatic valve.
  • Non-slip flooring.

Simpler options

  • A bath board or bath lift.
  • A shower over the bath with a seat.
  • A long-handled sponge.

Assessment and funding

Ask your council for an OT assessment. A Disabled Facilities Grant may help with major adaptations; arrangements differ across the UK.

While you wait

  • Wash sitting down.
  • Keep items within reach.
  • Have someone nearby if possible.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Do I need a full wet room?

Not always; an OT can suggest options.

Will the grant cover it?

It depends on assessment and finances.

Sources and further reading

  • GOV.UK: Disabled Facilities Grants
  • NHS: Home adaptations
  • NHS: Care services, equipment and care homes

article.content:
Quick answer: What arthritis means, the main types, common symptoms and when to seek advice.

Start with a manageable step

Arthritis can affect movement, energy and confidence in different ways. Begin with a short, comfortable activity and build gradually. Keep notes on what helps and what makes symptoms worse.

Practical ideas

  • choose low-impact movement such as walking, seated exercise or water-based activity;
  • add gentle strengthening when it feels safe;
  • take regular breaks and avoid pushing through severe pain;
  • ask a physiotherapist or GP for individual advice.

When to seek advice

Speak with a healthcare professional if symptoms persist, a joint becomes hot and swollen, or exercise causes a clear worsening that does not settle. This article is educational information and is not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

article.title: What Sustained Remission Means in RA
article.excerpt: Quick answer: Sustained remission in rheumatoid arthritis means stable minimal or no disease activity, not a cure. The article says it is a key treatment.
article.content:
Quick answer: Sustained remission in rheumatoid arthritis means stable minimal or no disease activity, not a cure. The article says it is a key treatment goal, often maintained through ongoing medication, monitoring, gentle regular movement and lifestyle support. It advises personalised clinician guidance, symptom tracking, pacing activity, and prompt review for swelling, fever, rapid function loss or medication side effects.

Overview

Remission isn't cure. Understanding the difference changes how you plan.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

The consensus among rheumatology experts and patient advocacy groups is that achieving remission in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a primary treatment goal. Systematic reviews of long-term studies consistently show that individuals who reach and maintain remission experience better quality of life, less joint damage, and improved physical function compared to those with ongoing disease activity. This evidence underpins current clinical guidelines, which strongly advocate for a 'treat-to-target' approach, meaning adjusting treatments until remission or very low disease activity is achieved.

However, clinical guidance also highlights that "remission" can be defined in different ways, from patient-reported outcomes to strict laboratory and physical examination criteria. Randomised trials examining various drug therapies often use these stricter definitions, showing that while remission is increasingly achievable, particularly with early and aggressive treatment, it often requires ongoing medication rather than being a permanent 'cure'.

Therefore, the evidence points to remission as a stable state of minimal or no disease activity, usually maintained through careful management, rather than a total eradication of the disease. This distinction is crucial for managing expectations and planning long-term care.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Stopping medication when feeling well: Your treatment is likely what's keeping you well; stopping without medical advice can cause flare-ups. *Always discuss medication changes with your doctor. Ignoring subtle symptoms: A slight stiffness or an odd ache could be an early warning sign, not just a 'bad day'. *Keep your symptom diary updated and discuss any new or worsening symptoms. Overdoing it on good days: Pushing too hard when you feel good can lead to a setback and increased fatigue. *Pace yourself and listen to your body, even in remission. Neglecting other health aspects: Diet, sleep, and stress management play a huge role in overall well-being with RA. *Focus on a holistic approach to your health, not just medication. Expecting a 'cure' instead of management: While remission is fantastic, it's usually ongoing management rather than a permanent fix. *Understand that sustained remission often means continued vigilance and treatment.

When to Speak to a Clinician

Even in sustained remission, it's important to be aware of signs that might indicate a change in your condition or require medical review. Persistent symptoms should always be checked out.

  • New, persistent joint pain or swelling: Especially if it lasts for more than a few days, or affects joints previously unaffected.
  • Unexplained fever or generally feeling unwell (malaise): These can sometimes indicate a flare or an infection.
  • Significant increase in fatigue: If your energy levels suddenly plummet and rest doesn't help.
  • Rapid loss of function in a joint: If you find you suddenly can't move a joint as you usually could.
  • Side effects from medication: Any new or worsening side effects from your prescribed drugs should always be discussed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I reduce my medication once I'm in sustained remission?

Sometimes, yes, but this must be done very carefully and under the guidance of your rheumatologist. Reducing medication needs to be a shared decision, considering your individual circumstances and risk of flare.

How is 'sustained remission' actually measured?

It's measured using a combination of factors, including your own report of symptoms (like how much pain or stiffness you have), your doctor's examination of your joints, and blood tests to check for inflammation markers. This data is often fed into a specific scoring system.

Does being in remission mean I can stop exercising?

No, regular exercise remains very important. It helps maintain joint flexibility, muscle strength, and overall well-being, even when you're feeling good. Your specialist or a physiotherapist can advise on suitable activities.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

article.content:
Here is a plain-English take on a wheelchair for distance, not for giving up: arthritis and frailty when arthritis and lower reserve share the same week. This UK guide looks at using wheels so you still get to the park in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Wales services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

Quick answer: Here is a plain-English take on a wheelchair for distance, not for giving up: arthritis and frailty when arthritis and lower reserve share the same week. This UK guide looks at using wheels so you still get to the park in a home setting, with practical steps, warning signs and Wales services. It is general information, not personal medical advice.

In Wales, clinicians may talk about frailty as a syndrome. You may simply feel that arthritis with frailty has stolen bounce from ordinary home tasks. Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis; a smaller group also live with frailty as a clinical syndrome. This article stays with using wheels so you still get to the park, not a generic arthritis recap. It is written in UK English for people, families and carers in Wales.

The overlap: pain in several joints and a frailer body

Clinicians sometimes use tools such as the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale in hospital. It is not a DIY label and it is not a moral judgement. Pain in several joints can make you look slower on a scale even when the driver is arthritis, so tell staff what is new this week versus what is your usual arthritis with frailty.

Around 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. Only some also live with frailty. The practical question is not the label. It is whether using wheels so you still get to the park is shrinking your home life — and what you can change this week without pretending pain is imaginary.

Living With Arthritis is an independent UK charity (1218461), not part of Arthritis UK. We write for patients and carers. We do not replace NHS Wales services via your GP and local health board.

What this can look like in a home

In a home, using wheels so you still get to the park is rarely one dramatic collapse. It is usually a stack of small avoidances. People with arthritis with frailty already know boom-and-bust. Frailty adds a longer payback: a quiet weekend can cost the following Thursday.

  • A hospital or infection week that ends with clothes feeling looser and stairs feeling taller.
  • A flare of arthritis with frailty that lasts, then a slower baseline even when the flare eases.
  • Shorter outdoor range, then shorter indoor range, then a home that has quietly rearranged itself around the chair.
  • Night toilet trips, poor lighting and stiff several joints stacking into a falls risk that nobody named.
  • Transfers that used to be boring — bed, chair, toilet, car — now need a pause, a push-up or a second person, especially when several joints are cold.

Who to talk to locally in Wales

Start with your GP practice and NHS Wales services via your GP and local health board. For urgent but non-emergency advice use NHS 111 Wales. For chest pain, suspected hip fracture, sudden new weakness, or a fall with a bang to the head on blood thinners, use 999.

In Wales, Dewis Cymru can help you browse local support. Rural travel, hills and limited buses matter as much as the joint diagnosis. Ask whether a community hospital, pharmacy service or home visit can cut the journey.

Self-management that respects arthritis with frailty

  • Book eye, foot and hearing checks as frailty care, not vanity. Arthritis with frailty already asks a lot of balance.
  • If stairs are the bottleneck, get an occupational therapy conversation on the list while you temporarily live downstairs — drifting is how a camp-bed becomes a lifestyle.
  • If cooking is the barrier, use tinned fish, eggs, yoghurt, beans or leftover protein foods rather than skipping meals. Muscle needs raw material as well as movement.
  • Ask a pharmacist to look at the whole list if dizziness, constipation or night sedation have arrived with the pain tablets. Do not add a new painkiller just in case.
  • If you live in a home, tell one other person the plan for a fall: who to call, where the spare key sits, whether you wear a pendant you can actually press.
  • Put the items you use at dawn — tablets, glasses, walking aid, phone — where you can reach them without a stretch that wrenches several joints.

Lifestyle changes that are really clinical care

Red flags — do not wait this out

  • Unplanned weight loss, repeated falls, or using wheels so you still get to the park that is clearly worsening week by week — book the GP and say you are worried about frailty as well as several joints.
  • Sudden confusion, new incontinence, or a crash in mobility over hours to days — think infection or delirium, not only arthritis.
  • A fall with a new inability to weight-bear, a shortened or rotated leg, or severe hip or groin pain — 999.
  • A hot, very swollen joint with fever, or feeling systemically unwell — seek urgent clinical advice. A joint infection is an emergency.
  • A knock to the head, especially if you take blood thinners — do not sleep it off as a plan.

Can frailty improve if I still have pain in several joints?

Sometimes the frailty part can shift even if arthritis with frailty remains. Strength, protein, reviewing dizzy medicines, treating a flare, and practising transfers can return reserve. Improvement is not guaranteed and it is rarely dramatic, but frailer this month is not always a one-way door. Work with clinicians rather than copying an online challenge.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by GP, community physio and, where it exists, a frailty team. If medicines are stacking, falls are repeating, or memory and continence are changing alongside arthritis with frailty, ask whether a comprehensive older-person assessment would help.

What should a carer do in the home without taking over?

Stand nearby for the risky bit, set the environment up (chair height, shoes, light), and leave the bits the person can still do. Taking over every transfer trains both of you into a hoist-by-default life. If moving and handling is already unsafe, stop DIY lifting and ask for a proper care and OT review.

Getting an NHS wheelchair

NHS wheelchair services can assess you if you need a wheelchair for regular use. Referral is usually through your GP, physiotherapist or occupational therapist.

  • Ask your GP or therapist how to be referred to your local wheelchair service, and how long the wait is.
  • Explain your arthritis, including whether you can self-propel with painful hands or shoulders.
  • Some areas offer a personal wheelchair budget towards a chair that meets your needs. Ask the service what applies locally.
