article.title: Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better
article.excerpt: Regular physical activity, including strength training, can make arthritis medication more effective by reducing pain, improving physical function.
article.content:
Quick answer: Regular physical activity, including strength training, can make arthritis medication more effective by reducing pain, improving physical function, and enhancing quality of life. This integrated approach, which combines medication with movement, is recommended in clinical guidelines. Exercise is thought to lower widespread inflammation, maintain healthy weight, strengthen muscles, and improve mood, all of which support treatment response.

Overview

Strength training improves drug efficacy by reducing systemic inflammation.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews looking at several individual studies consistently show that combining regular physical activity, especially strength training, with anti-arthritis medication can lead to better outcomes. These benefits include reduced pain, improved physical function, and a better quality of life compared to medication alone. Clinical guidelines from leading UK health bodies strongly recommend this integrated approach, highlighting that movement is a key component of effective arthritis management.

The exact way exercise helps medication work better isn't fully understood, but it's thought to be partly due to its ability to lower widespread inflammation in the body. Exercise also helps maintain healthy body weight, strengthens muscles around joints, and improves mood, all of which contribute to how well you respond to treatment.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Waiting for full pain relief before moving: Gentle movement can actually help reduce pain over time.
  • Only doing high-impact activities: Focus on low-impact options that protect your joints.
  • Overdoing it on good days: Stick to a consistent level of activity to avoid flare-ups.
  • Ignoring professional guidance: Your healthcare team can tailor advice to your specific condition and needs.
  • Comparing your progress to others: Everyone's journey with arthritis is unique; focus on your own improvements.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While movement is beneficial, there are times when you should always seek advice from your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. This is especially important if you notice new symptoms or a significant change in your condition.

  • Sudden, severe joint pain or swelling that doesn't settle with rest.
  • Fever, chills, or generally feeling unwell alongside joint symptoms.
  • New numbness, tingling, or weakness in a limb.
  • Rapid loss of movement or function in a joint.
  • Any symptoms that worry you or interfere with your daily life.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does gentle movement count, or do I need to do intense workouts?

Yes, gentle movement absolutely counts! Activities like walking, swimming, or tai chi can be very effective. The key is consistency and finding activities you enjoy that don't aggravate your joints. Intense workouts are generally not recommended for most people with arthritis.

How soon will I notice a difference in how my medication works?

It can take time to notice the full benefits of combining exercise with your medication. Most people find improvements gradually over several weeks or months. Keeping a symptom diary can help you track these changes and discuss them with your healthcare team.

Can exercise replace my arthritis medication entirely?

For most types of arthritis, exercise is a complementary treatment, not a replacement for medication. Your medicines work in specific ways to manage the underlying disease. Exercise helps reduce symptoms, improve function, and support your overall health alongside your prescribed treatment plan.

Practical next steps for Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better

If you came here about Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Quick questions about Exercise Makes Your Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

article.title: Cold home and arthritis: keeping warm and keeping moving (UK)
article.excerpt: Keep warm at home with arthritis without sitting still all day: rooms to heat, a five-minute warm-up, safer moving, and UK heating help to check.
article.content:
Quick answer: A cold home can make stiff joints feel worse and is risky if you are older or living with frailty. Heat the rooms you use, ideally to at least 18°C as the NHS suggests, wear layers, and get up and move for a few minutes every hour rather than staying wrapped up in one chair. Check GOV.UK for heating help and speak to your energy supplier if you are struggling.

When money is tight and joints are sore, it is tempting to heat one room, sit under a blanket and stay put. That keeps you a bit warmer for now, but long spells of sitting stiffen joints and weaken the muscles you need to get up, walk and stay independent. This guide is about staying warm and staying moving at home this winter, and where to get help with heating costs.

Why a cold home matters with arthritis

  • Many people say cold makes their joints stiffer and more painful. Research on why is mixed, but your experience is real
  • The NHS says cold homes raise health risks, especially for older people and people with long-term conditions
  • Cold, stiff muscles make it harder to get out of a chair, which can mean more sitting and a higher risk of falls

Keep warm without sitting still all day

  • Heat the rooms you use most, ideally to at least 18°C if you can. Keep the bedroom warm overnight and close curtains at dusk
  • Layer up: several thin layers, thermal socks, gloves and a hat trap more heat than one thick jumper
  • Move every hour: during TV adverts or every hour, stand up, march on the spot, or walk to the kitchen and back. A few minutes is enough to warm muscles and ease stiffness
  • Warm up stiff joints first: a warm shower, a wheat bag or a hot water bottle wrapped in a cover can ease morning stiffness. Do not sleep on a hot water bottle or electric blanket, and take care if your skin is thin or has poor feeling
  • Eat and drink warm: regular meals and hot drinks help keep your body warm and your energy up

A five-minute warm-up you can do at home

Do this once or twice a day, holding a sturdy chair or worktop for balance:

  1. March on the spot for one minute
  2. Sit to stand from a firm chair, five to ten times, using your hands if you need to
  3. Circle your shoulders and gently open and close your hands
  4. Rise up on your toes and back down, ten times
  5. Slowly bend and straighten each knee while sitting

Stay within comfort and scale back rather than stop on bad days. Our exercise hub and staying active in winter guide have more routines, and the knee and hip exercise guides help if those joints are the problem.

Make moving around the house safer

  • Keep paths clear and rooms well lit, with a night light on the way to the toilet
  • Wear well-fitting slippers with a back and a grippy sole
  • Raise a low chair or bed if getting up is a struggle; an occupational therapist can advise on equipment
  • Our falls prevention guide and joint protection guide have more ideas

Help with heating costs

Check GOV.UK for the Winter Fuel Payment, Cold Weather Payment and Warm Home Discount. Rules differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, so check the version for where you live. If you are struggling to pay, contact your energy supplier early to ask about payment plans and support.

Extra income can make heating affordable. If arthritis affects daily living, see our Benefits and PIP hub, and if you are over State Pension age, our Attendance Allowance guide. Carers may be able to get Carer's Allowance.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if someone is very cold and confused, drowsy, or has slurred speech or slow breathing. These can be signs of hypothermia
  • Get urgent advice if a joint becomes hot, red and swollen, especially with fever
  • See your GP if getting up from a chair or walking indoors is getting harder, or you have fallen. A physiotherapy or frailty review can help

Frequently asked questions

Is it better to rest stiff joints in the cold?

Short rests are fine, but long spells of sitting usually make stiffness worse. Little and often movement is the aim.

Can a carer help without taking over?

Yes. Set up the room, stay nearby for the risky part of a task and leave the parts the person can still do. A carer's assessment can help with support.

See also our cold weather and arthritis guide, vitamin D in winter and pain relief guide.

  • GOV.UK: Warm Home Discount Scheme
  • NHS: Hypothermia

Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.

article.title: Working with Arthritis – Your UK Employment Rights
article.excerpt: Know your employment rights when working with arthritis in the UK. Guide to reasonable adjustments, Equality Act protection, Access to Work scheme.
article.content:
Arthritis is recognised as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it has a substantial and long-term effect on your ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. This means you have legal protections at work.

Quick answer: If your arthritis significantly affects daily activities, it's considered a disability under the Equality Act 2010. This protects you from discrimination and harassment at work. Your employer must make reasonable adjustments, such as flexible hours or ergonomic equipment. The Access to Work scheme can also fund equipment and support. You are entitled to Statutory Sick Pay if you need time off.

Your Rights Under the Equality Act 2010

  • Protection from discrimination — your employer cannot treat you less favourably because of arthritis
  • Right to reasonable adjustments — your employer must make changes to remove disadvantages you face
  • Protection from harassment — colleagues cannot bully or mock you because of your condition
  • Protection from victimisation — you cannot be penalised for raising concerns about discrimination

Reasonable Adjustments

Your employer is legally required to make "reasonable adjustments" to help you do your job. Examples include:

  • Flexible working hours — starting later to manage morning stiffness
  • Ergonomic equipment — adjustable desk, ergonomic keyboard, supportive chair
  • Modified duties — avoiding heavy lifting or prolonged standing
  • Working from home — on flare days or regularly
  • Extra breaks — to stretch, move, or manage medication
  • Accessible parking — closer to the workplace entrance
  • Phased return — after illness or surgery

Access to Work Scheme

The government's Access to Work scheme can provide:

  • Funding for specialist equipment or workplace adaptations
  • Support worker costs
  • Help with travel costs if you can't use public transport
  • Mental health support

Apply at gov.uk/access-to-work. The scheme is available to employed and self-employed people.

Talking to Your Employer

  • You don't have to disclose your condition at interview, but it helps to tell your employer once employed so they can make adjustments
  • Ask for an occupational health referral — many employers provide this
  • Put requests for adjustments in writing
  • Keep records of any meetings about your condition

Sick Leave and SSP

If you need time off due to arthritis:

  • You're entitled to Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) — currently £109.40 per week for up to 28 weeks
  • Many employers offer enhanced sick pay beyond SSP
  • If you cannot return to work, you may qualify for Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)

Getting Help

  • ACAS — free workplace advice on 0300 123 1100
  • Citizens Advice — help with employment disputes
  • Disability Rights UK — factsheets on employment and arthritis

Knowing your rights empowers you to have productive conversations with your employer. Most employers want to support you — they just need to understand what you need.

article.title: Workplace Adjustment Letter Templates for Arthritis: Copy-and-Edit Letters and Plans (UK)
article.excerpt: Real, on-page templates you can copy and edit: a reasonable adjustments request, a statutory flexible working request with everything GOV.UK says it must include, a follow-up letter, an occupational health referral request, a request for reasons after a refusal, a phased return plan, a flare plan and an adjustments record.
article.content:
Quick answer: To ask for workplace adjustments for arthritis, write a short letter or email saying you have arthritis, explaining how it affects specific tasks, listing the changes you are asking for and how they would help, and asking for a meeting and a written reply. Keep a copy. For a change to hours, times, days or place of work, you can also make a statutory flexible working request.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Reasonable adjustments and GOV.UK: Flexible working. These templates are general information, not legal advice. Edit them to fit your situation.

Asking for help at work can feel awkward, especially if you are worried about how your manager will react. A clear, polite letter takes the pressure off a face-to-face conversation, makes it easier for your employer to act, and gives you a record. This page contains real templates you can copy into an email or document and edit. Replace everything in [square brackets].

Before you write: three things to know

  • Your employer has a legal duty. GOV.UK says employers must make reasonable adjustments so that workers with disabilities or health conditions are not substantially disadvantaged when doing their jobs. In England, Scotland and Wales this comes from the Equality Act 2010; in Northern Ireland, from the Disability Discrimination Act 1995. GOV.UK even gives the example of a special keyboard for someone with arthritis.
  • You may count as disabled if your arthritis has a substantial and long-term effect on your normal daily activities. Long-term usually means 12 months or more. You do not have to use the word "disabled" in your letter, but it can help to say you are asking for reasonable adjustments.
  • Be specific. "My hands are painful" is easy to overlook. "Typing for more than 20 minutes causes severe wrist pain, so I am asking for voice recognition software" is easy to act on.

If you have not yet worked out which tasks are hardest, start with Step 2 of our working with arthritis toolkit.

Template 1: Request for reasonable adjustments

Subject: Request for reasonable adjustments

Dear [manager's name],

I am writing to ask for some reasonable adjustments at work. I have [type of arthritis, for example rheumatoid arthritis / osteoarthritis of the knees], which I have had since [year]. It affects me in the following ways at work:

  • [for example: morning stiffness that lasts about [time], which makes early starts very difficult]
  • [for example: pain in my hands and wrists when typing for long periods]
  • [for example: pain when standing for more than [time]]

I would like to ask for the following adjustments:

  1. [adjustment, for example a start time of 10am on up to [number] days a week] – this would help because [reason].
  2. [adjustment, for example an ergonomic keyboard and vertical mouse] – this would help because [reason].
  3. [adjustment, for example a perching stool at my workstation] – this would help because [reason].

[Optional: My [GP / physiotherapist / occupational therapist / rheumatology team] has suggested [advice]. I am happy to be referred to occupational health if that would help.]

I would welcome a meeting to discuss this. Could you please let me know in writing by [date, for example two weeks from now] whether these adjustments can be made, or suggest alternatives? I would also like to agree a date to review how they are working.

Thank you for your support.

Yours sincerely,
[your name]
[job title, team]
[date]

Template 2: Statutory flexible working request

GOV.UK says all employees can make a flexible working request from their first day in a job, and can make 2 applications in any 12-month period. It says the request must include the date, a statement that it is a statutory request, details of how you want to work flexibly and when you want to start, and whether and when you have made a previous application. This template includes all of those. Your employer may have its own form; Acas also has a free template.

Subject: Statutory request for flexible working

Dear [manager's name],

Date of request: [date]

This is a statutory request for flexible working.

I would like to change my working pattern as follows: [describe the change, for example: to work from home on Mondays and Fridays / to start at 10am and finish at 6pm / to reduce my hours from 37.5 to 30 a week over four days].

I would like this change to start on [date].

[Choose one:] I have not made a previous application for flexible working. / I made a previous application on [date].

[Optional but helpful:] I am asking for this change because I have arthritis, and [explain briefly how the change would help, for example: travelling at peak times when my joints are stiffest causes significant pain]. I would also like this to be considered as a reasonable adjustment. I have thought about how this could work for the team: [for example, how cover, meetings or customer contact would be handled].

I look forward to discussing this with you.

Yours sincerely,
[your name]

GOV.UK says your employer must deal with the request in a reasonable manner, discuss it with you before refusing, and make a decision within 2 months unless you agree to longer. If they refuse, they must give the business reasons.

Template 3: Follow-up if you have not heard back

Subject: Follow-up: request for reasonable adjustments sent on [date]

Dear [name],

On [date] I asked for reasonable adjustments because of my arthritis (copy attached). I have not yet had a response. My symptoms are continuing to affect my work, particularly [example].

Could you please let me know by [date] when we can meet to discuss this, or who else I should contact?

Thank you,
[your name]

Template 4: Request for an occupational health referral

Subject: Request for occupational health referral

Dear [name],

I would like to ask for a referral to occupational health. I have [type of arthritis], and I would find it helpful to have independent advice on adjustments that could help me do my job well, particularly with [tasks].

Please let me know what information you need from me.

Kind regards,
[your name]

Template 5: Asking for reasons after a refusal

Subject: Response to my adjustment request

Dear [name],

Thank you for your reply dated [date] about my request for [adjustment]. I understand that you are not able to agree to this. So that I can understand the decision, please could you explain in writing:

  • the reasons the adjustment is not considered reasonable
  • whether any alternatives have been considered
  • whether Access to Work or occupational health advice has been sought

I would like to suggest the following alternative: [alternative]. I would be grateful for a meeting to discuss this further.

Yours sincerely,
[your name]

If you still think the refusal is unfair, get advice. GOV.UK says that you usually have to make an employment tribunal claim within 6 months of the problem, and you must contact Acas first. Northern Ireland has a different process.

Template 6: Phased return to work plan

A fit note can say you may be fit for work with a phased return. Use this table with your manager to agree the details.

WeekHours and daysDutiesAdjustments in placeCheck-in
1[e.g. 3 half days][e.g. desk-based tasks only][e.g. later start][date]
2
3
4

Agree in advance what happens if a week is too much: for example, staying at the same level for another week rather than stopping.

Template 7: Flare plan

My arthritis flare plan (agreed with [manager] on [date], review on [date])

  • Early signs of a flare for me: [e.g. more swelling in my hands, extreme tiredness]
  • How I will let you know: [e.g. text or phone call to [name] before [time]]
  • What I can usually still do: [e.g. work from home, shorter hours, lighter tasks]
  • Tasks that can be paused or covered: [list]
  • Who covers urgent work: [name]
  • How we will plan my return to full duties: [e.g. a short call after the flare]
  • How flare absence will be recorded: [e.g. as disability-related absence]

Template 8: Adjustments record

Some employers call this a reasonable adjustments passport. It saves you explaining everything again if you get a new manager.

AdjustmentWhy it helpsDate agreedWho arranges itReview date
[e.g. sit-stand desk][e.g. reduces back and hip pain]
[e.g. time off for rheumatology appointments]

Template 9: Time off for medical appointments

Arthritis often means regular appointments: rheumatology reviews, blood tests, physiotherapy or infusions. Agreeing an approach in advance avoids arguments each time.

Subject: Time off for arthritis appointments

Dear [name],

As part of the treatment for my arthritis, I need regular medical appointments. Over the next [period], I expect to need about [number] appointments, for example [blood tests every [number] weeks, a rheumatology review every [number] months]. Most last around [time], including travel.

I would like to agree how this time off will be handled, for example [paid time off / making up the time / using flexible start and finish times], and I am asking for this as a reasonable adjustment. Where I can, I will book appointments at the start or end of the day and give you as much notice as possible.

Kind regards,
[your name]

A short script for the conversation

If you are meeting your manager, it can help to have a few sentences ready:

  1. "I wanted to talk to you about my arthritis and how it affects my work."
  2. "On most days I manage well, but [task] is difficult because [effect], and on bad days [effect]."
  3. "These are the changes I think would make the biggest difference: [one, two, three]."
  4. "I am happy to see occupational health, and Access to Work may be able to help with some costs."
  5. "Could we agree what happens next, and a date to review it?"

Afterwards, send a short email summarising what was agreed.

Tips for getting a good outcome

  • Send it to the right person, usually your line manager, copying HR if that is your workplace's process.
  • Keep copies of everything, and note dates of conversations.
  • Offer solutions. Managers find it easier to say yes when you have thought about how it would work.
  • Mention Access to Work for equipment or support beyond what your employer must provide. See our Access to Work guide.
  • Ask for a review date so adjustments can change if your arthritis does.
  • Use your fit note. If you are off sick, ask the person writing your fit note to suggest changes. See our fit notes guide.

Free, independent advice

Acas gives free advice on workplace rights in England, Scotland and Wales, and the Equality Advisory and Support Service can help with discrimination questions. In Northern Ireland, contact the Labour Relations Agency or the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland. Citizens Advice, Scope, Disability Rights UK and trade unions can also help. We are not connected to these organisations. For more on the law itself, see your disability rights in the UK.

When to get medical help

If work is making your arthritis worse, speak to your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team. They can review your treatment and may suggest changes on a fit note. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with fever. If stress at work is affecting your mental health, talk to your GP.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to put my request for adjustments in writing?

No, you can ask in conversation. But writing it down makes it clearer, gives your employer something to act on, and gives you a record.

Do I need a letter from my doctor?

Not usually, but supporting advice from your GP, physiotherapist, occupational therapist or occupational health can help your employer understand what you need.

What is the difference between a flexible working request and a reasonable adjustment?

Any employee can make a statutory flexible working request. A reasonable adjustment is a legal duty that applies when you are disabled and the change would reduce a disadvantage caused by your condition. You can ask for a change in both ways at once.

How many flexible working requests can I make?

GOV.UK says employees can make 2 applications in any 12-month period.

How long does my employer have to reply?

For a statutory flexible working request, GOV.UK says the decision must be made within 2 months unless you agree to longer. There is no fixed deadline for adjustment requests, so ask for a reply by a specific date.

What if my employer refuses?

Ask for the reasons in writing, suggest alternatives, and get free advice from Acas or the Labour Relations Agency in Northern Ireland.

article.title: Wound care when reaching is hard with arthritis and frailty (UK)
article.excerpt: Looking after cuts and wounds when arthritis makes reaching hard: basic care, getting help from community nurses, and signs of infection to report.
article.content:
Slow-healing wounds can be a problem with frailty.

This guide covers wound care. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Minor cuts

Clean, dry and cover.

Getting help

  • Pharmacist.
  • Practice nurse.
  • Community nurse if housebound.

Signs of infection

  • Redness spreading.
  • Heat, swelling or pus.
  • Fever.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for heavy bleeding that will not stop.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Who dresses wounds at home?

District nurses can if you are housebound.

When should I worry?

If signs of infection appear.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Cuts and grazes

article.title: Wrist osteoarthritis and frailty: choosing a walking aid that does not hurt (UK)
article.excerpt: How to choose a walking aid when wrist arthritis makes gripping a stick or frame painful, including handle types, forearm supports and getting assessed.
article.content:
Walking aids can help you stay steady, but they put weight through your hands and wrists. With wrist osteoarthritis, this can be painful.

This guide explains options to discuss with a professional. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why wrists hurt with walking aids

  • Weight goes through the wrist at an angle.
  • Gripping a thin handle needs strong grip.
  • An aid at the wrong height increases strain.

Options that may help

  • Shaped or padded handles that spread pressure.
  • Forearm support frames or gutter frames that take weight through the forearm.
  • Wheeled walkers that need less lifting.
  • Making sure the height is correct.

Getting assessed

A physiotherapist or occupational therapist can assess which aid suits you and check the height. Ask your GP for a referral. Many aids are loaned free through community equipment services.

Caring for your wrists

Splints may help some people. Pain relief and hand exercises can be discussed with your GP or physiotherapist.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I stop using my stick if my wrist hurts?

Not without advice. Ask for an assessment for a different aid.

Can I buy my own walking aid?

You can, but an assessment helps ensure it is right for you.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Osteoarthritis
  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
  • NHS: Care services, equipment and care homes
  • NHS: Falls

article.title: X-Rays for Arthritis Explained: What They Show, Radiation and Your Report
article.excerpt: A plain-English UK guide to joint X-rays: what they show in osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis, when NICE recommends them, radiation in context, the day itself and how to read your report.
article.content:
Quick answer: An X-ray uses a small dose of radiation to show bone. In arthritis it can show joint space narrowing, bony spurs and erosions, but not cartilage, early inflammation or how much pain you have. NICE says osteoarthritis is usually diagnosed without imaging, but recommends hand and foot X-rays for suspected rheumatoid arthritis. A limb joint X-ray equals less than 1.5 days of natural background radiation.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against the NHS guide to X-rays, UK Health Security Agency patient dose information and NICE guidelines on osteoarthritis (NG226), rheumatoid arthritis (NG100) and spondyloarthritis (NG65).

X-rays are the oldest and most widely used scan for joints. They are quick, cheap and good at showing bone. But they have limits, and an X-ray result does not always match how a joint feels. This guide explains when X-rays are used for arthritis, what they can and cannot show, what happens on the day, how much radiation is involved and how to understand your report.

What is an X-ray?

The NHS describes an X-ray as a test that takes pictures of the inside of your body using a small amount of radiation. Dense tissues such as bone absorb more X-rays and show up white, while soft tissues appear in shades of grey. This makes X-rays good for looking at bones and the space between them, but poor at showing cartilage, ligaments, tendons or early inflammation.

What an X-ray can show in arthritis

  • Joint space narrowing. Cartilage does not show on X-ray, but the gap between bones indicates how much is left. A narrowed space suggests cartilage loss.
  • Osteophytes. Bony spurs at the edges of a joint, typical of osteoarthritis.
  • Subchondral sclerosis and cysts. Hardening and small cavities in the bone under the cartilage, also seen in osteoarthritis.
  • Erosions. Small areas where bone has been worn away at the joint edges, seen in inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, and in long-standing gout.
  • Bone thinning near joints, sometimes seen in inflammatory arthritis.
  • Changes in the sacroiliac joints and spine in established axial spondyloarthritis.
  • Calcium deposits in cartilage, which may suggest calcium pyrophosphate deposition (sometimes called pseudogout).
  • Alignment and deformity, and the position of a joint replacement.
  • Fractures and other bone problems that might explain pain.

What an X-ray cannot show

  • Cartilage, ligaments, tendons and the meniscus directly
  • Early inflammation in the joint lining
  • Early rheumatoid arthritis, before damage has happened
  • Early axial spondyloarthritis, which may only show on MRI
  • How much pain you are in

That last point matters. X-ray changes and symptoms often do not match well. Some people have marked changes on X-ray and little pain, while others have significant pain with mild changes. This is one reason NICE advises clinicians to use clinical assessment, rather than systems that numerically score severity, when deciding whether to refer someone for joint replacement.

When are X-rays used for arthritis?

Osteoarthritis

NICE says osteoarthritis can be diagnosed clinically without imaging in people who are 45 or over, have activity-related joint pain and have no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting 30 minutes or less. It advises against routine imaging unless there are atypical features, such as recent injury, prolonged morning stiffness, rapid worsening, deformity, a hot swollen joint, or concerns about infection or cancer. NICE also advises against routine X-rays for follow-up or to guide non-surgical treatment.

An X-ray may still be done if you are being considered for surgery, if the diagnosis is uncertain, or if something does not fit the usual pattern.

Rheumatoid arthritis

NICE recommends X-rays of the hands and feet for adults with suspected rheumatoid arthritis and persistent synovitis. When someone is newly diagnosed, NICE says X-rays of the hands and feet should be done to look for erosions, if not already done. Erosions at the start help predict how the disease might progress and can influence how intensively it is treated. Some teams repeat X-rays over time to check for new damage.

Axial spondyloarthritis

NICE's guideline describes using an X-ray of the sacroiliac joints as part of assessment, and requesting an MRI if the X-ray does not show clear changes.

Gout and other crystal arthritis

X-rays are not usually needed to diagnose gout, but they can show damage in long-standing gout or calcium deposits in other crystal conditions.

Back pain

NICE advises against routine imaging for low back pain in non-specialist settings.

How much radiation is involved?

The UK Health Security Agency publishes typical radiation doses from medical scans, compared with natural background radiation that we are all exposed to in everyday life:

X-ray ofEquivalent natural background radiationEstimated lifetime additional risk of fatal cancer
Limbs and joints (except hip)Less than 1.5 days1 in a few million
Chest3 days1 in a million
Hip7 weeks1 in 67,000
Pelvis4 months1 in 30,000
Lumbar spine (lower back)7 months1 in 15,000

Source: UKHSA patient dose information, updated 28 September 2026. X-rays of hands, feet, knees and other limb joints involve very low doses. The NHS says that if you have lots of X-rays there is a very small risk that radiation could cause cancer, and your doctor will weigh this up before offering one. This is another reason clinicians avoid X-rays that will not change your treatment.

Always tell the radiographer if you are or might be pregnant.

Preparing for an X-ray

Joint X-rays need very little preparation. The NHS says you may be asked not to wear anything with metal in it, such as jewellery, zips, poppers, underwired bras or hair clips. Tell the radiographer if you are pregnant or might be, are breastfeeding, take any medicines or have allergies.

Wear clothes that make it easy to uncover the joint, for example shorts or loose trousers for a knee X-ray. You may be asked to change into a gown.

If you would like a chaperone, someone you know or a trained member of staff, you can ask for one.

What happens during the X-ray

X-rays are usually done in a hospital or community diagnostic centre by a radiographer. The NHS says the X-ray itself only takes a few minutes:

  • The machine is lined up with the part of your body being X-rayed.
  • The radiographer moves behind a screen or leaves the room.
  • You keep very still for a few seconds while one or more images are taken. You will not feel anything.
  • You may be asked to move into different positions.

For knee and hip arthritis, X-rays are often taken while you stand, because this shows the joint space under load. If standing or holding a position is difficult, tell the radiographer. They can help you get into position and give you support.

In many places you can walk in for GP-requested X-rays without an appointment. Check the instructions on your request form.

Getting your results

The NHS says you should be told when you will get the results. This may be on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later. A radiologist or reporting radiographer writes a report that goes to the clinician who requested it. If you have not heard anything after a few weeks, contact the clinician who referred you or your GP.

Common terms in X-ray reports

TermWhat it usually means
Degenerative changeWear-related changes consistent with osteoarthritis, very common with age
Loss of joint space / joint space narrowingThinning of cartilage
OsteophytesBony spurs
Subchondral sclerosisHardening of the bone under the cartilage
ErosionsBone loss at joint margins, a sign of inflammatory arthritis
Periarticular osteopeniaThinning of bone around a joint
ChondrocalcinosisCalcium deposits in cartilage
EffusionExtra fluid in or around a joint
No acute bony injuryNo fracture seen

Words like "mild", "moderate" and "severe" describe what the bones look like, not how much pain or disability you have. Discuss your report with your clinician before drawing conclusions.

X-ray, ultrasound or MRI?

  • X-ray: best for bone, joint space, spurs and erosions. Quick, widely available, small dose of radiation.
  • Ultrasound: shows inflammation in joints and tendons in real time, with no radiation. Often done in rheumatology clinics.
  • MRI: shows soft tissues, early inflammation and the spine and sacroiliac joints in detail, with no radiation. Takes longer and is less widely available. See MRI scans explained.
  • DEXA scan: a different, low-dose X-ray that measures bone density to check for osteoporosis, which can be more common with some types of arthritis and long-term steroid use.

For an overview of the whole diagnostic process, see how arthritis is diagnosed.

If you were told you do not need an X-ray

It can feel frustrating to be told you do not need a scan. But for typical osteoarthritis, NICE is clear that diagnosis and treatment, including exercise, weight management and pain relief, do not depend on imaging. An X-ray would expose you to radiation without changing what you are advised to do. If your symptoms change, or new features appear such as a hot swollen joint, rapid worsening or a joint that looks deformed, ask your GP to reassess. Our list of questions to ask your consultant includes questions about tests.

Do I need repeat X-rays?

Not routinely. For osteoarthritis, NICE advises against using imaging for follow-up or to guide non-surgical treatment, because the plan (exercise, weight management, pain relief and support) does not depend on how the X-ray looks. Repeat X-rays may be done if symptoms change significantly, before surgery, or if a different problem is suspected.

In inflammatory arthritis, some rheumatology teams repeat hand and foot X-rays at intervals to check whether new erosions are developing, which can help show whether treatment is controlling the disease. Ask your team whether and when you will have them.

X-rays after a joint replacement

If you have had a hip, knee or shoulder replacement, X-rays are usually taken after the operation to check the position of the new joint, and sometimes at follow-up appointments. Later in life, an X-ray may be used if a replaced joint becomes painful, to look for loosening or wear. If you develop new pain, swelling, clicking or instability in a replaced joint, contact your GP or the surgical team rather than waiting for a routine review. Our checklist on preparing for joint replacement covers what to expect before surgery.

Practical tips for the day

  • Take your request form or appointment letter, and check whether you need to book or can walk in.
  • Take your usual pain relief beforehand if standing or positioning is likely to be uncomfortable.
  • Bring a list of previous X-rays or scans of the same joint, including where they were done, so they can be compared.
  • If you use a walking aid, bring it.
  • Ask when and how you will get the result before you leave.

When to get medical help

  • Same day (urgent GP appointment or NHS 111): a hot, swollen, very painful joint, especially with fever or feeling unwell; or sudden severe joint pain that started without injury.
  • A&E or urgent treatment centre: after a fall or injury if you cannot bear weight, the joint looks deformed, or you think you may have broken a bone.
  • Call 999 or go to A&E: back pain with numbness around the bottom or genitals or new problems controlling your bladder or bowels.
  • Routine GP appointment: if your arthritis is gradually getting worse or affecting new joints.

Frequently asked questions

Will an X-ray show arthritis?

It can show changes from osteoarthritis and from established inflammatory arthritis, such as narrowed joint spaces, bony spurs and erosions. It may look normal in early arthritis, because cartilage and inflammation do not show on X-ray.

Why does my X-ray look mild when my pain is severe?

X-ray appearance and pain often do not match. Pain is influenced by inflammation, muscles, nerves, sleep, mood and other factors that an X-ray cannot show.

Are X-rays safe?

Joint X-rays use very low doses of radiation. UKHSA estimates the dose from an X-ray of a limb joint is equivalent to less than 1.5 days of natural background radiation.

How long do X-ray results take?

The NHS says you may get results on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later. Contact the clinician who referred you if you have not heard after a few weeks.

Do I need an X-ray before a joint replacement?

Usually yes. Surgeons use X-rays to plan the operation, although NICE says the decision to refer for joint replacement should be based on clinical assessment, not on X-ray scores alone.

Can I have an X-ray if I am pregnant?

Tell the radiographer if you are or might be pregnant. They will consider whether the X-ray is needed now and how to minimise any risk.

Can an X-ray tell if I need a knee or hip replacement?

Not on its own. NICE says referral for joint replacement depends on how much your symptoms affect your quality of life and whether non-surgical treatment has worked, judged by clinical assessment rather than an X-ray score.

article.content:
Best yoga poses for ankylosing spondylitis stiffness — AS causes progressive spinal stiffness and can severely limit mobility over time. Yoga, when correctly adapted, is one of the best tools available for maintaining spinal mobility, reducing stiffness and managing pain in AS.

Quick answer: Best yoga poses for AS stiffness: cat-cow for spinal mobility, sphinx pose for gentle extension, supine spinal twist for rotation, child's pose for thoracic stretch, standing chest opener for rib cage. Avoid deep forward folds. Practice 1-2 hours after morning medication when stiffness has eased.

Yoga poses for spinal flexibility — openly licensed via Openverse

Why Yoga Specifically Helps AS

NICE guidelines recommend regular exercise, particularly exercises that promote spinal extension and rotation, as a cornerstone of AS management. Yoga provides systematic movement through the spine, hips and chest — exactly the areas where AS causes stiffness. A 2019 RCT found 12 weeks of yoga practice significantly improved spinal mobility, pain scores and quality of life in AS patients compared to a control group.

Recommended Poses for AS

Cat-Cow (Marjaryasana-Bitilasana)

On hands and knees. Inhale: arch back downward, lift head and tailbone (cow). Exhale: round spine upward, tuck chin and pelvis (cat). 10 slow repetitions. Gently mobilises the entire spine in flexion and extension.

Sphinx Pose (Salamba Bhujangasana)

Lie face down, forearms on the floor, elbows under shoulders. Press forearms gently to lift chest slightly. Hold 30–60 seconds. Gentle spinal extension that counteracts the forward-bending tendency of AS.

Supine Spinal Twist

Lie on back. Draw one knee to chest, then guide it across to the opposite side while extending that arm wide. Hold 30 seconds each side. Gentle thoracic and lumbar rotation.

Spinal mobility exercises — openly licensed via Openverse

Child's Pose (Balasana) — Modified

From kneeling, slowly lower hips toward heels and stretch arms forward. If hips do not reach heels, place a folded blanket between thighs and calves. Gently stretches thoracic spine and hips.

Standing Chest Opener

Stand in doorway, arms at 90 degrees on the frame. Lean forward gently until chest stretch is felt. Hold 20–30 seconds. Opens the anterior chest and rib cage — important in AS where chest expansion can be restricted.

AS-Specific Adaptations

  • Always warm up for 10 minutes before starting
  • Avoid deep forward folds — these can load already-fused or vulnerable spinal segments
  • Use props freely: blocks, bolsters, straps — they make poses accessible, not easier
  • Practice in the morning after medication has taken effect (typically 1–2 hours after taking NSAIDs)
  • Tell your yoga teacher about your AS before class — a good teacher will modify accordingly

Gentle movement therapy — openly licensed via Openverse

Q&A

Question: Is yoga safe during an AS flare?
Short answer: Very gentle movement (cat-cow, supine twist) is generally safe during mild flares. Avoid new poses or increased intensity during severe flares. Resume gradually as the flare settles.

Question: Should I see a physiotherapist before starting yoga for AS?
Short answer: Ideally yes — a physiotherapist specialising in inflammatory arthritis can assess your spinal mobility and advise on safe ranges before you begin a yoga programme.

Practical next steps for Best Yoga Poses for Ankylosing Spondylitis Stiffness

If you came here about Best Yoga Poses for Ankylosing Spondylitis Stiffness, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Quick questions about Best Yoga Poses Ankylosing

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

article.title: Yoga for Arthritis Beginners: A Safe and Gentle Starting Guide
article.excerpt: Start yoga safely with arthritis. Beginner-friendly poses, modifications for joint pain, and how to find arthritis-friendly yoga classes in the UK.
article.content:
Yoga has emerged as one of the most recommended complementary therapies for arthritis, endorsed by the NHS, NICE, Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) and the Arthritis Foundation globally. Yet many people with joint pain hesitate to try yoga, fearing it requires extreme flexibility or will worsen their symptoms. The truth is that yoga — when practised with appropriate modifications — is one of the safest and most beneficial forms of exercise for arthritis. This guide is designed specifically for beginners with arthritis, covering everything from choosing the right style to step-by-step poses you can start today.

Quick answer: Yoga is beneficial for arthritis as it combines gentle movement, stretching, strengthening, and mindfulness, helping manage various aspects of the condition. Recommended styles for beginners include Hatha, Iyengar, Restorative, and Chair yoga, which are adaptable and use props to support precise alignment and reduce joint strain. Always listen to your body and modify poses to avoid pain.

Why Yoga Works for Arthritis

Yoga combines gentle movement, stretching, strengthening and mindfulness — addressing multiple aspects of arthritis management simultaneously. Research supports its effectiveness:

  • A Johns Hopkins University randomised controlled trial found that people with rheumatoid and knee osteoarthritis who practised yoga twice weekly for 8 weeks showed significant improvements in pain, physical function and mental health compared to a control group
  • A systematic review in Rheumatology International concluded that yoga improves joint flexibility, muscle strength and overall well-being in arthritis patients
  • Yoga has been shown to reduce inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6) in multiple studies, suggesting benefits beyond simply improving flexibility
  • The mindfulness component of yoga helps with pain management, sleep quality and psychological well-being

Choosing the Right Yoga Style

Best Styles for Arthritis

  • Hatha yoga — The most accessible style. Slow-paced, holds poses for several breaths, allows time for modifications. Ideal for beginners
  • Iyengar yoga — Emphasises precise alignment and uses props (blocks, straps, bolsters, chairs) extensively. Particularly suited to people with physical limitations
  • Restorative yoga — Uses props to support the body in passive poses held for 5–10 minutes. Deeply relaxing and gentle on joints
  • Chair yoga — All poses performed seated or using a chair for support. Perfect for people with significant mobility limitations
  • Yin yoga — Slow, passive stretches held for 3–5 minutes targeting connective tissues. Good for flexibility but may need modification for inflamed joints

Styles to Approach with Caution

  • Vinyasa/Flow — Fast-paced transitions between poses may be too challenging initially
  • Bikram/Hot yoga — The 40°C room temperature may seem appealing for stiff joints but can cause overheating, dizziness and may mask pain signals, leading to overexertion
  • Ashtanga — Physically demanding and follows a set sequence that may not accommodate individual limitations

Beginner Poses for Arthritis

These poses are safe for most people with arthritis. Always listen to your body and skip any pose that causes sharp pain.

1. Mountain Pose (Tadasana)

The foundation of all standing poses. Stand with feet hip-width apart, weight evenly distributed. Lengthen your spine, roll shoulders back and down, arms relaxed at your sides. Breathe deeply for 30–60 seconds. This improves posture, body awareness and balance. Modification: hold the back of a chair for balance support.

2. Cat-Cow Stretch (Marjaryasana-Bitilasana)

Begin on hands and knees (use a folded blanket under knees for cushioning). As you inhale, drop your belly towards the floor, lift your chest and gaze forward (Cow). As you exhale, round your spine towards the ceiling, tucking chin to chest (Cat). Move slowly between the two positions 8–10 times. This gently mobilises the entire spine and is excellent for back stiffness. Modification: perform seated on a chair, placing hands on thighs.

3. Seated Forward Fold (Paschimottanasana)

Sit on the floor with legs extended (sit on a folded blanket if hamstrings are tight). Inhale and lengthen your spine. Exhale and hinge forward from the hips, reaching towards your feet. Only go as far as comfortable — use a yoga strap around your feet if you can't reach. Hold for 30 seconds. This stretches hamstrings, calves and the lower back.

4. Warrior II (Virabhadrasana II)

Stand with feet wide apart (about 3–4 feet). Turn your right foot out 90 degrees and left foot slightly in. Bend your right knee over your ankle (don't let it go past your toes). Extend arms out to the sides at shoulder height. Look over your right hand. Hold for 15–30 seconds, then switch sides. Strengthens legs, opens hips and improves balance. Modification: reduce the depth of the knee bend or practise against a wall for support.

5. Bridge Pose (Setu Bandhasana)

Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Press through your feet and lift your hips towards the ceiling. Hold for 15–30 seconds. Lower slowly. Repeat 3 times. Strengthens glutes, hamstrings and lower back. Good for hip and knee arthritis. Modification: place a yoga block under your sacrum for a supported bridge.

6. Child's Pose (Balasana)

Kneel on the floor, sit back on your heels, then fold forward with arms extended in front. Rest your forehead on the floor (or a pillow). Hold for 30–60 seconds. A resting pose that gently stretches hips, thighs and back. Modification: place a bolster or pillows under your torso for support, or keep your knees wider apart.

Essential Tips for Practising Yoga with Arthritis

  • Use props freely — Blocks, straps, bolsters, blankets and chairs are not signs of weakness — they're tools for safe, effective practice
  • Warm up first — Start with gentle movements (Cat-Cow, wrist circles, ankle rolls) before attempting deeper poses
  • Modify without guilt — Every pose has modifications. A smaller range of motion done safely is always better than pushing into pain
  • Breathe — Focus on slow, deep breathing throughout. Never hold your breath during a pose
  • Respect your limits today — Your range and tolerance will vary day to day. What felt fine yesterday might not work today, and that's completely normal
  • Avoid hyperextension — Don't lock out your knees or elbows. Keep a micro-bend in joints
  • Skip inversions initially — Poses like headstand or shoulder stand put significant pressure on joints and should only be attempted with expert guidance

Finding Arthritis-Friendly Yoga in the UK

  • NHS Exercise on Prescription — Some areas offer yoga as part of exercise referral schemes
  • Arthritis UK — Provides information about arthritis-friendly exercise classes across the UK
  • British Wheel of Yoga (bwy.org.uk) — The governing body for yoga in England. Search for qualified teachers near you
  • Yoga for Arthritis (arthritis.yoga) — An evidence-based programme developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins
  • YouTube — Free classes from channels like 'Yoga with Adriene' (search 'yoga for arthritis' or 'gentle yoga') provide accessible home practice
  • Local leisure centres and community halls — Many offer gentle or chair yoga classes at affordable rates

Building a Sustainable Practice

Start with just 10–15 minutes, 2–3 times per week. As your confidence and comfort grow, gradually extend to 20–30 minute sessions. Many arthritis patients find that a daily 15-minute practice provides more consistent benefits than occasional longer sessions. Keep a simple log of how you feel before and after each session — most people notice improvements in mood and stiffness within the first two weeks, with meaningful changes in pain and function after 6–8 weeks of regular practice.

Yoga is a journey, not a destination. There is no perfect pose — there is only the pose that works for your body today. Our virtual assistant can suggest specific yoga poses for your affected joints.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP or physiotherapist before starting yoga, particularly if you have severe or unstable joint disease.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, severe breathlessness, a suspected broken bone after a fall, or back pain with new loss of bladder or bowel control or numbness around your bottom or genitals.

Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever, or if your symptoms are getting rapidly worse.

Yoga for Arthritis: Gentle, Evidence-Based Relief

Yoga combines gentle stretching, strengthening, and mindfulness — making it one of the most holistic approaches to arthritis management. NICE recognises yoga as a beneficial activity for people with chronic pain.

What the Research suggests

A 2019 systematic review of 17 studies found yoga:

  • Reduced joint pain by 22% (moderate evidence)
  • Improved physical function by 20%
  • Decreased stiffness by 18%
  • Enhanced mental wellbeing and reduced depression
  • Was safe with no serious adverse events reported

8 Gentle Yoga Poses for Arthritis

1. Mountain Pose (Tadasana)

Stand tall, feet hip-width apart. Ground through your feet, lengthen your spine. Hold 30 seconds. Benefits: Improves posture and body awareness

2. Cat-Cow Stretch

On hands and knees, alternate between arching (cow) and rounding (cat) your spine. Benefits: Mobilises the entire spine, reduces stiffness

3. Warrior II (Modified)

Wide stance, front knee bent (not past ankle), arms extended. Use a chair if needed. Benefits: Strengthens legs, opens hips

4. Seated Twist

Sit tall in a chair. Place your right hand on your left knee, gently twist left. Hold 15 seconds each side. Benefits: Spinal mobility, reduces back stiffness

5. Bridge Pose

Lie on your back, knees bent. Slowly lift hips, hold 10 seconds. Lower slowly. Benefits: Strengthens glutes and core, supports hip and knee joints

6. Child's Pose

Kneel, sit back on heels (use a cushion if needed), extend arms forward. Benefits: Gentle back stretch, calming

7. Legs Up the Wall

Lie on your back with legs resting up a wall. Relax for 3–5 minutes. Benefits: Reduces swelling in legs and feet, deeply relaxing

8. Corpse Pose (Savasana)

Lie flat, arms by sides, eyes closed. Focus on breathing for 5 minutes. Benefits: Activates parasympathetic nervous system, reduces pain perception

Yoga Tips for Arthritis

  • Use props freely — blocks, straps, blankets, and bolsters reduce strain
  • Chair yoga is excellent if getting to the floor is difficult
  • Never push through pain — modify or skip any pose that causes sharp pain
  • Warm up first — gentle joint circles before poses
  • Practice regularly — 15–20 minutes daily is better than one long session

Finding the Right Class

  • Look for "gentle yoga", "restorative yoga", or "yoga for arthritis" classes
  • Many studios and NHS physiotherapy departments offer adapted classes
  • Online options: Yoga with Adriene (free YouTube), Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) yoga videos

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on yoga for arthritis: gentle poses that help. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.

article.title: Your Arthritis Care Team: Who Does What in the NHS
article.excerpt: Living with arthritis can mean seeing lots of different professionals. This guide explains who does what in the NHS, from GPs and first contact practitioners to rheumatology nurses, physios, OTs and podiatrists, and how to reach them.
article.content:
Quick answer: Your arthritis care team may include your GP or a first contact practitioner, a rheumatologist, a rheumatology specialist nurse, a physiotherapist, an occupational therapist, a podiatrist and a pharmacist, plus others such as surgeons or psychologists when needed. Many areas let you refer yourself to physiotherapy, and rheumatology departments usually run an advice line for patients under their care.

Why a team?

Arthritis affects more than joints. It can touch sleep, mood, work, feet, hands, medicines and everyday tasks. No single professional can cover all of that, so care in the NHS is shared between people with different skills. Knowing who does what helps you get the right help sooner and avoid being passed around.

Your first point of contact

GP

Your GP is usually your first port of call. They can assess new joint problems, arrange tests, prescribe medicines, refer you to specialists and manage other health conditions. For people on DMARDs, GPs often share care with the hospital, including prescribing and arranging monitoring blood tests.

First contact practitioner (FCP)

Many GP surgeries now have first contact practitioners. These are experienced physiotherapists who can see you directly for muscle, joint and back problems instead of a GP. They can assess and diagnose, give advice and exercises, arrange some tests and referrals, and issue fit notes. Ask at reception if your practice has one.

Community pharmacist

Pharmacists can advise on over-the-counter pain relief, medicine side effects and interactions, and help you manage your medicines. You do not need an appointment. Many offer a medicines review. See our guide to a pharmacist medication review.

Specialist rheumatology care

Rheumatologist

Rheumatologists are doctors who specialise in inflammatory and autoimmune conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis, lupus, vasculitis, gout that is hard to control, and polymyalgia rheumatica. They confirm the diagnosis, plan treatment such as DMARDs and biologics, and review you regularly. Most people with osteoarthritis are managed in primary care and do not need to see a rheumatologist.

Rheumatology specialist nurse

Specialist nurses are often the people you will speak to most. They teach you about your condition and medicines, show you how to do injections, review your progress, manage flares, and often run the rheumatology advice line. Ask for the advice line number and hours at your first appointment and save it in your phone.

Other hospital specialists

  • Orthopaedic surgeons carry out joint surgery such as joint replacements. See our surgery options guide.
  • Dermatologists treat psoriasis and skin problems, often jointly with rheumatology for psoriatic arthritis.
  • Ophthalmologists treat eye inflammation linked to some conditions and run hydroxychloroquine eye screening. See our hydroxychloroquine guide.
  • Pain specialists help with complex, long-term pain.
  • Radiographers and sonographers carry out X-rays and ultrasound scans.

Therapists who help you move and manage

Physiotherapist

Physiotherapists help you stay active, reduce pain and improve strength, balance and movement through exercise, education and hands-on treatment. In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy or musculoskeletal (MSK) services. Check your local NHS website or ask at your GP surgery.

Occupational therapist (OT)

Occupational therapists help you manage everyday activities at home and work, including joint protection, pacing, splints and equipment. See our guide to joint protection. Hand therapists are OTs or physiotherapists who specialise in hand and wrist problems. You can be referred through your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team, and your council's adult social care team can also arrange an OT assessment for home equipment.

Podiatrist

Podiatrists look after feet, which are often affected by arthritis. They can advise on footwear and insoles, treat painful skin and nail problems, and help with foot pain. NHS podiatry access varies, and some areas allow self-referral, particularly for people with inflammatory arthritis or diabetes.

Support for your wellbeing

  • Psychologists and talking therapies help with anxiety, low mood and coping with long-term pain. In England you can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies. See our guide to anxiety and arthritis.
  • Dietitians can help with weight management, nutrition and gut problems.
  • Social prescribers, often based in GP practices, connect you with local groups, activities and practical support.
  • Social workers and council teams help with care needs, carers' support and home adaptations.

Getting the most from your team

  • Keep a list of who is in your team, with contact numbers.
  • Keep your own record of medicines, test results and clinic letters. The NHS App can show many results and letters.
  • Write down questions before appointments and bring someone with you if you can.
  • Tell each professional about changes in your health or medicines.
  • If you are unsure who to contact, start with your rheumatology advice line (if you are under rheumatology care) or your GP practice.

If things go wrong

If you have concerns about your care, talk to the team first. If that does not resolve things, the Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS) at your hospital can help in England, and each nation has its own NHS complaints process. For urgent problems out of hours, use NHS 111. For emergencies, call 999 or go to A&E.

Who to contact for what: a quick guide

  • New joint pain or stiffness: GP or first contact practitioner, or self-refer to physiotherapy where available.
  • A flare of inflammatory arthritis: rheumatology advice line.
  • Side effects or questions about medicines: pharmacist, rheumatology nurse or GP.
  • Blood test results and monitoring: whoever arranged the tests, often your GP practice under shared care.
  • Struggling with daily tasks at home: occupational therapist or your council's adult social care team.
  • Foot pain or footwear problems: podiatrist.
  • Low mood or anxiety: GP or NHS Talking Therapies.
  • A hot, swollen joint with fever, or feeling very unwell: NHS 111 urgently, or 999 / A&E in an emergency.

Frequently asked questions

Can I refer myself to a physiotherapist on the NHS?

In many parts of the UK, yes. Check your local NHS website or ask at your GP surgery about self-referral to physiotherapy or MSK services.

What does a rheumatology nurse do?

Rheumatology specialist nurses provide education, monitor treatment, help with flares and injections, and often run the advice line for patients.

Do I need to see a rheumatologist for osteoarthritis?

Usually not. Most osteoarthritis is managed by GPs, first contact practitioners and physiotherapists, with referral to orthopaedics if surgery is considered.

What is a first contact practitioner?

An experienced physiotherapist based in a GP practice who can assess and manage muscle and joint problems without you seeing a GP first.

Who should I call during a flare?

If you are under rheumatology care, call the rheumatology advice line. Otherwise contact your GP practice, or NHS 111 out of hours.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Physiotherapy
  • NHS: Occupational therapy
  • NHS: Foot pain
  • NHS: Find NHS Talking Therapies
  • NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults

This guide is for general education and is not a substitute for personal medical advice. Everyone's situation is different, so always follow the advice of your own GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111.

article.title: Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010
article.excerpt: Arthritis can impact work performance due to its effects on physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. Many individuals with arthritis work.
article.content:
Quick answer: Arthritis can impact work performance due to its effects on physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. Many individuals with arthritis work successfully, often with workplace adjustments. Reasonable adjustments, which are a legal entitlement, include flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, and adjusted duties. You do not have to disclose your arthritis to your employer unless it poses a health and safety risk.

Overview

Reasonable adjustments are a legal entitlement, not a favour.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis editorial team using UK NICE guidance, NHS information and peer-reviewed sources. We aim to update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Systematic reviews consistently highlight the importance of early intervention and ongoing management in arthritis care. While there's no single cure, research from numerous randomised trials shows that a combination of pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments can significantly reduce pain, improve function, and enhance quality of life for people living with various forms of arthritis.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies reinforce this, recommending a personalised approach. This includes careful diagnosis, medication tailored to the individual's condition and symptoms, and a strong emphasis on self-management strategies. Evidence also points to the benefits of regular physical activity adapted to individual capabilities, education about the condition, and psychological support where needed.

The effectiveness of 'reasonable adjustments' in the workplace, for instance, is supported by evidence demonstrating that flexible working conditions and ergonomic adaptations can reduce absenteeism, improve productivity, and help retain experienced employees living with long-term health conditions. This isn't just about compliance; it's about creating a sustainable, inclusive work environment.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Ignoring early symptoms: Hoping pain will resolve on its own can delay effective treatment. *Fix: See a doctor for persistent joint pain or swelling. Overdoing it on good days: Pushing through pain can lead to flare-ups and setbacks. *Fix: Pace yourself and listen to your body, even when you feel well. Stopping medication too soon: Feeling better often means the medication is working, not that you no longer need it. *Fix: Always discuss medication changes with your doctor. Neglecting regular movement: Fear of pain can lead to inactivity, worsening stiffness and weakness. *Fix: Engage in gentle, low-impact exercise regularly. Lacking self-advocacy: Not clearly communicating your needs or asking for help. *Fix: Prepare for appointments and be clear about how arthritis affects your daily life.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While managing arthritis often involves day-to-day self-care, certain symptoms or changes warrant prompt medical advice. Catching potential issues early can prevent further complications and ensure your treatment plan remains effective.

  • Sudden, severe joint pain or swelling that doesn't improve with rest.
  • New symptoms like fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss accompanying joint pain.
  • Rapid loss of function or mobility in a joint.
  • Side effects from medication that are concerning or severely impacting your daily life.
  • Your current treatment plan no longer seems to be managing your symptoms effectively.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can arthritis affect my ability to do my job?

Yes, arthritis can impact various aspects of your work, including physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. However, many people with arthritis work successfully, often with the help of adjustments and support.

What kind of "reasonable adjustments" can I ask for at work?

Reasonable adjustments are changes that help you do your job effectively. Examples include flexible working hours, ergonomic equipment (like a special chair or keyboard), adjusted duties, or even a change of workstation.

Do I have to tell my employer I have arthritis?

You are not legally obliged to disclose your arthritis unless it poses a health and safety risk. However, telling your employer can help them understand your needs and allow you to request reasonable adjustments.

Practical next steps for Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010

If you came here about Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
